overview.text: Serengeti is a vast savanna region in East Africa, spanning northern Tanzania into Kenya; the famous Serengeti National Park occupies its core, but the wider ecosystem extends beyond park boundaries. Its landscape includes open short-grass plains, rocky outcrops, rivers and woodlands, supporting rich wildlife and large predators. The region is especially known for the annual, roughly circular movement of wildebeest, zebras and gazelles that follow seasonal rains and fresh grazing across Tanzania and Kenya. This migration links habitats across protected areas, making the Serengeti important not just for its spectacular wildlife but also as a connected ecosystem recognized by UNESCO as a World Heritage site.

key_facts.text: The Serengeti ecosystem crosses the Tanzania–Kenya border; the national park is at its heart, not the entirety of the ecosystem.
Its recognizable landscapes include short-grass plains, rocky outcrops called kopjes, rivers and woodlands.
Wildebeest, zebras and gazelles take part in an annual migration across the region, following seasonal rains and searching for pasture and water.
The migration and variety of habitats support abundant large mammals, including predators such as lions and hyenas.
Serengeti National Park was inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 1981.

overview.text: Borneo is a large island in Southeast Asia, crossed by the Equator and ranked the world’s third largest. Its territory is shared by Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei; the Indonesian portion is commonly called Kalimantan. The island’s landscapes include uplands, river corridors and coastal areas, with tropical rainforests supporting rich plant and animal life, including Bornean orangutans. Borneo is also home to many Indigenous and local communities. Its mix of distinctive environments, wildlife and human cultures makes the island important both as a natural region and as a place where people live and connect across national borders.

key_facts.text: Borneo is the world’s third-largest island.
Three countries share the island: Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei. The Indonesian part is known as Kalimantan.
A Borneo Studies director describes three broad physical zones: upland, riverine and coastal.
Borneo’s tropical forests are rich in species and provide habitat for Bornean orangutans.
Borneo has diverse Indigenous and local communities; the label “Dayak” covers many distinct native ethnic groups.

overview.text: Hoover Dam is a concrete arch-gravity dam in Black Canyon of the Colorado River, on the Nevada–Arizona border southeast of Las Vegas. Built as part of the federal Boulder Canyon Project, it was designed to help control floods, store water for farms and cities, and generate hydroelectric power. Construction began in 1931; the dam began impounding water in Lake Mead on February 1, 1935, and its last concrete was placed that May. The project reshaped the arid Southwest and became a landmark of large-scale engineering. First known as Boulder Dam, it was officially named Hoover Dam in 1947.

key_facts.text: The dam stands in Black Canyon, where the Colorado River forms the Nevada–Arizona border.
It is an arch-gravity dam, 726 feet above the riverbed; its concrete base is 660 feet thick.
The dam began holding back water to form Lake Mead on February 1, 1935. Its last concrete was placed May 29, 1935; President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated it that September.
Its planned roles included flood control, water storage for farms and cities, and hydroelectric power generation.
Congress officially designated it Hoover Dam in 1947, after it had also been called Boulder Dam.

overview.text: West Virginia is a U.S. state in the Appalachian Highlands, known as the Mountain State for its rugged, varied terrain. Long ridges, steep-sided valleys, high Allegheny Mountains, and deeply cut plateau country shape its landscape; the western two-thirds lies on the Allegheny Plateau. Most of the state’s drainage flows west toward the Ohio River, while the rest flows east toward the Potomac. West Virginia is also distinctive in U.S. history: it formed from Virginia during the Civil War after western Unionists moved to create a new state following Virginia’s secession. It became the 35th state on June 20, 1863. Spruce Knob, at 4,861 feet, is its highest point.

key_facts.text: West Virginia’s nickname, the Mountain State, reflects its rugged, mountainous terrain.
Spruce Knob, in Pendleton County, is the state’s highest point at 4,861 feet.
The Allegheny Front roughly marks the Eastern Continental Divide: about 85 percent of the state’s drainage flows west to the Ohio River, and 15 percent east to the Potomac River.
West Virginia became a state on June 20, 1863, after western Unionists pursued statehood during the Civil War.
The Allegheny Plateau covers the state’s western two-thirds; the Eastern Panhandle includes Ridge and Valley terrain.

overview.text: The Pentagon is a large, five-sided government building in Arlington, Virginia, across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C. It serves as the headquarters of the U.S. military department, making it both a working center of military leadership and a widely recognized national symbol. The building was constructed during World War II as the federal government sought more room for the expanding War Department: work began on September 11, 1941, and the Pentagon officially opened on January 15, 1943. Its five-sided exterior and central courtyard are among the features recognized in its National Historic Landmark designation. Its location also reflects Arlington’s local history: construction displaced Queen City, an African American neighborhood, and other East Arlington residents.

key_facts.text: The Pentagon stands in Arlington, Virginia, across the Potomac River from Washington, D.C.
It is the headquarters of the U.S. military department.
Construction began September 11, 1941; the building officially opened January 15, 1943.
Its distinctive five-sided shape and central courtyard are among the features recognized in its 1992 National Historic Landmark designation.
The Pentagon project displaced Queen City, an African American community, and other East Arlington residents.

overview.text: Morocco, officially the Kingdom of Morocco, is a North African monarchy with its capital at Rabat. Positioned between the Atlantic and Mediterranean, it lies at a crossroads between Africa and Europe. Its terrain ranges from coastal plains and green landscapes to the Rif and Atlas mountain ranges and arid Saharan regions; the High Atlas includes Jebel Toubkal, North Africa’s highest peak. Morocco’s location and layered heritage connect it with Mediterranean, African and European histories. Its long-standing U.S. connection dates to 1786, when it formally recognized the United States through a treaty of peace and friendship. ([diplomatie.gouv.fr](https://www.diplomatie.gouv.fr/fr/information-par-pays/maroc/presentation-du-maroc))

key_facts.text: Morocco’s official name is the Kingdom of Morocco; Rabat is its capital, and Casablanca, Fez, Tangier, Meknes, Marrakech, Salé, and Agadir are among its principal cities.
Morocco borders both the Atlantic Ocean and the Mediterranean Sea, and its position is described as a crossroads between Africa and Europe.
The High Atlas range stretches across Morocco; Jebel Toubkal, at 4,167 metres, is identified as North Africa’s highest peak.
The country’s landscapes include mountains, green plains, coasts, and Saharan desert regions.
Morocco formally recognized the United States in 1786 through a treaty signed at Marrakech by Sidi Muhammad, Sultan of Morocco, and U.S. Minister Thomas Barclay.

overview.text: Reykjavík is Iceland’s capital and most populous municipality, on the country’s southwest coast. Its name means “Smoky Bay,” referring to steam rising from nearby hot springs; geothermal water is also used to heat homes and swimming pools. The city is linked to Iceland’s earliest settlement: archaeological remains in its centre date to around 870. The traditional story that Ingólfur Arnarson chose the site by following pillars cast into the sea is a legend, not a confirmed account. Reykjavík’s urban growth began in the 18th century, and it received town rights in 1786. Government offices moved there in 1904, when it became Iceland’s capital and an important national centre.

key_facts.text: Reykjavík is Iceland’s capital and most populous municipality.
The name Reykjavík means “Smoky Bay,” linked to steam from the area’s hot springs.
Archaeological remains in the city centre date to around 870; the story of Ingólfur Arnarson following pillars to the site is presented as legend.
Reykjavík received town rights in 1786, after urban settlement began taking shape there in the 18th century.
Reykjavík became Iceland’s capital in 1904, when government offices were established there after Iceland gained Home Rule.
Geothermal water is used to heat homes and swimming pools in the city.

overview.text: Ontario is a province in east-central Canada and the country’s most populous province; it is also its second-largest by area. Toronto is Ontario’s capital, while Ottawa, on the Ottawa River, is Canada’s national capital—so both provincial and federal government centres are in Ontario. The province is closely associated with the Great Lakes, which lie along the Canada–United States border, and its southern communities are part of the Central Canada region. Beyond its cities, Ontario has abundant freshwater: lakes and rivers make up about one-fifth of its area. Ontario became one of Canada’s four founding provinces at Confederation in 1867.

key_facts.text: Ontario is Canada’s most populous province and second-largest province by area.
Toronto is the capital of Ontario; Ottawa, also in Ontario, is Canada’s national capital.
Ottawa was chosen as Canada’s capital in 1857 and sits on the Ottawa River.
Lakes and rivers cover about one-fifth of Ontario’s area.
Ontario became a province in 1867, when Confederation united four provinces.
Ontario and Quebec make up Central Canada, a region with many communities near the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River.

overview.text: Normandy (French: Normandie) is a region in northwestern France, facing the English Channel; its varied landscapes include a long coastline, plains, hills and river valleys. The name recalls the Norse “men of the North”: after Viking raids, a 911 agreement between Frankish king Charles the Simple and leader Rollo established a territory that developed into the Duchy of Normandy. Its dukes became influential in European history: William, born at Falaise, conquered England in 1066. Normandy returned to French royal control in 1204. The medieval duchy and the present-day administrative region are not the same entity; the region was reunified in 2016. Normandy is also associated with the Allied landings and Battle of Normandy in 1944.

key_facts.text: Normandy lies in northwestern France; its geography includes Channel coastline, plains, hills and river valleys. The modern region has five departments.
An agreement in 911 between Charles the Simple and Viking leader Rollo established a territory that became the Duchy of Normandy.
William, Duke of Normandy, was born at Falaise and became king of England after his victory at Hastings in 1066.
French forces brought Normandy under the French crown in 1204; Louis XI ended the duchy in 1469.
The modern administrative region was reunified in 2016. Normandy was also the site of the Allied landings and Battle of Normandy in 1944.

overview.text: Catalonia is a region in northeastern Spain, between the Mediterranean Sea and the Pyrenees, with Barcelona as its capital. It is one of Spain’s autonomous communities: under its Statute of Autonomy, it has its own parliament and government, called the Generalitat, and manages some public affairs while remaining within the Spanish state. Catalan, a Romance language, is a defining feature of Catalan identity and is official alongside Spanish; Aranese is also official in the region. Catalonia’s language, culture and institutional tradition distinguish it within Spain, and its distinct identity has figured prominently in a long-running movement for independence.

key_facts.text: Catalonia borders France and Andorra to the north and the Mediterranean Sea to the east; Barcelona is its capital.
The Generalitat’s institutions include Catalonia’s parliament, president and government. The Statute of Autonomy sets out their powers and relations with the Spanish state.
Catalan developed from Latin between the 8th and 10th centuries. It is also spoken beyond Catalonia, including in Andorra and the Balearic Islands.
Catalan, Spanish and Aranese are official languages in Catalonia.
Catalonia’s National Day on September 11 commemorates the loss of Catalan liberties and institutions after the 1714 defeat in the War of the Spanish Succession.

overview.text: Illinois is a U.S. state whose capital is Springfield and that includes Chicago; it borders Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Missouri and Wisconsin. It joined the Union on December 3, 1818, as the 21st state, and Springfield has been its capital since 1837. Its nickname, the Prairie State, reflects its once-extensive tallgrass landscape: glaciers shaped much of its northern terrain, while prairie and forest once formed contrasting regions. Most original prairie has since been converted, especially for agriculture. Illinois is also called the Land of Lincoln: Abraham Lincoln lived and worked there for decades before becoming president, and Chicago rose as a major city and economic center during the nineteenth century. The state’s mix of prairie heritage, Chicago’s urban influence and Lincoln’s history distinguishes Illinois.

key_facts.text: Illinois became the 21st state on December 3, 1818. Its capital moved from Kaskaskia to Vandalia and then to Springfield in 1837.
In 1820, Illinois had about 22 million acres of prairie and 14 million acres of forest; by 1900, most of its prairie had been converted, mainly to agriculture.
Glaciers shaped much of northern Illinois; the last major glaciation in the state was about 12,000 years ago.
Illinois’s official slogan is “Land of Lincoln,” referring to Abraham Lincoln’s years of residence and public life in the state before his presidency.
Before statehood, Illinois’s proposed northern border did not reach Lake Michigan; an amendment extended it north to make room for a future port city—Chicago—and access to lead-mining areas.

overview.text: The Great Wall of China is not one wall built at once but a vast defense network developed along northern China over many centuries. Earlier states built frontier barriers; around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang linked some existing sections into a broader system. Successive dynasties expanded or rebuilt it, with construction continuing into the Ming era (1368–1644); many familiar stone sections date from Ming rebuilding. UNESCO describes the listed system as more than 20,000 kilometers long, including varied routes and components such as walls, watchtowers, passes, and forts. It is a landmark of military engineering and a powerful symbol of Chinese history. The popular claim that it is visible from the Moon is false.

key_facts.text: Around 220 BCE, Qin Shi Huang joined some earlier fortifications into a wider northern defense system.
Successive Chinese empires built and expanded the system from the 3rd century BCE to the 17th century CE.
Its components include walls, watchtowers, horse tracks, shelters, fortresses, and passes.
The Ming dynasty (1368–1644) undertook major rebuilding; many familiar stone sections are from that era.
The Wall is difficult to make out even from low Earth orbit; it cannot be seen from the Moon with the naked eye.

overview.text: The Hawaiian Islands are a volcanic archipelago in the central Pacific and include the islands of the U.S. state of Hawaiʻi. Their land is the exposed summits of volcanic mountains built up from the ocean floor by repeated eruptions. The chain’s defining pattern reflects the Pacific Plate moving northwest over a relatively fixed hotspot: Hawaiʻi Island lies above the active hotspot, while older volcanoes extend northwest. After volcanism weakens, erosion gradually reshapes the islands. This ongoing process makes the archipelago a clear example of how plate motion and volcanism can build a long island chain; politically, Hawaiʻi became the 50th U.S. state on August 21, 1959.

key_facts.text: The Hawaiian Archipelago stretches about 1,500 miles across the central Pacific.
The islands are exposed peaks of volcanic mountains built from the seafloor by repeated eruptions.
The Pacific Plate’s movement over a relatively fixed hotspot helps explain the chain’s age pattern: Hawaiʻi Island is above the active hotspot, and older volcanoes lie northwest.
As volcanic activity weakens, erosion reshapes the islands.
Hawaiʻi became the 50th U.S. state on August 21, 1959.

overview.text: Moscow (Russian: Moskva) is Russia’s capital and largest city, on the Moskva River. Its historic core grew around the Kremlin, a fortified center of government and religious life whose earliest written mention dates to 1147; that date marks a record, not necessarily the city’s founding. The Kremlin’s walls, towers, churches and palaces stand beside Red Square, together forming a UNESCO World Heritage site recognized for architectural importance and links to major Russian political events. Moscow served as Russia’s capital before the early-18th-century move to St. Petersburg and regained that role in 1918. The city remains a national political and economic center.

key_facts.text: Moskva is the Russian name for Moscow; the city stands on the river of the same name.
Moscow’s earliest written mention is dated to 1147. This is a documentary reference, not proof that the city was founded that year.
The Kremlin developed as a fortified center of state and religious power; UNESCO describes it as Moscow’s oldest part and a historic center of Russian political life.
The Kremlin and Red Square form a UNESCO World Heritage site, recognized for architectural works including the Kremlin’s churches and the St. Basil’s Basilica.
Russia’s capital moved from Moscow to St. Petersburg in the early 18th century and returned to Moscow in 1918.

overview.text: Belgium is a small country in western Europe, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg and France. Its landscape rises from low coastal areas through central plateaus to the wooded Ardennes in the south. After a revolution in 1830, a provisional government declared independence from the Netherlands on October 4; a constitution followed in 1831, and Leopold I became the first king that year. Today Belgium is a federal constitutional monarchy, with Dutch, French and German as official languages and decision-making shared among federal, regional and community institutions. Its capital, Brussels, is also one of the official seats of European Union institutions.

key_facts.text: Belgium lies in western Europe and shares borders with the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg and France.
The country has three broad elevation zones: lower, central and upper Belgium; the Ardennes are in the south.
A provisional government declared independence on October 4, 1830; the National Congress adopted a constitution on February 7, 1831.
Belgium is a federal constitutional monarchy with three official languages—Dutch, French and German—and three regions: Flanders, Brussels-Capital and Wallonia.
Brussels is Belgium’s capital and one of the three official seats of European Union institutions.

overview.text: Cleveland is an Ohio city on the southern shore of Lake Erie, founded in 1796 and incorporated in 1836; its name honors survey leader Moses Cleaveland. Rail and water routes, along with iron and oil, helped make it an important industrial and commercial center. The Cuyahoga River cuts through the city’s Flats, a former dock-and-factory district that today mixes commerce, industry, nightlife, and homes. Nearby Ohio City, once a separate municipality, is among Cleveland’s oldest neighborhoods and is home to the West Side Market. The Cleveland Orchestra, founded in 1918 and based at Severance Music Center, adds a prominent cultural dimension through performances, education, recordings, and tours.

key_facts.text: The Connecticut Land Company’s survey established Cleveland in 1796; the city was named for General Moses Cleaveland and incorporated in 1836.
The Flats are low-lying land along the Cuyahoga River; canals, lake shipping, and railways helped turn the area into a center for docks, warehouses, and factories.
Ohio City became an independent municipality in 1836 and was annexed by Cleveland in 1854.
Ohio City’s West Side Market traces its beginnings to a public market site set aside in 1840; its present market building opened in 1912.
The Cleveland Orchestra was founded in 1918; Severance became its permanent home in 1931, and the ensemble began touring Europe in 1957.

overview.text: Mount Kilimanjaro is a volcanic massif in northern Tanzania, rising in isolation above the surrounding plains. At 5,895 metres, it is Africa’s highest mountain. Its three major volcanic peaks are Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira: Kibo holds the summit, Mawenzi is rugged and sharply ridged, and Shira is an older collapsed cone forming a plateau. The massif’s summit includes craters and fumaroles, while its elevation creates a striking sequence of landscapes—from montane forest through heath, moorland and alpine desert to the summit zone. UNESCO identifies Kilimanjaro’s height, form, ice and isolated setting as an outstanding natural phenomenon.

key_facts.text: Kilimanjaro’s highest summit is Kibo, at 5,895 metres; Mawenzi is its second-highest peak.
The three principal volcanic peaks are Kibo, Mawenzi and Shira; geologically, they are overlapping volcanic edifices.
Shira is an older collapsed peak that forms a plateau.
The Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program reports no known Holocene eruptions; its cited research places the latest known volcanic activity roughly 150,000–200,000 years ago.
UNESCO describes five main vegetation zones, from lower slopes and montane forest to heath and moorland, alpine desert and summit.

overview.text: Arthur Rimbaud (1854–1891) was a French poet born in Charleville whose celebrated poetic career lasted only a few intense years. His best-known works include the visionary poem “The Drunken Boat,” the prose-poetry book A Season in Hell, and Illuminations. Rimbaud challenged conventional poetic forms and used startling images, sound, and sensory associations to suggest experiences beyond ordinary perception; his writing helped reshape modern French poetry and continued to inspire later artists. His life also took an unusual turn: around age twenty, he stopped writing poetry and spent much of his remaining adulthood traveling and working abroad.

key_facts.text: He was born in Charleville on October 20, 1854, and died in Marseille on November 10, 1891, aged 37.
He wrote poetry for about five years, ending around 1875; the city museum describes his major poetic period as spanning ages 17 to 21.
His notable works include “The Drunken Boat,” A Season in Hell, and Illuminations; A Season in Hell was the only collection he arranged to publish himself.
In “Vowels,” he associated vowel sounds with colors, exemplifying his experimentation with language and sensory imagery.
After leaving poetry, he traveled and worked abroad, including in Aden and Harar; his later work life included commerce and arms trading.

overview.text: Grendel is the monstrous first antagonist of the Old English epic Beowulf. The poem presents him as a hostile outsider who repeatedly raids King Hrothgar’s hall, Heorot, killing and eating the king’s men; the attacks end when Beowulf confronts him. In the poem’s Christian narration, Grendel belongs to Cain’s cursed lineage, linking the monster to biblical fratricide and evil; this is part of the poem’s religious storytelling, not a historical claim. Beowulf defeats him bare-handed, tearing off an arm, and Grendel escapes to the fens with a mortal wound. His mother then attacks to avenge him, making Grendel’s defeat the first of the epic’s three major conflicts.

key_facts.text: The poem’s Christian framing connects Grendel’s lineage to Cain, who killed his brother Abel.
Grendel repeatedly attacks Hrothgar’s hall and kills the Danes there; the attacks last twelve years before Beowulf fights him.
Beowulf tears off Grendel’s arm, inflicting a mortal wound; Grendel escapes to the fens.
After Grendel’s defeat, his mother attacks Hrothgar’s people to avenge her son.
The British Library describes Grendel’s fight with Beowulf as the first of the poem’s three main sections; the other two concern Grendel’s mother and a dragon.

overview.text: David Foster Wallace (1962–2008) was an American novelist, short-story writer, and essayist whose work established him as a significant literary figure. His best-known novel, *Infinite Jest*, appeared in 1996; its settings—a tennis academy and a halfway house for people recovering from addiction—frame questions about entertainment, pleasure, and human connection. Wallace also published *The Broom of the System*, story collections such as *Oblivion*, and essay collections including *A Supposedly Fun Thing I’ll Never Do Again* and *Consider the Lobster*. A regionally ranked junior tennis player himself, he brought the sport into his fiction. His final novel, *The Pale King*, was unfinished at his death and published in 2011.

key_facts.text: Wallace was born in Ithaca, New York, in 1962 and grew up in Illinois; he died in 2008.
He studied philosophy and English at Amherst College; his senior English thesis became his first novel, *The Broom of the System*.
As a teenager, Wallace was a regionally ranked tennis player. *Infinite Jest* features a tennis academy alongside a halfway house for people recovering from addiction.
Published in 1996, *Infinite Jest* explores entertainment, its place in people’s lives, and how it relates to human connection.
His last novel, *The Pale King*, was unfinished when he died and was published posthumously in 2011.

overview.text: The March family are the fictional New England household at the center of Louisa May Alcott’s *Little Women*, first published in parts in 1868–69. Its four daughters—Meg, Jo, Beth, and Amy—grow from girlhood toward adulthood during the Civil War era. Their distinct temperaments shape the story: Jo is quick-tempered and yearns for independence; Beth is devoted to home and family; Meg wants fashionable comforts; and Amy can be self-absorbed. Alcott drew on her own family and childhood, and the novel follows ordinary family life—playacting, sibling rivalry, reconciliation, friendship, romance, and loss. Yet the sisters are fictional characters, not exact copies of Alcott’s sisters.

key_facts.text: The March sisters are the four central characters of *Little Women*, which Alcott’s publisher asked her to write as a book for girls.
The novel is set in a small New England town during the Civil War and Reconstruction; its first parts appeared in 1868–69.
The sisters’ contrasting traits include Jo’s independence, Beth’s devotion to home and family, Meg’s interest in pretty clothes, and Amy’s self-absorption.
Alcott adapted episodes and people from her own childhood, including her sisters, but said the March girls were only suggestions of her real sisters—not exact portraits.
The sisters’ story traces their progress toward adulthood through family adventures, rivalries, reconciliations, friendships, romance, and loss.

overview.text: The Kite Runner, Khaled Hosseini’s 2003 debut novel, follows Amir from his childhood in Kabul into adulthood in the United States and back to Afghanistan. As a privileged boy, Amir is close to Hassan, the son of his father’s servant; after Amir wins a kite-fighting contest, a traumatic event and his failure to help Hassan leave him burdened by guilt. Years later, amid Afghanistan’s political upheaval, Amir returns seeking to make amends. The novel connects this personal story to conflict, migration, and social divisions, while exploring friendship, betrayal, fathers and sons, and the possibility—but not certainty—of redemption.

key_facts.text: The novel was first published in 2003 and was Hosseini’s first novel.
Kite fighting in the story is a contest in which participants try to cut down other kites; a kite runner retrieves a kite after it falls.
Amir and Hassan’s relationship is shaped by unequal wealth and status as well as affection; the AQA overview also connects their characters to ethnic and religious divisions represented in the novel.
The story’s changing settings reflect upheaval in Afghanistan and the effects of political events on ordinary people; its historical setting is part of a fictional narrative.
Amir’s adult return to Afghanistan is presented as an effort to atone, but the ending offers hope rather than guaranteeing that Sohrab has healed.

overview.text: William Wordsworth’s “I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud,” often called “Daffodils,” is a celebrated English Romantic poem first published in 1807, then revised into the four-stanza version widely read today in 1815. Its speaker sees golden daffodils beside a lake, and the flowers’ motion seems to join the dancing waves. Vivid comparisons transform a brief encounter with nature into an exuberant scene. The poem’s distinctive turn comes later: alone and reflective, the speaker recalls the flowers through an “inward eye,” and the remembered scene renews his pleasure. Its lasting appeal lies in the connection it makes between close attention to nature, imagination, and the joy memory can bring.

key_facts.text: Wordsworth composed the poem in 1804, after he and his sister Dorothy saw daffodils by Ullswater in April 1802.
Dorothy recorded the daffodil sighting in her journal; her account may have influenced Wordsworth’s later poem.
The poem first appeared in 1807 under its opening line rather than a separate title; “Daffodils” is a common alternate name.
The 1807 manuscript has three six-line stanzas; Wordsworth added a stanza for the revised 1815 version.
The later stanza emphasizes that the remembered flowers can bring pleasure when the speaker is alone and reflective.

overview.text: Created by author and illustrator Jeff Kinney, Diary of a Wimpy Kid is a humorous children’s book series told through middle-schooler Greg Heffley’s journal entries. Greg writes about trying to get through school, friendships, family life, embarrassing moments, and other everyday troubles. Short passages of writing are paired with cartoons, giving the books a distinctive illustrated-journal feel. Kinney began developing the idea with jokes and drawings in journals, then published installments online before the first print book appeared in 2007. The series stands out for turning familiar growing-up problems into comic adventures narrated in Greg’s self-focused, imperfect voice.

key_facts.text: Jeff Kinney created and illustrates the series; Greg Heffley is its middle-school narrator.
The series combines Greg’s journal entries with cartoons and humor.
Kinney says he began writing the series in 1998; the official series history says online installments began in May 2004.
The first printed book was published in 2007.
Dog Days and Cabin Fever are installments in the series.

overview.text: Isabel Allende is a novelist and memoirist born in Lima to Chilean parents and raised mostly in Chile. After the 1973 military coup, she went into exile in Venezuela; there, a letter to her dying grandfather grew into her first novel, The House of the Spirits (1982). The novel brought her wide recognition and blends family history and political upheaval with supernatural elements, following generations of women. Across her fiction, Allende connects personal lives with historical change and often centers women challenging restrictive expectations. The House of the Spirits, Daughter of Fortune, and Portrait in Sepia form a trilogy, though each novel can be read independently.

key_facts.text: Allende was born in Lima in 1942 to Chilean parents and grew up mostly in Chile.
After Chile’s 1973 coup, she lived in exile in Caracas, Venezuela.
A letter she began to her dying grandfather became the basis of The House of the Spirits, published in 1982.
The House of the Spirits combines a multigenerational family saga with Chilean political history and magical elements.
The House of the Spirits, Daughter of Fortune, and Portrait in Sepia are linked novels that can each be read on its own.

overview.text: Franz Kafka’s unfinished novel *The Trial* (written in 1914–15 and published posthumously in 1925) follows Josef K., a bank officer who is arrested without receiving clear information about the accusation against him. As he tries to understand his case and the anonymous court system, his search for clarity only deepens his confusion, and the story ends with his execution. The unexplained arrest and inaccessible bureaucracy give the novel a distinctive atmosphere of uncertainty. A major work of European modernism, it is often read as a critique of bureaucratic power or as an existential or theological parable, though no single interpretation settles its meaning.

key_facts.text: Kafka wrote the novel in 1914–15; it was published in 1925, after his death.
Josef K. is a bank officer who is suddenly arrested but cannot get clear information about the charge against him.
As Josef K. seeks truth and clarity, the story describes his growing confusion and ends with his execution.
Kafka died before completing any of his full-length novels; his friend Max Brod published his unpublished work despite Kafka’s request that it be destroyed.
Readers have interpreted the novel as a parable of modern bureaucracy and through existential or theological ideas; these are interpretations, not a single settled meaning.

overview.text: Charles Dickens’s short ghost story A Christmas Carol, first published in 1843, follows Ebenezer Scrooge, a miser who rejects Christmas cheer and charity. On Christmas Eve, his dead business partner Jacob Marley warns him, and the spirits of Christmas Past, Present, and Future confront him with memories, the people affected by his choices, and the lonely fate awaiting him. Scrooge awakens changed and begins treating Bob Cratchit’s family with generosity. Blending supernatural episodes and festive scenes with concern for poverty and social responsibility, the tale became the first and most famous of Dickens’s Christmas books, and its associations between Christmas and ghost stories have endured. ([britishlibrary.cn](https://www.britishlibrary.cn/en/works/charles-dickenss-christmas-carol/))

key_facts.text: The book was published in 1843 by Chapman and Hall; the first edition appeared on December 19.
It was the first of Dickens’s series of Christmas books.
Jacob Marley’s ghost visits Scrooge before the three spirits of Christmas Past, Present, and Future.
The children Ignorance and Want make the story’s concern with poverty and social neglect vivid.
The first edition had lavishly colored illustrations; its price was capped to make it more affordable to readers.

overview.text: “Dulce et Decorum Est” is a World War I poem by British poet and soldier Wilfred Owen, drafted in 1917 while he was being treated at Craiglockhart War Hospital. It follows exhausted soldiers caught in a gas attack and focuses on one man who fails to put on his gas mask in time; the speaker’s recurring nightmare makes the scene feel both immediate and lasting. The Latin title completes a saying by Roman poet Horace that dying for one’s country is sweet and fitting. Owen turns that praise into bitter irony, challenging people who present war deaths as glorious.

key_facts.text: Owen drafted the poem at Craiglockhart War Hospital in 1917, while recovering after fighting in the war.
The poem’s title comes from a line by the Roman poet Horace; Owen uses its patriotic message ironically.
A sudden gas attack interrupts the soldiers’ march; one soldier does not get his mask on in time.
The central episode depicts an unnamed soldier’s death and ends by attacking the idea that such deaths are glorious.
The poem survives in four original manuscripts, and its early drafts were revised; the exact place and timing of later revisions are uncertain.

overview.text: Truman Capote’s *Breakfast at Tiffany’s* is a 1958 novella centered on Holly Golightly, a restless young woman making a life in Manhattan. A writer recalls his friendship with Holly, his neighbor, whose unsettled habits include throwing parties and refusing to feel bound to a stray cat she has taken in. Capote presents her as more than a glamorous socialite: literary critic Robert Pranzatelli describes her as someone who invents a public identity while seeking acceptance and struggling with uncertainty. The story’s mix of wit, poignancy, and vulnerability helps explain Holly’s lasting place in American literature; her name and style have entered the literary landscape.

key_facts.text: Capote’s novella was published in 1958.
The story is told through a writer’s recollection of his friendship with Holly, his neighbor in a Manhattan apartment building.
Holly Golightly is a self-invented identity; literary critic Robert Pranzatelli connects her reinvention to the search for social acceptance.
Holly takes in a stray cat but insists that neither belongs to the other; her regret after sending it away reveals her attachment.
A publisher’s description notes Holly’s wit and poignancy and says her name and style have become part of the American literary landscape.

overview.text: “Ulysses” is a dramatic monologue by Victorian poet Alfred, Lord Tennyson, published in 1842. Its speaker is the legendary Greek hero also called Odysseus, now an aging king on Ithaca. Dissatisfied with ruling at home, he recalls past voyages and battles, leaves the kingdom to his son Telemachus, and calls his former mariners to sail with him in search of new experience and knowledge. The poem’s famous final resolve affirms striving despite age, yet the expedition’s success is uncertain: Ulysses admits the sea may overwhelm them. Tennyson said he wrote the poem soon after his friend Arthur Hallam died, expressing a need to continue through life’s struggles; the poem also draws on Dante’s contrasting account of Ulysses.

key_facts.text: The poem is a dramatic monologue: Tennyson writes in the voice of Ulysses, the Roman name for the Greek hero Odysseus.
Ulysses leaves the rule of Ithaca to his son Telemachus and addresses his former mariners, inviting them on another voyage.
The voyage is uncertain rather than a guaranteed triumph: Ulysses allows that the sea may destroy them, or that they may reach the Happy Isles.
Tennyson connected the poem, written soon after Arthur Hallam’s death, with the need to go forward and face life’s struggles.
The poem draws on Dante’s account of Ulysses in the Inferno, but Tennyson presents the hero’s restless aspiration more positively than Dante does.

overview.text: Erich Maria Remarque’s 1929 novel, originally published in German as Im Westen nichts Neues, follows Paul Bäumer, a young German soldier on the Western Front during World War I. Through Paul and his fellow recruits, it presents combat not as heroic adventure but as trench warfare’s misery, fear, and losses, while showing the friendships soldiers depend on and the distance between front-line life and the ideals that sent them there. Remarque’s own wartime service and the loss of comrades informed the work. Its stark portrayal of young soldiers’ suffering made it an international bestseller and drew both pacifist praise and nationalist condemnation, establishing it as a major antiwar novel.

key_facts.text: The novel was published in 1929 under its German title, Im Westen nichts Neues.
Remarque was drafted into the German army, served on the Western Front, and was wounded in 1917; the museum says his experiences and the loss of comrades inspired the novel.
The story centers on Paul Bäumer and his fellow young German soldiers, emphasizing trench warfare’s brutality and the bonds formed among comrades.
The book’s pacifist stance earned praise from liberal and leftist critics, while Nazis and conservative nationalists condemned it.

overview.text: Tragedy is a dramatic genre that presents a serious, connected action through characters’ words and deeds, often showing suffering, a reversal of fortune, or a protagonist’s downfall. In Aristotle’s influential account, tragedy arouses pity and fear and brings about “catharsis,” but scholars disagree about what that effect means; it should not be reduced to one settled definition. The genre’s early history is especially associated with ancient Athens, where tragedies were probably performed at a spring festival for Dionysos. Greek tragedy and later forms, including Shakespearean plays, show how writers use intense conflict and loss to explore human choices and their consequences.

key_facts.text: Aristotle describes tragedy as enacted drama representing a serious, complete action, rather than a story told by a narrator.
In Aristotle’s theory, pity and fear are central to tragedy; the meaning of catharsis remains disputed among scholars.
The roots of Greek tragedy are thought to lie in an Athenian spring festival honoring Dionysos, though the Met notes that little is known about its origins before Aeschylus.
Most of the few surviving Greek tragedies draw on heroic myths; Aeschylus’ Persians is a notable exception.
Aristotle’s Poetics mainly treats tragedy in its surviving portion; the work’s section on comedy is now lost.

overview.text: In Homeric epic, Odysseus (called Ulysses in Latin) is the Greek hero and king of Ithaca whose defining aim is to get home after the Trojan War. The Odyssey, a poem attributed to Homer and dated by the Ashmolean to the eighth century BCE, centers on his return voyage: after Troy falls, a further ten years of adventures separate him from Ithaca. The poem moves between the homecoming and earlier episodes Odysseus recounts, including encounters with the Cyclops Polyphemus and the enchantress Circe. His intelligence and resourcefulness set him apart among the Greek warriors, while his long, difficult return has made him a lasting subject of retelling and art.

key_facts.text: Odysseus is also known as Ulysses, the Latin form of his name.
In the Odyssey, he is king of Ithaca and returns there after the Trojan War.
The Ashmolean dates the poem, attributed to Homer, to the eighth century BCE.
The poem’s adventures include Odysseus’s encounter with the Cyclops Polyphemus and his test of wills with Circe.
The Ashmolean describes him as a clever strategist as well as a great fighter, emphasizing the contrast between his skill and his difficult journey home.

overview.text: Ender’s Game is a science-fiction novel by Orson Scott Card about Andrew “Ender” Wiggin, a gifted child selected for military training against an alien enemy. At an orbiting Battle School, Ender and other young recruits practice strategy in mock battles in a zero-gravity Battle Room. The story combines military competition with Ender’s loneliness, peer rivalry, and pressure from adult commanders, making the experience of a child soldier central to the plot. Card says he expanded an earlier, shorter “Ender’s Game” story into the novel. The novel won the 1985 Nebula and 1986 Hugo Awards for Best Novel, distinguishing it as an award-winning work of science fiction.

key_facts.text: The protagonist is Andrew “Ender” Wiggin, recruited to train at an orbiting Battle School.
The young recruits practice combat in the zero-gravity Battle Room.
Ender’s training involves loneliness, rivalry with other students, and pressure from adult instructors.
Card describes the novel as a longer reworking of an earlier, shorter story titled “Ender’s Game.”
The novel won the 1985 Nebula Award and the 1986 Hugo Award, both for Best Novel.

overview.text: Eugene Gladstone O’Neill (1888–1953) was an American playwright whose work helped make the U.S. stage a venue for psychologically intense, serious drama. The son of actor James O’Neill, he drew on family tensions and difficult experiences while also experimenting with theatrical form, including the inner monologues of Strange Interlude. He received the 1936 Nobel Prize in Literature, the first American playwright to do so, and four Pulitzer Prizes for Drama. His major plays range from Mourning Becomes Electra, which reshapes Greek tragedy in post-Civil War America, to The Iceman Cometh, about barroom dreamers, and the autobiographical Long Day’s Journey Into Night, portraying a family over one day and published after his death.

key_facts.text: O’Neill was born in New York City on October 16, 1888, and died in Boston on November 27, 1953.
His 1936 Nobel Prize made him the first American playwright to receive the Literature award.
Beyond the Horizon, his first major success, premiered in 1920 and won his first Pulitzer Prize for Drama.
Mourning Becomes Electra retells the Oresteia in post-Civil War America.
Long Day’s Journey Into Night won the 1957 Pulitzer Prize for Drama after O’Neill’s death.

overview.text: “Easter, 1916” is a political lyric by Irish poet William Butler Yeats, composed on September 25, 1916, in response to the Easter Rising, an armed revolt in Dublin begun that April to establish an Irish republic. The rebels surrendered after several days, and British authorities executed many of its leaders. Yeats names four of the dead in the poem’s closing stanza, preserving them in verse while also questioning whether their sacrifice was necessary. Its recurring “terrible beauty” refrain holds admiration and horror together: the poem memorializes the Rising without presenting violence as simple heroism. That tension makes it both an elegy for individuals and a reflection on political change.

key_facts.text: Yeats dated the poem September 25, 1916.
The Rising began on Easter Monday, April 24, 1916; rebels proclaimed an Irish Republic from Dublin’s General Post Office.
After the rebels surrendered on April 29, British authorities executed fourteen Rising leaders between May 3 and May 12.
The final stanza names Thomas MacDonagh, John MacBride, James Connolly, and Patrick Pearse.
The refrain “A terrible beauty is born” returns in the poem’s first, second, and final stanzas, linking political violence with change and rebirth.
Yeats restricted an early private printing to 25 copies; he allowed open publication in November 1920.

overview.text: Juliet Capulet is the young heroine of William Shakespeare’s tragedy Romeo and Juliet and the daughter of Lord and Lady Capulet. At a party hosted by her family, she meets Romeo, whose Montague family is locked in a feud with the Capulets; neither initially knows the other’s identity, but they fall in love. Juliet recognizes that Romeo’s family name makes him her enemy, yet questions whether a name defines a person, and the two arrange a secret marriage with Friar Lawrence. When her father pressures her to marry Count Paris, Juliet seeks the Friar’s help and takes a potion that makes her appear dead. A failed plan leads to both lovers’ deaths, which finally help end the feud.

key_facts.text: Juliet belongs to the Capulet household, one of the two families at the center of Verona’s feud.
She and Romeo fall in love at a Capulet party before learning that their families are enemies.
In the orchard scene, Juliet questions the importance of Romeo’s Montague name, a defining moment in the play’s treatment of identity and family allegiance.
Juliet and Romeo secretly marry with Friar Lawrence’s help, hoping their union may help reconcile their families.
When Juliet’s father insists she marry Paris, she takes a potion that makes her seem dead; the plan fails, and her death with Romeo contributes to the families’ reconciliation.

overview.text: Daniel Defoe (c. 1660–1731) was an English writer whose career joined fiction with journalism and political writing. In his own lifetime he was especially known as a journalist and political agent, and his output ranged across books, pamphlets, and periodicals. Today he is best known for Robinson Crusoe (1719), a novel often regarded as an early landmark in English fiction; the Folger Shakespeare Library notes that its castaway story drew on Alexander Selkirk’s experience. Defoe also wrote Moll Flanders (1722) and A Journal of the Plague Year (1722), set during London’s 1665 epidemic. Crusoe and Friday’s adventures became lasting touchstones in Western literary history.

key_facts.text: Defoe lived from about 1660 to 1731; reference sources differ slightly on his birth year, so it is often given approximately.
He worked as a journalist and political writer, and wrote across books, pamphlets, and periodicals.
Robinson Crusoe appeared in 1719 and is often regarded as a foundational early English novel.
The Folger Shakespeare Library connects Robinson Crusoe’s castaway story with Alexander Selkirk’s experience on an uninhabited island.
Moll Flanders and A Journal of the Plague Year were published in 1722; the latter is set during London’s Great Plague of 1665.

overview.text: W. W. Jacobs’s “The Monkey’s Paw” is a supernatural horror story first published in 1902 and collected that year in The Lady of the Barge. Its plot begins when Sergeant-Major Morris brings the White family a dried monkey’s paw, which he says was enchanted to grant three wishes to each of three men as a warning against interfering with fate. Mr. White wishes for £200, and the wish is fulfilled through a devastating loss; later wishes deepen the family’s grief. Jacobs builds suspense by setting ominous warnings and strange events against ordinary family life, while leaving room for characters to explain events as coincidence. The story is remembered as a horror classic and has been anthologized and adapted.

key_facts.text: The story first appeared in Harper’s Monthly in 1902 and was collected in The Lady of the Barge that same year.
In Morris’s account, the dried paw is said to grant three wishes to each of three men; he warns the family about trying to change fate.
Mr. White wishes for £200, which arrives as compensation after his son Herbert is killed in a workplace accident.
The story has three numbered sections, tracing the family’s wishes and their increasingly painful consequences.
Jacobs was known mainly for humorous writing during his lifetime, while this story became his most famous work and a horror classic.

overview.text: Amy Tan’s The Joy Luck Club (1989) is a linked-story novel about four Chinese immigrant mothers and their American-born daughters in San Francisco. The mothers’ mah-jong gatherings give the stories a meeting point, while memories of China and the daughters’ lives in the United States reveal how family histories shape identity and how love can coexist with cultural and generational misunderstanding. Tan first conceived the book as a collection of stories; its interwoven episodes are arranged in four sections, each opening with a Chinese fable before turning to mothers’ and daughters’ accounts. The book became an international bestseller and remains significant for its focus on immigrant family perspectives and its connected narrative design.

key_facts.text: Amy Tan’s book was published in 1989; she initially wrote it as connected stories, which came to be read as a novel.
The story is told through four mother-daughter pairs; each of the book’s four sections opens with a Chinese fable.
In the novel, four Chinese women who immigrated to San Francisco meet to play mah-jong, remember the past, and share stories.
The opening narrative follows Jing-mei “June” Woo as she takes her late mother Suyuan’s place at the club and later travels to China to find her mother’s lost daughters.
Tan’s official biography describes the book as a collection of connected stories and reports that it became a bestseller.

overview.text: Joseph Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was a British poet, novelist, and short-story writer, born in Bombay (now Mumbai) and shaped by his childhood and early journalism in India. He became known for stories and poems portraying colonial India, British soldiers, and animal characters. His best-known works include The Jungle Book (1894), Kim (1901), and the poem “Gunga Din.” In 1907, he became the first English writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature. His work remains influential, but also contested: Kipling supported British imperialism, and his portrayals of colonized peoples have drawn criticism.

key_facts.text: Kipling was born in Bombay in 1865 and returned to India as a teenager, where he worked as a journalist and editor.
The Jungle Book, published in 1894, features animal stories; its Mowgli stories became especially well known.
Kim, a novel about Indian life, was published in 1901.
“Gunga Din” appeared in Barrack-Room Ballads (1892), a collection of Kipling’s poems.
Kipling’s 1899 poem “The White Man’s Burden” expressed imperialist views that have been criticized as racist and elitist.
In 1907, Kipling became the first English writer to receive the Nobel Prize in Literature.

overview.text: Giovanni Boccaccio’s *The Decameron* is a fourteenth-century Italian prose work whose frame is set during the 1348 plague in Florence. In this fictional frame, seven women and three men leave the afflicted city for the countryside; over ten storytelling days, they tell one tale each, making a collection of one hundred stories. Their tales explore everyday human behavior—including desire, wit, trickery, and the turns of fortune—against a backdrop of social disruption. The work is notable for bringing vernacular Italian prose to a high artistic level and for giving women prominent roles as storytellers. Its lively, sometimes bawdy stories also left a literary legacy, with later writers drawing on Boccaccio’s themes and tales.

key_facts.text: The frame’s ten young Florentines—seven women and three men—are fictional characters who flee the plague-stricken city for the countryside.
Each storyteller tells one tale on each of ten days, creating a collection of one hundred stories.
The stories portray human behavior and relationships, including desire, cleverness, trickery, and the effects of fortune.
Boccaccio wrote the work in Italian vernacular prose, which Duke’s literature professor describes as raising vernacular prose to an art form.
Duke’s account notes Shakespeare’s borrowing of themes from Boccaccio and scholarly suggestions of connections between the work and some of Chaucer’s tales.

overview.text: Jules Verne’s Around the World in Eighty Days (French: Le tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours) is an adventure novel first serialized in 1872 and issued as a book in 1873. It follows Phileas Fogg, a methodical Englishman who wagers that he can circle the globe within eighty days, and his French valet, Jean Passepartout. Their deadline turns railway and steamship connections into the story’s central challenge: missed links, detours, and changing transport keep the journey uncertain. The contrast between Fogg’s precision and Passepartout’s more emotional, adaptable character adds humor and personality to a tale shaped by expanding nineteenth-century travel networks.

key_facts.text: The original French title is Le tour du monde en quatre-vingts jours; Jules Verne (1828–1905) wrote the novel.
It appeared as a serial in Le Temps from November 6 to December 22, 1872, then as a book from Hetzel in 1873.
Fogg bets his Reform Club companions that he can make the journey in eighty days or less; Passepartout joins him as his valet.
The premise relies on the era’s expanding travel connections, including railways and steamships, which the BnF identifies as central to the story.
The text has Fogg use many forms of transport, including steamers, railways, carriages, a yacht, a trading ship, sledges, and elephants.

overview.text: In Geoffrey Chaucer’s The Canterbury Tales, the Knight is a fictional pilgrim and experienced warrior whom the frame narrator introduces as a model of chivalric conduct: loyal, honorable, generous, and courteous. He has campaigned in distant lands and arrives in practical, travel-worn clothing rather than showy dress. On the pilgrimage to Canterbury, drawing lots makes him the first to tell a story. His tale, a romance about Palamon and Arcite competing for Emily, features love, rivalry, and a tournament. The pairing of this seasoned knight with an elevated tale of aristocratic life makes him a memorable voice in Chaucer’s varied company of pilgrims; Shakespeare and John Fletcher later adapted the tale as The Two Noble Kinsmen.

key_facts.text: The Knight travels with a diverse group of pilgrims headed to Canterbury to visit the shrine of Thomas à Becket.
The frame narrator associates him with chivalry, fidelity, honor, generosity, and courtesy.
The poem describes him as widely traveled in warfare, including campaigns in Christian and non-Christian lands; this is the character’s literary description, not evidence about a historical knight.
The Knight’s Tale is a romance about Palamon and Arcite, who love Emily and become rivals; it includes a tournament.
Shakespeare and John Fletcher’s The Two Noble Kinsmen is based on The Knight’s Tale.

overview.text: Western fiction, often called the Western, is a popular literary genre set mainly in an imagined American Old West, especially the nineteenth-century frontier. Familiar stories feature cowboys, outlaws, sheriffs or marshals, ranch or settlement conflicts, and struggles between law and lawlessness. Owen Wister’s The Virginian (1902) helped establish a recognizable pattern: a cowboy hero, a code of the West, and a climactic shootout. Inexpensive dime novels and later pulp magazines carried such adventures to mass audiences and helped shape popular images of the cowboy. Westerns are fiction, not straightforward history: the genre’s nostalgic frontier is partly myth, and later writers have challenged its older formulas and narrow portrayals.

key_facts.text: Traditional Westerns often stage conflicts between law and lawlessness in a romanticized Old West, commonly set on the Great Plains or in the Southwest during the nineteenth century.
Owen Wister’s The Virginian (1902) helped establish familiar conventions including a cowboy hero, a “Code of the West,” and a climactic shootout.
Beadle’s Dime Novels began as a weekly series in 1860, publishing mass-market adventures about the Western frontier.
Common plot patterns included ranching disputes, cattle drives, and stories of outlaws who become marshals; the genre’s conventions later grew less rigid.
Some later Western writers gave women more prominent roles and added greater historical and geographical detail, complicating earlier genre conventions.

overview.text: Philip Milton Roth (1933–2018) was an American novelist born and raised in Newark, New Jersey, a city that also became the setting for much of his fiction. His novels repeatedly explored Jewish-American experience and questions of identity, politics, race, and American life, often combining comedy, satire, and self-conscious storytelling. Portnoy’s Complaint (1969), a provocative comic novel framed as a patient’s confession to a psychoanalyst, brought him wide attention. Roth also created Nathan Zuckerman, a recurring writer-character who narrates several novels. Among these is American Pastoral (1997), which won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1998. His varied work—from comic satire to novels examining national history and social change—made him a major figure in twentieth-century American literature.

key_facts.text: Roth grew up in Newark, the setting for much of his fiction, and earned degrees in English from Bucknell University and the University of Chicago.
His first book, Goodbye, Columbus (1959), won the National Book Award in 1960.
Portnoy’s Complaint (1969) is a comic, confessional monologue addressed to a psychoanalyst; its publication made Roth a widely noticed literary figure.
Nathan Zuckerman first appeared in The Ghost Writer (1979) and returned as a character in several later novels.
American Pastoral (1997), narrated by Zuckerman and set in the Vietnam era, won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 1998.

overview.text: Li Bai (also known as Li Po; 701–762) was a Chinese poet of the Tang dynasty, a period when Chinese literature and art reached a classical high point. He traveled widely, and his poetry often turns encounters with landscapes into reflections on solitude, friendship, and home. In “Quiet Night Thoughts,” moonlight leads the speaker to remember his homeland; in another poem, Li imagines sitting alone with a mountain after birds and clouds disappear. Li’s fellow poet Du Fu was his contemporary and friend. Recognized as one of the Tang era’s most important poets, Li’s work later influenced writers and artists around the world.

key_facts.text: Li Bai is also known by the romanized name Li Po; the Academy of American Poets gives his birth year as likely 701 and his death year as 762.
Li traveled widely and met fellow Tang poet Du Fu in 744; the two were friends who wrote to each other in their poems.
In “Quiet Night Thoughts,” moonlight appears like frost, and the speaker’s thoughts turn toward home.
A poem by Li Bai portrayed in a Metropolitan Museum of Art collection entry links solitude with nature, depicting the speaker sitting with a mountain after birds and clouds vanish.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes the eighth century as a classical period of Chinese art and literature and identifies Li Bai and Du Fu among its leading poets.
The Academy of American Poets notes that Li Bai’s work influenced poets and artists around the world, including Ezra Pound.

overview.text: Rodrick Heffley is a fictional character in Jeff Kinney’s Diary of a Wimpy Kid books and Greg Heffley’s older brother. He plays drums in the rock band Löded Diper, and his teasing of Greg makes him a vivid source of sibling conflict. Rodrick takes a central role in Rodrick Rules, the second book, where he knows about an embarrassing secret Greg is trying to hide. The series later returns to the band in Diper Överlöde, when Greg joins and discovers the unglamorous work behind musical fame. Kinney has said his own older brother, who played drums in a band, inspired Rodrick, while noting that the character differs from his sibling.

key_facts.text: Rodrick is Greg’s older brother and the drummer in Löded Diper, a rock band.
Rodrick Rules is the second book in the series and spotlights the brothers’ rivalry.
In Rodrick Rules, Rodrick knows about an embarrassing incident Greg wants to keep secret.
In Diper Överlöde, Greg joins Rodrick’s band and learns that pursuing fame involves setbacks.
Jeff Kinney said his older brother, who played drums in a basement band, was an original inspiration for Rodrick; he also said the character differs from his brother.

overview.text: Fyodor Dostoevsky’s *Notes from the Underground*, first published in 1864, centers on an unnamed former civil servant in St. Petersburg. Its two sections pair his argumentative, self-contradictory reflections with earlier episodes showing his isolation and strained encounters with others. Through this difficult narrator, Dostoevsky challenges the idea that people can be fully explained or made happy by rational systems: the Underground Man argues that people may choose against their own advantage to assert their freedom. The novella is often read as an important precursor to existentialist literature, although the narrator’s views should not be treated as a straightforward statement of Dostoevsky’s own conclusions.

key_facts.text: The novella first appeared serially in 1864 in the Russian magazine *Epoch*.
The narrator calls himself sick and spiteful, says he has liver trouble, and refuses to consult a doctor out of spite.
Part I, “Underground,” is largely reflection; Part II, “À Propos of the Wet Snow,” recounts earlier events in the narrator’s life.
The narrator often contradicts himself, so readers cannot easily tell whether his philosophical claims are sincere or reliable.
His resistance to rational utopian schemes foregrounds a conflict between calculated self-interest and the desire to act freely.

overview.text: Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941), often called Gurudev, was a Bengali poet and creative polymath whose work included novels, short stories, plays, songs, painting, education, and philosophy. His poetry collection Gitanjali (Song Offerings) became widely known in an English version assembled from his translations of poems from several Bengali collections; it was central to the recognition that brought him the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature. Tagore also founded an experimental school at Santiniketan, where he sought to combine Indian and Western traditions. His song Jana Gana Mana was adopted as India’s national anthem in 1950, giving his writing and music a lasting place in the country’s public life.

key_facts.text: Tagore was born in Calcutta on May 7, 1861, and died there on August 7, 1941.
In 1913, he became the first non-European recipient of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
The English Gitanjali: Song Offerings gathered Tagore’s translations of religious poems from several Bengali collections, not just the Bengali book Gitanjali.
Tagore founded an experimental school at Santiniketan in 1901; it became Visva-Bharati University in 1921.
India adopted Tagore’s Jana Gana Mana as its national anthem on January 24, 1950.

overview.text: Neil Gaiman’s 2001 fantasy novel American Gods follows Shadow, recently released from prison, whose wife has died and who accepts work from the mysterious Mr. Wednesday. Gaiman’s synopsis frames their journey as part of a struggle for America’s soul. Blending reinvented deities, legends, mythic creatures, and folk heroes with an American setting, the novel asks how inherited stories and beliefs shape cultural identity. Its gods come from varied traditions and survive in the memories and stories of immigrants who brought them to the United States. Through this premise, the book explores American beliefs and contradictions, using supernatural conflict to examine the country’s culture.

key_facts.text: The novel was published in 2001; its opening setup has Shadow leaving prison after his wife’s death and meeting Mr. Wednesday, who offers him a job.
Its imagined gods come from varied traditions and persist in the stories, beliefs, and memories of immigrants who brought them to the United States.
The novel reworks deities, legends, mythic creatures, and folk heroes in an American setting, connecting mythology to questions about American culture and identity.
Gaiman’s website lists the novel as a winner of the Hugo, Bram Stoker, Locus, and Nebula awards.

overview.text: For Whom the Bell Tolls is Ernest Hemingway’s 1940 novel set during the Spanish Civil War. It follows Robert Jordan, an American volunteer aligned with the Republic, who is ordered to work with Spanish guerrillas to destroy a bridge. During the mission he falls in love with Maria and confronts the human risks of wartime action. Hemingway’s experience reporting from Spain informed the book, but its characters and plot are fiction. By joining a suspenseful military task with a love story and reflections on loyalty, courage, defeat, and the value of human life, the novel became a major work of war literature. Its title draws on John Donne’s Meditation XVII, used as the book’s epigraph.

key_facts.text: The novel was first published in 1940.
Jordan’s mission is to help guerrillas destroy a bridge; the operation gives the story its central wartime objective.
Hemingway reported on the Spanish Civil War, and his experience informed the novel.
The novel’s themes include war, love, loyalty, courage, and defeat.
The title comes from John Donne’s Meditation XVII, which is used as the novel’s epigraph.

overview.text: Ernest Hemingway’s *A Farewell to Arms* (1929) is a novel set on the Italian front during World War I. Its narrator, American ambulance volunteer Lieutenant Frederic Henry, looks back on his wartime experience and love for English nurse Catherine Barkley. Their relationship unfolds amid injury, military retreat, and loss. The novel draws on Hemingway’s own service as an ambulance driver and wartime injury, but its characters and events are fictionalized rather than a literal memoir. Its significance lies in joining a tragic love story to an unsentimental portrayal of war; Hemingway’s spare, restrained prose lets readers infer much that is left unstated.

key_facts.text: The novel was published in 1929.
Frederic Henry is an American serving with an ambulance unit in Italy; Catherine Barkley is an English nurse he meets during the war.
Hemingway’s ambulance service and injury in Italy informed the novel, but its story is described as fictionalized and semiautobiographical—not as a direct account of his life.
The National Archives describes the novel as a critique of war’s glorifying language and notes that its tragedy is not simply caused by combat.
Hemingway’s short, restrained prose and omissions—often associated with his “iceberg” approach—are key features of the novel’s style.

overview.text: Rudyard Kipling’s The Jungle Book is a collection first published in 1894, not a single continuous novel. Its central thread follows Mowgli, a human child raised by wolves in an imagined Indian jungle, learning its rules with help from the bear Baloo and panther Bagheera. Yet Mowgli is not the book’s only subject: the contents range from “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” in which a mongoose confronts cobras, to stories of a white seal and elephants. Poems and songs accompany the prose. This mixture of characters and forms is a defining feature; Mowgli’s unusual ability to move between human and animal worlds connects some stories, while others stand apart.

key_facts.text: The first edition was published by Macmillan and Co. in London and New York in 1894.
Mowgli is accepted into the Seeonee Wolf Pack; Baloo teaches him the Jungle Law, and Bagheera helps guide him.
The Mowgli stories are central, but the collection also includes independent animal tales such as “The White Seal,” “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” and “Toomai of the Elephants.”
In “Rikki-Tikki-Tavi,” a mongoose fights the cobras Nag and Nagaina to protect a family.
The book combines prose stories with poems and songs, including “Hunting-Song of the Seeonee Pack” and “Mowgli’s Song.”

overview.text: Hedda Gabler is a four-act play by Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen, published in 1890 and first performed in 1891. It is known as a psychological drama: rather than focusing only on outward events, it closely examines Hedda’s discontent and her attempts to influence the people around her. Newly married to Jørgen Tesman, Hedda becomes entangled in the fate of writer Eilert Løvborg and his manuscript. She secretly burns it, and later Judge Brack uses what he knows about a pistol to threaten her. As Tesman and Thea work to recreate the manuscript, Hedda sees her control slipping away and dies by suicide. The play’s tense relationships and focus on a complex central character distinguish it.

key_facts.text: The play has four acts; it was published in 1890 and first performed in 1891.
Hedda is General Gabler’s daughter and is newly married to Jørgen Tesman when the play begins.
Hedda burns Eilert Løvborg’s manuscript, which he had written with help from Thea Elvsted.
Judge Brack learns that Løvborg’s pistol belonged to Hedda’s father and plans to use this knowledge against her.
The play is described by Store norske leksikon as a psychological drama and a study of Hedda’s struggle to find meaning in life.

overview.text: Hikaru Genji, often translated as “Shining Genji,” is the fictional protagonist of Murasaki Shikibu’s early-eleventh-century Heian-period novel The Tale of Genji. In the story, he is born a son of Emperor Kiritsubo but gives up royal status and receives the surname Minamoto. Celebrated for his beauty, sensitivity, poetic talent, and romances, he represents an aristocratic ideal, while the narrative also explores complicated feelings and relationships. His life unfolds in the refined court society around Heian-kyō, today’s Kyoto; important relationships include those with his first wife, Aoi, and lifelong companion, Lady Murasaki. Genji is a literary creation, not a historical prince, and his central role makes him one of Japanese literature’s most memorable characters.

key_facts.text: “Hikaru Genji” means “Shining Genji”; the National Diet Library says his exceptional beauty earned him this name and the related title “Shining Prince.”
In the tale, Genji is the son of Emperor Kiritsubo, relinquishes royal status, and receives the surname Minamoto.
His poetic nature, gentleness, beauty, and romances make him an idealized figure in the story.
The tale’s settings include real places in and around Heian-kyō, the former capital now known as Kyoto.
Genji is fictional. The National Diet Library lists several possible historical inspirations, not one definitive real-life identity.

overview.text: Published in 1981, Nadine Gordimer’s *July’s People* is a South African political novel set in an imagined revolutionary crisis. When violence reaches the cities, white couple Bam and Maureen Smales and their children flee with help from July, their Black servant, who takes them to his village. Their dependence on July overturns the familiar employer-servant balance and brings racial power and strained relationships into focus. The story imagines a violent upheaval; it is not a record of how apartheid ended. The novel’s political fable probes what happens to identities and relationships when South Africa’s racial order is challenged. Gordimer received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1991.

key_facts.text: The novel appeared in 1981 and was Gordimer’s eighth novel; a literary scholar describes it as a psychological and political fable.
In the story, July shelters the Smales family in his village after violence drives them from South African cities.
As the family relies on July, the former employer-servant relationship shifts, highlighting racial and social power.
The title can refer both to July’s white employers and to his own Black family and villagers.
The imagined upheaval is distinct from South Africa’s actual transition: a chapter abstract notes that black majority rule was achieved in 1994.

overview.text: Jim Hawkins is the young central character and principal narrator of Robert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 adventure novel Treasure Island. He helps his widowed mother at the Admiral Benbow inn until the discovery of a pirate’s map draws him into an expedition aboard the Hispaniola. As cabin boy, Jim overhears Long John Silver’s mutiny plans while hiding in an apple barrel; once ashore, he encounters marooned Ben Gunn and repeatedly acts on his own, sometimes taking reckless risks. These experiences make Jim’s growth in judgment and independence central to the novel’s coming-of-age dimension. The British Library credits Jim’s adventures with helping popularize familiar pirate imagery, including parrots, rum, and treasure marked with an X.

key_facts.text: Jim’s story begins at the Admiral Benbow inn; a map found among Billy Bones’s belongings sets the treasure voyage in motion.
Aboard the Hispaniola, Jim hides in an apple barrel and overhears Silver’s plan for a mutiny.
The novel’s narration briefly shifts to Dr. Livesey during several chapters, then returns to Jim.
On the island, Jim meets Ben Gunn, who was marooned after an earlier unsuccessful search for the treasure.
The BBC describes Treasure Island as a coming-of-age novel, with Jim’s experiences shaping his character and outlook.
