overview.text: Astronomical distance describes how far a celestial object is from an observer and is fundamental to mapping the universe and determining objects’ intrinsic properties. Astronomers use the light-year—the distance light travels in a year—and the parsec, about 3.26 light-years. For nearby stars, parallax measures their apparent shift against background stars as Earth moves around the Sun: smaller shifts indicate greater distances. Beyond the reach of direct parallax, a calibrated “distance ladder” uses standard candles—objects whose known intrinsic brightness can be compared with how bright they appear. On cosmic scales, galaxy redshift interpreted through Hubble’s law also helps estimate distance, linking spectral shifts to the universe’s expansion.

key_facts.text: A light-year is the distance light travels in one year; one parsec equals about 3.26 light-years and corresponds to a parallax angle of one arcsecond.
As Earth orbits the Sun, nearby stars appear to shift against the distant background; the smaller the parallax, the farther the star.
A standard candle’s known intrinsic brightness can be compared with its apparent brightness to estimate its distance.
Cepheid variable stars are useful standard candles because their pulsation period is related to their luminosity.
Galaxy redshift measures shifts in spectral lines; interpreted with Hubble’s law, it can help estimate distance while reflecting the universe’s expansion.

overview.text: Soil is the natural material at Earth’s surface where rooted plants can grow. Unlike bare, unaltered rock, it contains mineral particles, organic matter, water and air, and it often has distinct layers called horizons. Its ingredients and properties vary from place to place: particle sizes such as sand, silt and clay influence texture, while climate, organisms, landscape and time help shape the soil. Living things in soil—including fungi, bacteria and animals—break down organic remains and cycle nutrients. Soil matters because it supports plant life and also helps regulate water flow, filter pollutants and provide habitat.

key_facts.text: Soil includes solid minerals and organic matter, plus liquid water and gases such as air.
Sand, silt and clay are mineral particle sizes that contribute to soil texture.
Soil forms through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, topography and time; these influences can produce distinct horizons.
Soil organisms, including fungi, bacteria, nematodes and earthworms, contribute to decomposition and nutrient cycling.
Soil helps sustain plants and animals, regulate water flow, and filter or buffer pollutants.

overview.text: Escherichia coli (E. coli) is a Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium commonly found in the lower intestine of warm-blooded animals. Most strains do not cause illness, but certain strains have traits that let them cause disease, including diarrhea; Shiga toxin-producing strains can sometimes lead to serious kidney complications. E. coli is also important in science and biotechnology: researchers can manipulate it readily, grow it quickly and inexpensively, and use its well-studied genetics and available laboratory tools to produce recombinant proteins. Its distinguishing significance is this contrast: the same bacterial species includes ordinary gut inhabitants, disease-causing strains, and laboratory strains useful for research and production.

key_facts.text: E. coli is a Gram-negative, facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium.
It commonly lives in the gastrointestinal tract, and most strains do not cause illness.
Disease-causing strains differ in their virulence traits; Shiga toxin-producing E. coli, particularly some O157 strains, can cause hemolytic uremic syndrome, which can damage the kidneys.
Certain extraintestinal pathogenic strains cause urinary tract infections; CDC reports that E. coli causes 80–90% of UTIs.
E. coli is widely used to produce recombinant proteins because it is relatively easy to manipulate and grow, and researchers have many compatible laboratory tools and strains.

overview.text: Crystals are solids distinguished by an ordered microscopic arrangement of particles that repeats in space; unlike amorphous solids such as glass, their internal structure has long-range order. A crystal’s pattern can be described by a tiny repeating building block called a unit cell, and the cell’s dimensions and symmetry help classify crystal systems. Their structure matters because it helps determine recognizable forms and properties, aiding mineral study and identification. For example, salt commonly forms cube-shaped crystals, while quartz and topaz have distinct crystal systems. A mineral’s color may change with small amounts of other elements without changing its characteristic crystal structure.

key_facts.text: A unit cell’s side lengths and angles describe the repeating pattern that builds a crystal lattice.
The USGS describes minerals as having an orderly internal structure and characteristic composition; rocks are aggregates of minerals or mineral matter.
Crystals contain imperfections: vacancies can help atoms diffuse, while line defects can affect mechanical strength.
Salt commonly forms cube-shaped crystals; the museum also shows diamond, muscovite, quartz, and topaz with different crystal systems.
Small amounts of other elements can change a mineral’s color, even when its characteristic crystal structure remains the same.

overview.text: The Pauli exclusion principle, named for physicist Wolfgang Pauli, is a rule of quantum mechanics first proposed in 1925 while scientists were working to understand atomic shells and the periodic table. It says that identical fermions—particles with half-integer spin, including electrons—cannot occupy the same complete quantum state. For electrons in atoms, a state is specified by four quantum numbers, including a spin value. As a result, an orbital can hold at most two electrons, and they must differ in spin. By limiting how electrons fill atomic shells and subshells, the principle helps explain the structure of atoms and the chemical patterns of the elements.

key_facts.text: Pauli proposed the principle in 1925 in the context of atomic shell completion and the periodic system.
The rule applies to identical fermions, which have half-integer spin; electrons and protons are examples.
For an electron in an atom, four quantum numbers specify its state; two electrons in the same orbital can differ in their spin projections.
The principle limits a subshell with orbital quantum number l to 2(2l + 1) electrons; for an s subshell, that means two.
The principle helps explain electron configurations and the resulting physical and chemical patterns among elements.

overview.text: Search algorithms are procedures that look through data or a possible solution space to find a target, decide it is absent, or identify a best option. For a list, linear (sequential) search checks entries one by one and works even when they are unsorted, but may inspect every entry. Binary search is faster on sorted data: it checks the middle and repeatedly discards the half that cannot contain the target, taking logarithmic rather than linear growth in the worst case. Searching also applies to graphs: pathfinding algorithms explore connections between places, and Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight routes when edge weights are nonnegative. These methods matter because the chosen procedure affects how much work a computer needs to solve a search task.

key_facts.text: Linear search checks a list from the beginning; if the target is absent, it must inspect all n entries.
Binary search requires sorted data. Each middle-value comparison lets it discard half of the remaining possibilities, so its worst-case work grows logarithmically with list size.
Dijkstra’s algorithm finds lowest-total-weight paths in a directed graph whose edge weights are nonnegative; “shortest” refers to the sum of weights, not necessarily the fewest edges.
Search procedures can report whether an item is present or absent, and the algorithm’s steps can be written as pseudocode before being implemented as code.

overview.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a research field within computer science concerned with building systems that perform tasks associated with intelligence, such as learning from experience, solving problems, recognizing patterns, planning, or working with language. It is not one particular kind of machine: AI includes approaches ranging from programs that use explicit logic and rules to machine-learning systems that improve through data. Machine learning is therefore a branch of AI, not a synonym for the whole field. The term was coined by computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955; a 1956 Dartmouth workshop helped establish the emerging field, though participants disagreed about how to create intelligent machines. AI can imitate selected abilities without necessarily thinking as people do.

key_facts.text: Computer scientist John McCarthy coined the term “AI” in 1955.
At a 1956 Dartmouth workshop, researchers named the emerging field artificial intelligence, but disagreed about how to build intelligent machines.
Machine learning is one part of AI: it studies how systems can improve their perception, decisions, or actions using experience or data.
Symbolic AI uses logic and rules to work with symbols; neural networks are a different approach, loosely inspired by brain structures.
Narrow AI focuses on particular tasks, while artificial general intelligence describes the aim of broadly capable, context-aware machines.

overview.text: Graphene is a form of carbon consisting of a single atomic layer in a repeating hexagonal, honeycomb-like arrangement. It is the basic building sheet of graphite: stacked layers make the material used in pencil cores. Unlike ordinary graphite, an isolated graphene sheet is only one atom thick, yet it is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well. Isolating and studying individual sheets helped establish research into two-dimensional materials. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov isolated graphene at the University of Manchester in 2004 by peeling layers from graphite with adhesive tape; their experiments on graphene received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

key_facts.text: Graphene is one layer of carbon atoms arranged in a honeycomb lattice.
It is a building block of graphite, the material used in pencil cores.
Geim and Novoselov isolated graphene at Manchester in 2004 using adhesive tape to peel layers from graphite.
Graphene is flexible and conducts heat and electricity exceptionally well despite being one atom thick.
The researchers’ graphene experiments were recognized with the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

overview.text: Lanthanides are a family of metals conventionally comprising the 15 elements from lanthanum (La, atomic number 57) through lutetium (Lu, 71), usually shown in a detached row beneath the periodic table’s main body. IUPAC prefers “lanthanoids” as the collective name, while recognizing the common inclusion of lanthanum. The 14 elements from cerium through lutetium are associated with progressive filling of the 4f sublevel; this distinction helps explain why descriptions of the series and the f-block boundary can differ. Lanthanides matter in technology: members are used in optical devices and alloys, and rare-earth elements are used in electronics and magnets.

key_facts.text: The commonly defined 15-element series spans atomic numbers 57–71, from lanthanum to lutetium.
The 4f sublevel is progressively filled across cerium–lutetium; lanthanum is included in the broader named series by common usage.
The series is commonly displayed as a separate row at the bottom of the periodic table.
Lanthanides are metals; examples of their uses include alloys, petroleum refining, and optical devices.
The EPA notes that rare-earth elements, including the lanthanides, are used in modern electronics and magnets.

overview.text: Protein folding is the process in which a newly made chain of amino acids takes on a particular three-dimensional shape. The chain’s amino-acid sequence influences that shape, while interactions among parts of the chain help it become compact and organized. Folding can begin while the chain is still being made and continue afterward. The resulting shape is important because it helps determine what the protein can do. Some proteins fold without assistance; others are helped by cellular proteins called chaperones, which can reduce incorrect folding or clumping. Folding is not simply a random search through every possible shape: proteins reach their structures through pathways shaped by their chemistry.

key_facts.text: A polypeptide is a chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds; folding may start during translation and continue afterward.
The amino-acid sequence helps specify a protein’s three-dimensional shape, though the chemical environment also matters.
In many proteins, water-avoiding (hydrophobic) amino-acid side chains tend to cluster inside, helping the chain become compact.
Some proteins fold spontaneously, while chaperones help others fold and can prevent them from aggregating.
A protein’s folded shape is important to its function; abnormal temperature or pH can interfere with correct folding.

overview.text: A submarine is a self-propelled watercraft designed to travel and operate underwater for extended periods. Its ballast tanks take in water to help it dive; compressed air expels that water to help it rise, while ballast adjustments and diving planes control depth and trim. Because its hull is windowless, a periscope can give the crew a limited view of the surface, though sonar and electronic sensors are also vital. Submarines have mattered as naval vessels and as vehicles for exploring the undersea world. They should not be confused with many small research submersibles, which make short excursions from a support ship.

key_facts.text: Flooding ballast tanks adds water and helps a submarine submerge; blowing water out with compressed air helps it surface.
Ballast adjustments and diving planes help control a submarine’s depth and trim while it is underwater.
A periscope provides a limited view outside the otherwise windowless hull; modern submarines also use sonar and electronic sensors.
Sonar lets a submarine detect sounds or echoes underwater, without needing to rise to periscope depth.
Submarines have served naval purposes and helped people explore underwater; many small research submersibles instead make short excursions from a support ship.

overview.text: A diode is a two-terminal electronic component designed to conduct much more readily in one direction than the other. In the common semiconductor version, doped p-type and n-type regions meet at a p–n junction, where a depletion layer helps control charge movement. Connecting the p-side to the positive supply and n-side to the negative supply forward-biases the diode and allows substantial current; reversing the polarity greatly reduces current, though practical diodes are not perfect one-way gates. This directional behavior makes diodes useful for rectifying alternating current in power supplies. A light-emitting diode (LED) is a specialized diode that emits light when forward-biased; its semiconductor material helps determine the light’s color.

key_facts.text: In a p–n junction diode, forward bias narrows the depletion layer; reverse bias widens it and strongly reduces current.
A real diode is not a perfect one-way switch: a small reverse leakage current can flow, and sufficiently high reverse voltage can cause breakdown.
Diodes have a nonlinear current–voltage response: forward current rises steeply as voltage increases, rather than following a resistor’s simple linear relationship.
A rectifier uses one or more diodes to convert alternating current into current of a single polarity; rectifier circuits are used in power supplies.
An LED is a diode designed to emit light when forward-biased; the semiconductor material affects the emitted light’s color.
This overview describes common semiconductor diodes; earlier diodes also included devices based on thermionic emission rather than a p–n junction.

overview.text: The Avogadro constant (Nₐ) is the exact conversion factor between amount of substance, measured in moles, and counts of specified entities: 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹. One mole therefore contains exactly that many entities, which may be atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, or specified groups; it matters to state what is being counted. The constant connects the particle counts used in chemistry to the amount of substance in a sample. It is one of seven SI defining constants, and fixing its value defines the mole. The name honors Amedeo Avogadro, but he did not invent the mole; that term appeared much later.

key_facts.text: Its symbol is Nₐ, and its exact SI value is 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
A mole contains exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ specified elementary entities.
Entities counted can include atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, or specified groups of particles.
The entity being counted should be identified precisely, for example by naming a molecule’s chemical formula.
The name commemorates Amedeo Avogadro, but the mole was not his invention; the term appeared nearly 1900.

overview.text: Chemical concentration describes how much of a chosen component—often a dissolved substance called a solute—is present relative to a specified amount of a mixture or solution. It helps chemists compare solution compositions and calculate amounts used in chemical reactions. Concentration can be described qualitatively as dilute or concentrated, or quantitatively using units with different denominators. Molarity (M) is moles of solute per liter of the entire solution; molality (m) is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Because solution volume can change with temperature, molarity may change as temperature changes, while molality, based on mass, does not. The denominator is the key distinction between these two units.

key_facts.text: Concentration expresses the relative amount of a component in a specified amount of solvent or solution.
Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution; its symbol is capital M.
Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent; its symbol is lowercase m.
Molarity can vary with temperature because solution volume changes; molality does not, since it uses mass.
Molarity can be used to calculate quantities in chemical reactions and solution calculations.

overview.text: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and one of the solar system’s two ice giants, with an interior rich in water, ammonia, and methane “ices”—unlike the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn. Its atmosphere is mostly hydrogen and helium, with methane that absorbs red light and gives the planet its blue-green color. Uranus’s extreme axial tilt—about 98 degrees—makes it rotate almost on its side, producing unusually long seasons. Faint rings and dozens of moons surround the planet. Its distinctive tilt, rings, and moon system make Uranus an important world for understanding the outer solar system, but it has been visited up close by only one spacecraft: Voyager 2.

key_facts.text: Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1781 and was the first planet discovered with the aid of a telescope.
Its axis is tilted about 98 degrees relative to its orbit; the cause is uncertain, though a major collision is one proposed explanation.
Methane in Uranus’s atmosphere absorbs red light, helping give the planet its blue-green appearance.
Uranus has 13 faint rings: nine inner rings and two outer rings, alongside narrow ring structures described by NASA.
Voyager 2 made the only spacecraft close approach to Uranus, in January 1986.
Uranus’s moons include five major ones—Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon—and are named mainly for characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.

overview.text: An unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), often called a drone, is an aircraft with no pilot aboard. It may be controlled remotely by a person on the ground or fly autonomously; “unmanned” does not mean that people are uninvolved. The Federal Aviation Administration distinguishes the aircraft from an unmanned aircraft system (UAS), which includes the equipment needed to operate it. UAVs are useful for scientific observation and other work in remote or hazardous places, where flying without an onboard pilot can reduce risks to people. Their tasks include observing Earth, surveying land and crops, supporting firefighting, and military reconnaissance. Designs range from radio-controlled models to aircraft built for long-duration research flights.

key_facts.text: A UAV has no onboard pilot; it can be remotely controlled or autonomous.
A UAS includes the unmanned aircraft and the equipment needed to operate it.
People may still operate, monitor, or support a UAV from the ground.
NASA examples include using unmanned aircraft for Earth observation, wildfire support, and surveying land or crops.
Unmanned aircraft have been used for research in hazardous flight conditions and for military reconnaissance.

overview.text: The Mohs scale ranks minerals by their resistance to scratching. Friedrich Mohs devised it in 1822, using ten reference minerals ordered from softest to hardest. In a scratch test, a harder mineral can scratch a softer one; comparing an unknown sample with known materials helps estimate its hardness and identify it, especially in the field. The numbers are ordinal, not equal measurement steps: each increase does not represent the same change in absolute hardness. The reference minerals range from talc (1), gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase feldspar, quartz, topaz and corundum to diamond (10), which is far harder than corundum.

key_facts.text: Talc is the softest reference mineral at 1; diamond is the hardest at 10.
The ten reference minerals, in order, are talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, orthoclase feldspar, quartz, topaz, corundum and diamond.
A mineral that scratches another is harder than the material it scratches; this comparison helps estimate an unknown mineral’s position.
The scale is useful for field identification because comparisons can be made with familiar objects such as a fingernail, penny or nail.
Mohs numbers are not evenly spaced measures: diamond is about four times harder than corundum.

overview.text: An mRNA (messenger RNA) vaccine gives some of the body’s cells temporary instructions for making a chosen antigen—a molecule the immune system can recognize. Unlike vaccines that supply a weakened or inactivated germ, mRNA vaccines supply the message for making an antigen. Cells use it to produce a harmless protein piece; immune defenses respond by making antibodies and activating other immune cells, while immune memory can help the body respond faster after later exposure. COVID-19 vaccines provide a familiar example: their mRNA directs cells to produce a piece of SARS-CoV-2’s spike protein. This approach trains immune defenses without requiring the vaccine to contain the whole virus.

key_facts.text: The mRNA carries instructions; it is not the antigen itself. Cells use the instructions to make a protein or protein piece for the immune system to recognize.
For COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the instructed protein piece comes from the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein.
After cells make the protein piece, they break down and remove the mRNA.
The immune response includes antibodies and other immune cells; immune memory can help the body respond faster if it encounters the same pathogen again.
Researchers have studied mRNA vaccine technology for decades, including for diseases beyond COVID-19.

overview.text: A glacier is a long-lasting mass of land ice—often mixed with snow, rock, and sediment—that forms where snowfall builds up faster than it melts. Gravity makes the ice flow downhill: ice crystals deform internally, and the glacier may also slide over or shear its bed. Debris trapped in the ice grinds and plucks rock, carving features such as U-shaped valleys and cirques. As ice melts, it leaves debris, including ridges called moraines, while meltwater can carry and sort sediment farther away. A glacier’s end can advance or retreat as its gains and losses change, but the ice continues to flow. Glaciers reshape terrain and store freshwater.

key_facts.text: Glaciers form where snow accumulation exceeds melting; accumulated snow is compressed into ice.
Glacier movement combines deformation within the ice with motion at its base, such as sliding or shearing sediment.
Abrasion grinds and scratches bedrock; plucking removes rock chunks that the ice can carry.
Moraines are piles of sediment deposited by glaciers; meltwater can transport and rework sediment as outwash.
A glacier’s terminus may retreat while its ice keeps flowing downhill; retreat happens when melting exceeds accumulation.

overview.text: Hydronium is the positively charged ion H₃O⁺: a water molecule that has accepted a proton. It is water’s conjugate acid, and water’s self-ionization is commonly represented as two H₂O molecules forming H₃O⁺ and OH⁻. Hydronium is important in aqueous acid–base chemistry because acids transfer protons to water, producing this ion. Through water’s leveling effect, an acid stronger than H₃O⁺ transfers its proton to water, making hydronium the strongest acid species ordinarily represented as persisting in water. Chemists often use H⁺(aq) as shorthand, but that notation does not mean a bare proton floats freely in water.

key_facts.text: Formula: H₃O⁺; it is a positively charged ion, or cation.
Hydronium is the conjugate acid of water: water accepts a proton to form H₃O⁺.
Water’s self-ionization is represented by 2 H₂O ⇌ H₃O⁺ + OH⁻.
In water, stronger acids transfer their protons to water; this leveling effect makes H₃O⁺ the strongest acid species in aqueous solution.
H⁺(aq) is commonly used as shorthand for hydronium, but it does not represent a free proton in water.

overview.text: Lithium (Li) is chemical element 3, a group 1 alkali metal and the lightest metal. At room temperature it is a soft, silvery solid with exceptionally low density, but it reacts vigorously with water; it occurs naturally in minerals and brines rather than as pure metal. Its standout modern role is in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries used in portable electronics and electric vehicles: lithium-containing electrolytes and compounds are part of cells that also contain other electrode materials. Lithium compounds are also used in specialty glass and ceramics, while lithium alloys can make some metals stronger and lighter. These applications make this lightweight element important to electronics and transport.

key_facts.text: Symbol Li; atomic number 3; located in group 1 of the periodic table.
A soft, silvery solid at room temperature, lithium is the least dense of the metals and reacts vigorously with water.
Lithium is found in nature in minerals and brines, not as pure metal.
Lithium-ion batteries are used in electronics and vehicles; their cells include lithium-containing electrolytes and other electrode materials.
Lithium compounds are used in glass and ceramics, and lithium alloys can help make metals stronger and lighter.

overview.text: Glucose is a simple sugar (a monosaccharide) with six carbon atoms and the formula C6H12O6. It is important because cells break it down during cellular respiration to make ATP, a usable form of energy. Plants make glucose and may join extra molecules into starch for storage; animals store glucose mainly as glycogen, while plants also use glucose units to build cellulose, a strong part of cell walls. In people, glucose carried in blood is called blood sugar: when its level rises, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps glucose enter cells. In water, glucose is usually in a ring-shaped form.

key_facts.text: Glucose is a six-carbon sugar, or hexose, and its chemical formula is C6H12O6.
Glucose is a monosaccharide—the single-unit sugar that can serve as a building block for larger carbohydrates.
Cells use energy released from glucose in cellular respiration to help make ATP.
Starch and glycogen store glucose; cellulose is made of glucose units and helps strengthen plant cell walls.
When blood glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, which helps glucose move into cells for energy.

overview.text: The Heisenberg uncertainty principle is a rule of quantum mechanics: for a particle, position and momentum cannot both have arbitrarily small uncertainties at once. In its standard form, ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2, where Δx and Δp describe the spreads in position and momentum, and ħ is the reduced Planck constant. A smaller spread in position requires a larger spread in momentum. This is not simply a problem with imperfect instruments; the limit is built into quantum theory and connected to matter’s wave-like behavior. German physicist Werner Heisenberg presented the principle in 1927. Its effects are important for atomic particles but generally unnoticeable for everyday objects.

key_facts.text: The principle applies to position and momentum, not just position and speed; momentum is mass times velocity.
The position–momentum relation is ΔxΔp ≥ ħ/2; the product of their uncertainties has a nonzero lower limit.
The uncertainty is not merely caused by faulty or imprecise measuring equipment; it is inherent in quantum mechanics.
Heisenberg presented the idea in 1927; the American Institute of Physics exhibit describes his work on it as arising amid debates over quantum theory.
The effect is significant for quantum particles but generally too small to notice in everyday macroscopic objects.

overview.text: The weak nuclear force, also called the weak interaction, is one of nature’s fundamental forces. Unlike the strong force, it does not bind protons and neutrons; instead, it can change a quark’s type, converting a neutron into a proton or vice versa. This makes it central to beta decay, in which a nucleus can change its number of protons and become a different element. The force is carried by the charged W boson and the neutral Z boson; their large masses give the interaction an extremely short range. It is also significant because electroweak theory connects the weak and electromagnetic forces as aspects of one interaction.

key_facts.text: In beta-minus decay, a neutron changes into a proton and the process produces an electron and an electron antineutrino.
The W boson carries electric charge; the Z boson is neutral.
The large masses of the W and Z bosons limit the weak force to an extremely short range—about 10⁻¹⁸ metres, according to CERN.
In the 1960s, Sheldon Glashow, Abdus Salam, and Steven Weinberg developed the theory connecting the weak and electromagnetic forces.
CERN reports that W and Z bosons were first observed in 1983, supporting a key part of the Standard Model.

overview.text: A volcanic eruption occurs when gases, rock fragments, and/or molten rock escape from within Earth through a vent. Molten rock underground is magma; after it reaches the surface, it is called lava. Eruptions range from relatively quiet outpourings of fluid lava to explosive blasts. Their style depends on magma’s composition, viscosity, gas content, and eruption rate: runny magma lets gas escape more easily, while sticky, gas-rich magma can build pressure and shatter into ash and larger fragments. Eruptions shape volcanic landforms, but lava, ash, hot fragment-laden clouds, and gases can threaten people and damage nearby areas. In major explosive eruptions, sulfur dioxide can form reflective sulfate aerosols high in the atmosphere, temporarily reducing sunlight and cooling climate.

key_facts.text: Magma is molten rock below Earth’s surface; once it erupts, it is called lava.
Effusive eruptions tend to produce lava flows or fountains with little ash; explosive eruptions can send large amounts of ash high into the atmosphere.
Magma composition, viscosity, gas content, and eruption rate help determine how explosive an eruption is.
Volcanic ash is made of small rock fragments; larger fragments may also be thrown out during explosive eruptions.
Large eruptions can send sulfur dioxide into the atmosphere, where it can form reflective sulfate aerosols that temporarily cool climate.

overview.text: Bone, also called osseous tissue, is hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Individual bones—such as the femur, ribs, and skull bones—support the body, provide levers moved by muscles at joints, and protect organs including the brain, heart, and lungs. Bone’s matrix combines collagen fibers with mineral crystals, giving it strength and some flexibility. Living bone is continually remodeled as bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts work in balance. Most bones contain dense compact tissue and lighter, lattice-like spongy tissue. Spongy bone can contain red marrow, which produces blood cells; marrow can also store fat. Bones additionally store and release minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus.

key_facts.text: Compact bone is organized into osteons, with central Haversian canals that carry blood vessels and nerves.
Spongy bone is a lattice of trabeculae; its spaces make bone lighter, and some contain red marrow.
Osteoblasts form bone, osteoclasts break it down, and osteocytes are mature bone cells; their activity helps maintain and remodel bone tissue.
Red marrow produces blood cells, while yellow marrow contains fat used for energy storage.
Bone stores minerals, especially calcium and phosphorus, and can release them into the bloodstream.

overview.text: Enrico Fermi (1901–1954) was a physicist born in Rome who later became a U.S. citizen. He combined mathematical theory with experiment, contributing to quantum and nuclear physics. In 1938, he received the Nobel Prize in Physics for research on new radioactive elements and nuclear reactions produced by slow neutrons. His 1926 statistical laws for particles governed by Pauli’s exclusion principle later gave their name to fermions, including electrons. In Chicago, Fermi led the team that built Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor; on December 2, 1942, it achieved the first human-made, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction. This milestone showed that a controlled chain reaction could be sustained, paving a path toward nuclear energy and weapons.

key_facts.text: Fermi was born in Rome in 1901, earned his doctorate in physics at the University of Pisa in 1922, and became a U.S. citizen in 1944.
He received the 1938 Nobel Prize in Physics for discoveries involving radioactive elements and nuclear reactions caused by slow neutrons.
His work included Fermi–Dirac statistics and a theory of beta decay, alongside research in nuclear and elementary-particle physics.
Fermi and his colleagues found that slowing neutrons could increase the production of radioactive elements in their experiments.
Chicago Pile-1 achieved its self-sustaining chain reaction beneath the University of Chicago’s Stagg Field on December 2, 1942.

overview.text: Crop rotation is the planned sequence of different crops grown on the same field over time. Instead of repeatedly planting one crop, farmers choose a sequence suited to their crops and local conditions. Changing crops can interrupt the spread of pests, diseases, and weeds that thrive when a preferred host is repeatedly available. Different crops also explore soil at different depths, helping use nutrients and water from varied layers. Including legumes such as peas or clover can add nitrogen to the farming system and benefit crops that follow. Rotation is one way to manage soil nutrients and support soil health, though the best sequence depends on the farm.

key_facts.text: A rotation is defined by the order of crops planted on the same field; it may extend across multiple seasons or years.
Changing crops can reduce pest, disease, and weed pressure, but pests that move widely may be harder to control through rotation alone.
Some legumes support nitrogen fixation, and legumes in a rotation can provide nitrogen for a following crop.
Crops with different rooting depths can draw on different soil layers; rotations can also help distribute water and nutrients through the soil profile.
Rotation plans should account for the crops and local conditions: the previous crop can affect later disease risks, soil fertility, and soil structure.

overview.text: Plague is an infectious disease of humans and other mammals caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which circulates naturally among wild rodents and their fleas. People most often become infected through flea bites, but contact with infected animal tissue and inhaling droplets from an infected animal or person can also spread it. Its forms include bubonic plague, which typically causes painful swollen lymph nodes called buboes; septicemic plague, which infects the bloodstream; and pneumonic plague, which affects the lungs. Only pneumonic plague is known to spread person to person through infectious respiratory droplets. Historically, plague was known as the Black Death during the fourteenth century. Antibiotics can treat plague when it is diagnosed promptly.

key_facts.text: Yersinia pestis circulates naturally among rodents and their fleas; infected flea bites are the most common way people get plague.
Bubonic plague commonly causes a tender, swollen lymph node called a bubo.
The main forms include bubonic, septicemic (bloodstream), and pneumonic (lung) plague.
Pneumonic plague can spread between people through infectious respiratory droplets; other forms are not spread person to person.
Plague was known as the Black Death during the fourteenth century, and antibiotics can be effective when treatment begins early.

overview.text: Laika was a small stray dog from Moscow, selected by Soviet scientists for an early spaceflight experiment. On November 3, 1957, she rode in a sealed cabin aboard Sputnik 2, becoming the first animal to orbit Earth. She was not the first animal in space: earlier flights carried animals beyond the atmosphere without putting them into orbit. Laika’s flight tested whether a living creature could endure spaceflight, as the Soviet program prepared for human missions. Sputnik 2 had no plan to bring her back, and NASA reports she likely survived only a few hours in orbit. Her historic flight was a milestone in space exploration, but one with a tragic outcome.

key_facts.text: Laika launched aboard Sputnik 2 on November 3, 1957, and became the first animal to orbit Earth.
She was a stray dog from Moscow; NASA describes her as a small mongrel.
Sputnik 2’s sealed cabin included air-regeneration and temperature-control equipment, food, and medical instruments.
The spacecraft had no reentry plan, and NASA says Laika likely survived only a few hours in orbit.
Earlier animals had reached space on suborbital flights, but Laika was the first to orbit Earth.

overview.text: Deuterium (hydrogen-2, written ²H or D) is a stable, naturally occurring but minor isotope of hydrogen. Its nucleus has one proton and one neutron; the most common hydrogen isotope, protium, has only a proton, so deuterium is roughly twice as massive. Its atomic mass is about 2.014, and its proportion varies among natural hydrogen sources. Deuterium is important in research: fusion scientists investigate combining it with radioactive tritium, a reaction that produces helium and an energetic neutron, as a possible route to future power. The isotope’s experimental identification in 1931 provided striking evidence that hydrogen, too, has isotopes.

key_facts.text: Deuterium is the minor stable isotope ²H; its symbol is D, and its listed atomic mass is about 2.014 Da.
A deuterium nucleus contains one proton and one neutron. The most common hydrogen isotope, protium, has one proton and no neutrons.
Deuterium’s natural abundance varies among hydrogen sources; CIAAW lists a range rather than one universal percentage.
Experiments reported in 1932 established hydrogen-2’s existence; Harold Urey, George Murphy, and Ferdinand Brickwedde identified its spectral lines in enriched samples.
Deuterium-tritium fusion is being investigated as a possible future energy source; the reaction produces helium and an energetic neutron.

overview.text: SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein (S) is a sugar-decorated protein projecting from the virus’s outer envelope. It forms a three-part assembly, and each part has an S1 region, which includes the receptor-binding domain (RBD), and an S2 region that helps fuse viral and cell membranes. The RBD shifts between tucked-down and exposed-up positions; the up position can bind ACE2, a receptor on human cells. After attachment and protein activation, S2 refolds to drive membrane fusion and viral entry. Spike’s essential role and surface exposure make it a key target of neutralizing antibodies and vaccines: mRNA vaccines instruct cells to make a harmless spike piece, prompting immune recognition.

key_facts.text: The spike is a trimer: three protein units form its projecting structure, and each unit contains S1 and S2 regions.
The ACE2-binding site is in S1’s RBD; moving into the exposed “up” position allows it to bind ACE2.
S2 helps fuse the virus and host-cell membranes, a step that enables viral entry.
Neutralizing antibodies can target spike; some block its interaction with ACE2, while others affect spike’s shape or activity.
COVID-19 mRNA vaccines instruct cells to make a harmless piece of spike, which prompts an immune response.

overview.text: A nebula (plural: nebulae) is a cloudlike concentration of interstellar gas—mostly hydrogen and helium—and dust. Some nebulae are stellar nurseries: gravity gathers cloud material, and young stars can reshape it while making new stars. Others are matter shed by dying stars or debris from supernova explosions, so nebulae help reveal different stages of stellar life. Their appearance reflects how they interact with light: emission nebulae glow after energetic starlight ionizes gas, reflection nebulae scatter nearby starlight, and dark nebulae obscure light behind them. “Planetary nebula” is a historical misnomer: these expanding shells come from aging stars, not planets. The range from star-forming clouds to stellar remains makes “nebula” a broad family, not a single object type.

key_facts.text: Nebulae are clouds in the interstellar medium, made chiefly of gas—mostly hydrogen and helium—and fine cosmic dust.
Emission nebulae glow when nearby stars energize and ionize their gas; the Orion Nebula is an example.
Reflection nebulae scatter nearby starlight, while dark nebulae block light from objects behind them.

Planetary nebulae are expanding shells of gas expelled by low- to medium-mass stars near the end of their lives; the name comes from their planetlike appearance in early telescopes, not a connection to planets.
A supernova remnant contains material from an exploded star and interstellar material swept up by the explosion; the Crab Nebula is one example.

overview.text: Melatonin is a hormone made by the pineal gland in the brain. It acts as a time signal linking the light–dark environment with the body’s internal clock: light information reaching the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) helps control its production, which normally increases after dark and falls in daylight. This daily pattern helps set the timing of circadian rhythms—roughly 24-hour cycles that shape sleep patterns and other bodily functions. Melatonin can signal readiness for sleep, but it is not an on/off switch required for sleep. The body’s natural hormone rhythm is distinct from melatonin taken as a supplement, whose usefulness depends on the condition.

key_facts.text: The pineal gland releases more melatonin at night as light entering the eyes diminishes; light exposure can reduce its production.
The SCN, a group of nerve cells in the brain, helps control melatonin production based on light information received from the eyes.
Circadian rhythms are roughly 24-hour cycles and influence sleep patterns, hormone release, appetite and digestion, and body temperature.
Melatonin signals the body to prepare for sleep, but it is not necessary for a person to sleep.
Melatonin supplements are distinct from the hormone naturally produced by the body; most supplements are made synthetically.

overview.text: A solid is a state of matter that typically keeps its own shape and volume instead of flowing to fit a container. Its atoms, ions, or molecules are close together and held near set positions; they can vibrate, but do not move freely past one another as liquid particles do. Solids are not all built alike: crystalline solids have an orderly repeating arrangement, while amorphous solids such as glass lack that repeating pattern. The arrangement and attractions between particles help determine properties: metals can bend and conduct heat and electricity, whereas many ionic solids are brittle. Solids can melt into liquids or, in some conditions, change directly into gas by sublimation.

key_facts.text: Solids generally have a definite shape and volume; unlike liquids, they do not take the shape of their container.
In the basic particle model, particles in a solid stay near set positions and vibrate rather than moving freely past one another.
Crystalline solids have a repeating particle pattern; amorphous solids, including glass, do not have that ordered internal structure.
Solids can have very different properties: metals such as copper conduct heat and electricity and are malleable, while ionic solids tend to be brittle.
A solid can become a liquid by melting or change directly into a gas by sublimation.

overview.text: A blackbody is an idealized object that absorbs all electromagnetic radiation falling on it, reflecting none; in thermal equilibrium it also emits radiation. Its emitted spectrum—the distribution of radiation across wavelengths—is determined by its temperature. A useful near-example is a tiny opening in a hollow cavity: incoming light bounces repeatedly inside and is unlikely to escape, so the opening behaves almost like a perfect absorber. As temperature rises, the spectrum’s peak shifts toward shorter wavelengths, helping astronomers estimate star temperatures. Explaining the blackbody spectrum led Max Planck in 1900 to propose that energy exchanges occur in discrete amounts, a key step toward quantum physics.

key_facts.text: A perfect blackbody absorbs all incident electromagnetic radiation; real materials only approximate this ideal.
A small hole in a cavity is a practical close approximation: light entering it reflects repeatedly inside the cavity.
The blackbody spectrum depends on temperature; as temperature increases, its peak moves to shorter wavelengths.
Astronomers can use the peak wavelength of a star’s radiation to estimate its temperature.
Planck’s explanation of the spectrum introduced energy exchanges in discrete amounts, helping lay groundwork for quantum physics.

overview.text: A tokamak is an experimental device for studying controlled nuclear fusion. Its name comes from a Russian acronym meaning “toroidal chamber with magnetic coils.” Inside its doughnut-shaped chamber, fuel becomes plasma, a hot, electrically charged gas. Magnetic coils create fields that guide the plasma around the torus; combined, these fields twist and help confine it away from the chamber walls. Researchers use tokamaks to investigate conditions needed for fusion, but the machines are research devices, not commercial power stations. Developed through Soviet research in the late 1950s, the design’s first machine, T-1, began operating in Russia in 1958.

key_facts.text: A torus is the doughnut-like shape of a tokamak’s plasma chamber.
The toroidal magnetic field runs the long way around the torus; a poloidal field runs the short way around it.
Together, these magnetic fields form a twisted field that confines charged plasma particles.
The first tokamak, T-1, began operation in Russia in 1958.
ITER is designed to study fusion plasma; it is not designed to convert its fusion heat into electricity.

overview.text: Talc is a naturally occurring hydrous magnesium silicate, a mineral rather than a product such as talcum powder. Its standout trait is extreme softness: it ranks 1 on the Mohs hardness scale, and its layered structure helps make it easy to crush or cut. Talc can feel greasy or soapy. In massive rock form, talc-rich material is called steatite; soapstone refers to an impure massive variety. Talc’s softness, whiteness, fragrance retention, and other useful properties have made it valuable both in familiar powders and in industry, including ceramics, paint, paper, and plastics.

key_facts.text: Talc is a hydrous magnesium silicate.
It has Mohs hardness 1; its layered structure contributes to its softness.
Talc may feel greasy or soapy, a useful clue to its identity.
Steatite is massive talcose rock; soapstone is an impure massive variety.
Talc is used in talcum powder and in industrial products such as ceramics, paint, paper, and plastics.

overview.text: The stratosphere is Earth’s second atmospheric layer, above the troposphere and below the mesosphere. It begins around 10 km above the ground at middle latitudes and reaches roughly 50 km, though its lower boundary shifts with location and season. Its ozone layer absorbs ultraviolet energy from the Sun, helping shield life at Earth’s surface and warming the surrounding air. As a result, temperature generally rises with altitude here—the opposite of the usual pattern in the troposphere. This temperature structure limits vertical mixing, making the stratosphere relatively stable; commercial passenger jets fly in its lower region partly to avoid turbulence.

key_facts.text: The tropopause is the stratosphere’s lower boundary; its upper boundary is the stratopause.
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, converting that energy into heat.
The stratosphere is much drier than the troposphere, so few clouds form there; polar stratospheric clouds are an exception.
The lower stratosphere is less turbulent than the troposphere, making it a route for commercial passenger aircraft.
Its lower boundary varies with latitude and season, ranging from about 7 km near the poles in winter to as high as 20 km near the equator.

overview.text: Proteins are large biological molecules built from one or more chains of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. The order of amino acids helps determine how a chain folds into a distinctive three-dimensional shape, which in turn helps determine what the protein does. Proteins carry out many essential jobs: some speed up chemical reactions as enzymes, while others provide structural support, transport substances, transmit signals, or help defend the body. Proteins also matter in nutrition: foods provide protein that the body uses to build and maintain tissues such as muscles, bones, and skin. Their varied shapes and jobs distinguish proteins from other major biological molecules.

key_facts.text: Amino acids are linked into protein chains by peptide bonds.
The amino-acid sequence helps determine a protein’s three-dimensional shape and specific function.
Protein roles include catalyzing reactions, providing structure, transporting substances, sending signals, and defending against foreign particles.
Proteins in foods help the body build and maintain bones, muscles, and skin.
OpenStax describes 20 common amino acids found in proteins; differences in their side chains give them different chemical properties.

overview.text: Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was a Serbian-American inventor and electrical engineer, born in Smiljan—then in the Austro-Hungarian Empire, now Croatia—to Serbian parents. He became known for developing polyphase alternating-current motors and related power-system technologies. Unlike direct current, Tesla’s AC system could support efficient transmission over long distances; its practical use helped electricity move from local generating stations to wider networks. A key feature was the induction motor: alternating current creates a rotating magnetic field that induces motion in the rotor. Working with George Westinghouse, Tesla’s patents helped put AC technology into practice, including at Niagara Falls. His lasting significance is his contribution—not sole invention—to the electrical infrastructure used today.

key_facts.text: Tesla was born in Smiljan in 1856 to Serbian parents and arrived in New York in 1884.
His notable contribution was developing polyphase AC motors and related technologies—not inventing alternating current itself.
In an induction motor, AC produces a rotating magnetic field that induces currents and motion in the rotor.
George Westinghouse bought Tesla’s AC-motor patents in 1888, helping bring the technology into commercial use.
The Niagara Falls generating station, opened in 1895, used two-phase AC techniques associated with Tesla and demonstrated long-distance transmission in practice.

overview.text: A nephron is the kidney’s microscopic functional unit: a connected renal corpuscle and renal tubule that filter blood plasma and adjust the resulting fluid to form urine. In the renal corpuscle, a tuft of capillaries called the glomerulus sits within Bowman’s capsule; water and small dissolved substances enter the tubule, while blood cells and most proteins remain in circulation. As filtrate travels through winding tubule sections—including the loop of Henle—needed water, salts, and nutrients are reabsorbed into nearby blood vessels, while some wastes and other substances are secreted into the tubule. This selective processing removes wastes and helps maintain the body’s fluid and mineral balance; each kidney contains roughly a million nephrons.

key_facts.text: The renal corpuscle includes the glomerulus, a capillary network, and Bowman’s capsule, which encloses the start of the tubule.
The tubule’s path includes the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule; the loop lies mostly in the kidney’s medulla.
Filtration lets fluid and small substances pass from glomerular blood into the tubule, while blood cells and larger proteins remain in the blood.
Tubules return much of the filtered water and useful nutrients and salts to the blood, and can secrete additional substances into the filtrate.
Each kidney has approximately one million nephrons; individual counts vary.

overview.text: A colloid is a mixture in which tiny particles or droplets of one substance remain spread through another, called the continuous phase. Its dispersed particles are larger than molecules or ions dissolved in a true solution, yet generally small enough not to settle like the larger particles in a suspension. Colloids may look uniform to the eye, but their components remain dispersed rather than forming a true molecular solution. Their particles can scatter light, making a beam visible through the mixture; this is the Tyndall effect. Colloids are useful to recognize because they occur in familiar materials, including milk, fog, paint, whipped cream, and gelatin.

key_facts.text: A colloid has a dispersed phase—the particles or droplets—and a continuous phase, the material they are spread through.
Colloidal particles are larger than particles in a true solution but smaller than those in a suspension; unlike suspension particles, they generally do not settle when left standing.
The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles, which can make a beam’s path visible; it can help distinguish a colloid from a true solution.
Milk is an emulsion, a type of colloid: butterfat is dispersed in water, with casein helping stabilize the mixture.
Colloids can take different forms: examples include fog (liquid droplets in gas), paint (solid particles in liquid), and whipped cream (gas in liquid).

overview.text: RNA, or ribonucleic acid, is a nucleic acid that helps cells use and regulate genetic information. It is made by copying DNA in transcription and is often—but not always—single-stranded; its four bases are adenine, uracil, cytosine, and guanine. RNA is not just a temporary message: messenger RNA (mRNA) carries protein-making instructions to ribosomes, transfer RNA (tRNA) delivers amino acids, and ribosomal RNA (rRNA) helps form ribosomes and catalyze protein assembly. Other RNAs regulate gene activity; for example, small interfering RNAs can guide the breakdown of matching mRNA, reducing protein production. This variety makes RNA central to gene expression and control.

key_facts.text: RNA is often single-stranded, but some RNA molecules are not; RNA contains the bases A, U, C, and G.
Ribosomes read mRNA in three-nucleotide units called codons to help assemble proteins.
tRNA folds into a distinctive L-shape; one end matches an mRNA codon, while another carries an amino acid.
In RNA interference, small interfering RNA (siRNA) guides a complex to matching mRNA, which can then be cleaved and degraded.
Other gene-regulating RNAs include microRNAs, which can block protein production, and long noncoding RNAs, which have varied regulatory roles.

overview.text: The Field Museum of Natural History is a Chicago museum where visitors explore Earth’s life, human cultures, and the past through exhibits, while scientists study and care for extensive collections. Its roots lie in objects from Chicago’s 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition: the museum opened in 1894 and was named for benefactor Marshall Field. Today its work spans anthropology, botany, geology, and zoology, connecting public learning with research and conservation. A standout specimen is SUE, a Tyrannosaurus rex discovered by Sue Hendrickson in South Dakota in 1990. With about 250 of roughly 380 T. rex bones, SUE is especially complete and gives researchers evidence about the dinosaur’s growth, biology, and behavior.

key_facts.text: The museum’s original collections included objects displayed at Chicago’s 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition; it opened to the public in 1894.
Its scientific work includes anthropology, botany, geology, and zoology, with research connected to conservation and public education.
SUE is named for Sue Hendrickson, who discovered the T. rex fossil in South Dakota in 1990.
The Field Museum describes SUE as about 90 percent complete, with 250 of approximately 380 known T. rex bones; the skull on display is a cast, while the real skull is displayed separately for study.
The Field Museum’s first home was the Palace of Fine Arts built for the 1893 World’s Columbian Exposition; that building later became the Museum of Science and Industry.

overview.text: Dark matter is the name for unseen matter inferred from its gravitational effects; scientists have not directly identified what it is. Unlike ordinary matter, it emits, absorbs, or reflects little to no electromagnetic radiation, but its mass affects how stars and galaxies move. Astronomers infer its presence from galaxy rotation speeds that visible matter alone cannot explain and from gravitational lensing, in which gravity bends light from more distant objects. Evidence accumulated after Fritz Zwicky’s 1933 study of the Coma Cluster and Vera Rubin’s later measurements of spiral galaxies. Dark matter is thought to help shape galaxies and larger cosmic structures. Its composition remains unknown, and it is distinct from dark energy.

key_facts.text: Dark matter is inferred from gravity rather than seen directly; it does not emit, absorb, or reflect light in the way ordinary matter does.
Stars far from the centers of spiral galaxies move faster than estimates based on visible matter alone would predict, providing evidence for additional unseen mass.
Gravitational lensing—distortion of background light by gravity—lets astronomers map mass in galaxies and clusters, including matter they cannot see.
Fritz Zwicky proposed unseen matter to explain the Coma Cluster’s motions in 1933; Vera Rubin’s later studies of spiral galaxies added strong evidence.
Dark matter and dark energy are different: dark matter’s gravity helps bind structures, while dark energy is associated with the universe’s accelerating expansion.

overview.text: Torque—also called the moment of force or turning moment—is how strongly a force tends to twist an object about a chosen pivot or axis. It is the rotational counterpart of force: net torque can change an object’s angular motion, while torques that cancel produce no angular acceleration. Its vector form is τ = r × F; its magnitude is rF sin θ, or force multiplied by the perpendicular lever arm. That is why a door is easier to open when pushed far from its hinges and at right angles. Torque’s SI unit is the newton-metre (N·m), not the joule, despite the units having equivalent dimensions.

key_facts.text: The position vector r runs from the pivot or axis to where the force is applied. The lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the force’s line of action.
Torque’s magnitude is τ = rF sin θ. A force parallel to the position vector produces no torque; a perpendicular force produces the greatest torque for the same force and distance.
Torque has direction as well as magnitude. In a three-dimensional description, the right-hand rule gives the direction of r × F; in a plane, the turning sense is clockwise or counterclockwise.
When several forces act, their torques about the chosen axis add to give the net torque. Zero net torque means zero angular acceleration.

For a given rotational inertia, a larger net torque produces a larger angular acceleration. Torque is measured in newton-metres (N·m); although that has the same unit dimensions as a joule, torque is not energy.

overview.text: Sodium chloride (NaCl), commonly called table salt, is an ionic compound in which sodium atoms transfer an electron to chlorine atoms, producing positively charged sodium ions and negatively charged chloride ions. These opposite charges attract, arranging ions in an alternating pattern that forms cubic crystals. In nature, sodium chloride occurs as the mineral halite. Salt seasons food and serves as an industrial raw material for making chlorine and caustic soda; rock salt is also spread on roads to reduce ice. Historically, salt helped preserve food through curing and became a valuable commodity, with access to deposits sometimes connected to trade and conflict.

key_facts.text: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, forming positive sodium ions and negative chloride ions that attract.
Sodium and chloride ions alternate in salt crystals, which have a cubic shape.
Halite is the mineral form of sodium chloride (NaCl).
Salt is used to season food, deice roads, and manufacture chlorine and caustic soda.
Salt curing helped preserve food, and historical accounts describe disputes over access to salt deposits.

overview.text: Melanin is a pigment made by melanocytes, specialized pigment-producing cells. It contributes color to skin, hair, and eyes, and is also present in the retina, where it has a role in normal vision. Human melanocytes make two forms, eumelanin and pheomelanin; their relative amounts help shape skin and hair color, with eumelanin associated with brown or black hair and darker skin, and pheomelanin with red or blond hair, freckles, and lighter skin. Eumelanin helps protect skin from ultraviolet damage, while melanin absorbs some harmful rays. Sunlight can stimulate extra melanin production and darken skin, but this protection is incomplete.

key_facts.text: Melanocytes are specialized cells that produce melanin.
Eumelanin and pheomelanin are two forms of melanin; their relative amounts help determine skin and hair color.
Melanin contributes to skin, hair, and eye color; it is also found in the retina, where it plays a role in normal vision.
Eumelanin helps protect skin from UV damage, but melanin does not provide complete protection from the sun.
Sunlight can cause skin to produce more melanin, making it darker; the resulting tan fades as skin cells are replaced.

overview.text: Transition metals are metallic elements in the central d-block of the periodic table, commonly shown in groups 3–12. The label has a qualification: a stricter electronic definition requires an incompletely filled d subshell in an atom or one of its ions, so group 12 is sometimes excluded. Their d electrons help many of these metals adopt more than one oxidation state and bind surrounding atoms or ions called ligands, forming coordination complexes. These flexible combinations give transition-metal chemistry unusual variety: complexes can differ in shape and stability and may show vivid colors or magnetism. Transition metals are therefore versatile building blocks in inorganic chemistry.

key_facts.text: The usual periodic-table grouping places transition metals in groups 3–12; a stricter d-electron definition can exclude group 12.
Many transition metals occur in several stable oxidation states; iron commonly forms +2 and +3 ions.
A coordination complex has a central metal atom or ion surrounded by attached atoms or ions called ligands.
Transition-metal complexes can display color and magnetism; these properties depend on their electronic structure and metal–ligand interactions.

overview.text: CPU cache memory is a small, high-speed store near the processor that keeps data and instructions a program may use again, helping avoid some slower trips to main memory. It matters because cached information can reach the processor more quickly, improving performance. Cache designs take advantage of locality: recently used information may be needed again soon, and nearby memory locations may be needed next. Many processors arrange caches in levels: L1 is typically closest, smallest, and fastest; L2 and L3 are generally larger and slower, though designs vary. A hit means the requested data is present; a miss sends the request onward, often to main memory. Caches commonly transfer data in blocks called cache lines.

key_facts.text: Three cache levels—L1, L2, and L3—are common, but some processors use a different arrangement. L1 is typically the smallest and fastest level, closest to the processor.
A cache hit occurs when requested information is already cached; a miss means the processor must request it from a slower level, such as main memory.
Caches exploit temporal locality (information used recently may be needed again) and spatial locality (nearby memory locations may be accessed soon).
Caches transfer data in blocks, often called cache lines, so a request for one location can bring nearby information into the cache too.
L1 caches commonly keep instructions and data in separate sections, because programs access them in different patterns.

overview.text: The octet rule is a useful bonding guideline: many main-group atoms form ions or covalent bonds in ways that give them eight electrons in their outer (valence) shell, like a noble gas. In ionic bonding, electrons may be transferred; in covalent bonding, shared electron pairs count for both atoms. Chemists use Lewis dot symbols and structures to track these electrons and predict common bonding patterns, especially for many lighter nonmetals. The rule is not universal: hydrogen is usually stable with two electrons, boron compounds such as BF₃ can leave boron with six, and PCl₅ can be drawn with ten around phosphorus. Such cases show why it is a guide, not a law.

key_facts.text: The rule describes a tendency for main-group atoms to form enough bonds to reach eight valence electrons.
Lewis symbols show valence electrons as dots; Lewis structures show bonding pairs and lone pairs.
Hydrogen is a common exception: its first shell is filled with two electrons.
In BF₃, boron has an incomplete octet, with six electrons around it in the Lewis structure.
Exceptions include incomplete octets, odd-electron molecules, and expanded octets; in the Lewis structure of PCl₅, phosphorus has ten electrons around it.

overview.text: Ferromagnetism is a form of magnetism found in materials such as iron, cobalt, and nickel. Quantum-mechanical interactions make neighboring atomic magnetic moments—arising partly from electron spins—align within small regions called domains. In an unmagnetized piece, domains point in different directions, so their effects largely cancel; an applied field can shift and reorient domains, creating strong net magnetization. Ferromagnetic materials can retain magnetization after the field is removed. This history-dependent response is called hysteresis and makes magnetic recording possible. Ferromagnetism disappears above a material-specific Curie temperature, when thermal motion disrupts long-range magnetic order.

key_facts.text: Within each magnetic domain, many atomic magnetic moments align in the same direction; a domain therefore has a net magnetic moment.
A bulk ferromagnetic object can have little net magnetization when its domains point in different directions, even though each domain is magnetized.
An applied magnetic field can reorient domains and enlarge those pointing with the field, producing strong net magnetization.
Hysteresis means magnetization depends on the material’s magnetic history; some magnetization can remain after the applied field is removed.
Above a material’s Curie temperature, ferromagnetic order disappears; iron, cobalt, and nickel are examples of ferromagnetic elements.

overview.text: Sharks are a diverse group of cartilaginous fishes in class Chondrichthyes, related to rays and skates; the great white, also called the white shark, is just one species. Their skeletons are made mainly of cartilage rather than bone, and most sharks have five separate gill slits on each side (some have six or seven). Many have several rows of teeth that are continually replaced. Their senses include a lateral line that detects water movement and ampullae of Lorenzini—sensory pores that detect weak electric fields, useful for finding concealed prey. Many sharks are predators that help shape marine food webs, but shark species differ greatly in size, diet, habitat, and behavior.

key_facts.text: Sharks, rays, and chimaeras belong to the cartilaginous-fish class Chondrichthyes; a shark’s skeleton is made mainly of cartilage.
Most sharks have five gill slits on each side of the head, while some species have six or seven.
Sharks continually shed and replace teeth; tooth shapes vary with what different species eat.
The lateral line senses water movement, while ampullae of Lorenzini detect weak electric fields that can help sharks find hidden prey.
Shark skin is covered in tiny scales called dermal denticles, which reduce drag as the shark moves through water.
Sharks are predators that can help keep prey populations in check, contributing to the ecological balance of their environments.

overview.text: A dwarf planet is a Sun-orbiting body massive enough for gravity to make it nearly round. It has not cleared its orbital neighborhood of similarly sized objects and is not a moon. The International Astronomical Union (IAU) created this separate category in 2006, distinguishing dwarf planets from the eight planets by their orbital surroundings rather than by small size alone. The change classified Pluto as a dwarf planet after discoveries of similar distant worlds. NASA lists five recognized dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris; Ceres is the only one in the inner solar system.

key_facts.text: Under the IAU’s 2006 definition, a dwarf planet orbits the Sun, is nearly round, has not cleared its orbital neighborhood, and is not a satellite.
NASA’s dwarf-planet overview lists Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, and Eris as the five recognized examples.
Ceres is in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter and is the only dwarf planet in the inner solar system.
Ceres was discovered in 1801, first classified as a planet, later as an asteroid, and designated a dwarf planet in 2006.
The IAU’s 2006 resolution established dwarf planets as a class distinct from planets and identified Pluto as an example.

overview.text: Atoms are tiny building blocks of ordinary matter, and their structure helps identify elements and distinguish isotopes and ions. Each has a compact central nucleus containing positively charged protons and, in most atoms, neutral neutrons; negatively charged electrons occupy the space around it. An atom’s proton count, called its atomic number, determines its element. Atoms of the same element can have different neutron counts and thus be different isotopes. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, but gaining or losing electrons makes it electrically charged—an ion—without changing its proton-defined element. The nucleus is extremely small relative to the whole atom.

key_facts.text: Protons are positive, neutrons have no electric charge, and electrons are negative.
Protons and neutrons are in the nucleus; electrons are outside it.
The atomic number is the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus and identifies its element.
Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons; gaining or losing electrons forms an ion.

overview.text: The strong interaction (strong force) is a fundamental interaction of the Standard Model, described by quantum chromodynamics (QCD). At the smallest scales, it acts on quarks and gluons: gluons carry the interaction, and it binds quarks into protons, neutrons, and other hadrons. Its distinctive color charge is a physics label, not visible color; quarks and gluons are confined inside composite particles rather than found alone in ordinary matter. A residual effect of this interaction also binds protons and neutrons into atomic nuclei, counteracting the electrical repulsion between positively charged protons. Unlike a simple long-range pull, its behavior varies with distance, becoming weaker at very short quark separations.

key_facts.text: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD) is the theory that describes the strong interaction.
Gluons carry the strong interaction, which binds quarks into protons, neutrons, and other composite particles.
A residual effect of the interaction binds protons and neutrons in nuclei, helping overcome the electrical repulsion between protons.
“Color” names a type of charge in this theory; it does not mean that quarks or gluons have visible colors.
The interaction’s strength depends on distance: it is weaker at very short quark separations and stronger as quarks are pulled farther apart.

overview.text: ʻAʻā (pronounced “ah-ah”) describes a rough-surfaced form of lava flow, especially familiar from basaltic volcanoes. Its top is broken into sharp, jagged chunks called clinkers, unlike the smoother, often rope-like crust of pāhoehoe. The contrast is more than a difference in appearance: ʻAʻā’s surface breaks apart under strain as the flow moves, while its interior can remain dense and massive. Greater viscosity, faster flow or a higher rate of lava discharge can favor ʻAʻā, and a flow may change from pāhoehoe to ʻAʻā as it cools and loses gas. Geologists use these textures to learn about conditions during a flow’s movement.

key_facts.text: ʻAʻā is a Hawaiian term; USGS gives its pronunciation as “ah-ah.”
The jagged surface fragments are called clinkers; they form a rubbly layer over the flow’s denser interior.
Pāhoehoe is the useful contrast: it usually has a smoother, billowy or rope-like surface.
Flow texture depends on physical conditions such as viscosity, strain and discharge rate; the two forms need not have significantly different composition.
A flow can begin as pāhoehoe and transition to ʻAʻā as it cools or conditions change.

overview.text: Vitamin D, also called calciferol, is a fat-soluble vitamin with two main sources: certain foods and supplements, and vitamin D₃ made in the skin after exposure to ultraviolet light. Before the body can use it fully, it is converted first in the liver and then mainly in the kidneys. Its key role is helping the intestine absorb calcium; it also helps maintain phosphate levels needed for normal bone growth and mineralization. Too little vitamin D can weaken bones and cause rickets in children or osteomalacia in adults. The two main forms are D₂ (ergocalciferol) and D₃ (cholecalciferol); some foods, including milk in the United States, are fortified with it.

key_facts.text: Vitamin D is fat-soluble and is also known as calciferol.
Ultraviolet light can trigger vitamin D production in the skin; the amount produced varies with factors such as season and skin pigmentation.
Vitamin D helps the gut absorb calcium, supporting normal bone formation and mineralization.
The two main forms in foods and supplements are D₂ (ergocalciferol) and D₃ (cholecalciferol).
In the United States, most milk is fortified with vitamin D; few foods naturally contain much of it.

overview.text: Ultraviolet (UV) radiation is electromagnetic energy with wavelengths shorter than visible light but longer than X-rays. The World Health Organization defines its range as 100–400 nanometers; humans cannot see it. UV occurs naturally in sunlight and can also come from artificial sources. Scientists divide it into UVA, UVB, and UVC bands. As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, ozone and other gases absorb all UVC and most UVB, so the UV that reaches the ground is mainly UVA with some UVB. This makes the ozone layer an important shield, not a complete barrier. UV exposure can harm skin and eyes, and excessive exposure is associated with sunburn, skin cancers, cataracts, and immune-system effects.

key_facts.text: UV is invisible to humans and occupies the part of the electromagnetic spectrum between visible light and X-rays.
The bands are commonly defined as UVA (315–400 nm), UVB (280–315 nm), and UVC (100–280 nm).
Sunlight and artificial sources—including some lamps and tanning devices—produce UV radiation.
The atmosphere absorbs all UVC and most UVB from sunlight; UVA is less affected, so surface UV is mainly UVA with a smaller UVB component.
UVB can damage DNA; excessive UV exposure is associated with skin cancer and eye damage, including cataracts.

overview.text: Ants are insects in the family Formicidae and order Hymenoptera, which also includes bees and wasps. Typical ants have elbowed antennae and a narrow, pinched waist; most workers are wingless. A defining feature is cooperation within colonies: queens reproduce, while female workers typically gather food, care for young, maintain nests, or defend them. Ants communicate through chemical signals, and their coordinated behavior can make a colony function like a “superorganism.” Ants are ecologically varied: some harvest seeds or prey on other animals, while leafcutter ants grow fungus gardens for food, and some species protect aphids and feed on their honeydew.

key_facts.text: Ants belong to the family Formicidae and the insect order Hymenoptera.
Elbowed antennae and a constricted waist are useful features for recognizing ants.
In typical colonies, queens reproduce and female workers do jobs such as foraging, caring for young, nest-building, and defense. Workers—not the queen—decide which tasks to perform.
Ants use chemical signals, including pheromones, to communicate and coordinate activities.
Leafcutter ants bring plant material to underground gardens, where they grow fungus for food.
Some ants protect aphids and other honeydew-producing insects, then feed on their sugary secretion.
