overview.text: Eyes are sensory organs that begin vision by collecting light; seeing also depends on the brain, which interprets signals sent from each retina. Light first passes through the clear cornea, which helps focus it; the pupil is the opening that admits light, while the iris adjusts its size. Behind it, the clear lens further focuses light onto the retina, a light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eyeball. Retinal photoreceptors convert light into electrical signals, carried along the optic nerve to the brain. The macula supports central vision, and its fovea is where vision is sharpest.

key_facts.text: The cornea is the clear, dome-shaped covering at the front of the eye and helps focus light.
The pupil is an opening in the iris; the iris changes its size to regulate how much light enters.
The lens sits behind the iris and focuses light on the retina, helping the eye focus on near and far objects.
Retinal receptor cells called rods and cones respond to light and send electrical impulses through the optic nerve to the brain.
The macula is a retinal area needed for central vision; its center, the fovea, is where vision is sharpest.

overview.text: The Van Allen radiation belts are two broad, doughnut-shaped zones of energetic charged particles held around Earth by its magnetic field. The particles follow magnetic field lines, bouncing between northern and southern regions; the belts are not solid rings but changing populations of trapped radiation. Typically there is an inner belt and a more variable outer belt, with protons and electrons present in different proportions. Explorer 1 and Explorer 3 detected trapped radiation in 1958, and follow-up spacecraft helped reveal the outer belt. The belts matter because energetic particles can disrupt or damage spacecraft electronics, so scientists study them to understand near-Earth space and protect satellites. Brief extra belts can sometimes appear during space-weather disturbances.

key_facts.text: Earth’s magnetic field traps charged particles in two belts that generally have a doughnut-like shape.
Particles travel along magnetic field lines, bouncing between polar regions.
Explorer 1 and Explorer 3 detected trapped radiation in 1958; later spacecraft helped identify the outer belt.
The belts’ energetic particles can damage spacecraft electronics, making the region important for satellite design and space research.
The two main belts are not the only possible arrangement: a temporary third ring was observed in 2012 and lasted about a month.

overview.text: A wave is a traveling disturbance that carries energy from one place to another; in many waves, the material involved oscillates around its usual position rather than traveling along with the disturbance. Waves include sound, ripples on water, earthquakes, and light. Mechanical waves, such as sound, need a substance called a medium to travel through, while electromagnetic waves, including light, can cross empty space. Waves are distinguished by how their disturbance moves: in a transverse wave it is perpendicular to the direction the wave travels, and in a longitudinal wave it is parallel. Some waves combine both kinds of motion.

key_facts.text: Waves transfer energy, but mechanical waves generally do not carry the medium’s material along with them; its particles oscillate around equilibrium.
Sound and water waves are mechanical waves that require a medium; electromagnetic waves such as light do not.
Transverse disturbances move perpendicular to wave travel; longitudinal disturbances move parallel to it. Sound in air is longitudinal.
Amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium; wavelength is the distance between matching points, such as consecutive crests.
Frequency counts cycles passing a point per unit time; it is the inverse of period and is commonly measured in hertz (Hz).

overview.text: Aluminum (Al; aluminium is an alternate spelling) is chemical element 13, a silvery-white, lightweight metal and the most abundant metal in Earth’s crust. It is rarely found as a pure metal in nature, so industry obtains it from bauxite: the Bayer process refines the ore into alumina, then the Hall–Héroult process uses electrolysis of alumina dissolved in molten cryolite to make aluminum. Its low density, ability to be shaped into thin sheets or wires, electrical conductivity, and resistance to corrosion make it useful in foil and cans, electrical lines, buildings, vehicles, and aircraft. Because pure aluminum is relatively soft, many structural parts use stronger aluminum alloys.

key_facts.text: Its chemical symbol is Al, and its atomic number is 13.
Aluminum is abundant in Earth’s crust but is usually bound in minerals rather than occurring as free metal.
Aluminum is malleable and ductile; its low density and corrosion resistance help make it useful in many applications.
Foil, cans, electrical transmission lines, building components, and aircraft parts are among its uses.
Primary production involves refining bauxite into alumina with the Bayer process, then using electrolysis in the Hall–Héroult process.

overview.text: Spiders are arachnids in the order Araneae. Unlike insects, they have eight legs, two main body regions, and no antennae. They are predators, but they do not all hunt alike: some wait in webs, while others ambush or chase prey. All spiders produce silk from spinnerets near the rear of the abdomen; webs are only one use, alongside egg coverings, shelters, and safety draglines. Orb webs, a familiar design, have radiating support threads and spiral capture threads, but spider webs take many forms. By capturing insects through varied hunting strategies, spiders play a useful role in ecosystems.

key_facts.text: Spiders belong to the arachnid order Araneae; arachnids also include mites, ticks, and scorpions.
A spider’s body has two main regions and eight legs; unlike insects, spiders have no antennae.
All spiders produce silk, but not all build webs to catch prey; jumping spiders can pursue prey, and crab spiders can ambush it.
Spinnerets on the abdomen produce silk, which can harden in air and serve uses such as egg cases, shelters, draglines, and webs.
Orb webs use radiating threads and spiral threads; other web designs include tangles, sheets, and spring traps.

overview.text: Velocity describes how an object's position changes over time. Average velocity is displacement—the vector from the starting position to the ending position—divided by elapsed time, not total path length divided by time. Because velocity is a vector, it includes both magnitude and direction; speed is its magnitude and does not specify direction. Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a particular moment. Along a curved path, its direction is tangent to the path. Velocity is commonly measured in meters per second (m/s), and a change in either speed or direction changes velocity.

key_facts.text: Average velocity equals displacement divided by elapsed time: v_avg = Δx/Δt.
Velocity is a vector, so a complete description includes direction; speed is scalar and gives only magnitude.
Average velocity can be zero on a round trip even when the traveler covers a nonzero distance, because the final position matches the starting position.
Instantaneous velocity describes motion at a specific moment; it equals average velocity over an interval when velocity is constant.
For motion along a curved path, the instantaneous velocity vector points tangent to the path.

overview.text: Mercury (Hg), atomic number 80, is a naturally occurring metal distinguished by being liquid at ordinary room temperatures: it freezes at about −38.8 °C, so it stays liquid around 20 °C. Its shiny silver appearance and high density (about 13.5 g/cm³) make it recognizable; its old name, quicksilver, reflects its silvery, flowing look. Mercury is historically important because its ability to form amalgams with gold helped recover gold from ores, and liquid mercury was used in thermometers and electrical devices. It is seldom found as free metal in nature; it is chiefly obtained from cinnabar ore. Elemental mercury can evaporate into harmful vapor, while methylmercury and other compounds are chemically different forms with distinct exposure risks.

key_facts.text: Mercury’s chemical symbol is Hg and its atomic number is 80.
It is a silvery liquid at 20 °C; its melting point is about −38.8 °C and its density is about 13.53 g/cm³.
Mercury rarely occurs uncombined in nature; cinnabar, or mercury sulfide, is a principal ore.
Mercury forms amalgams with metals such as gold; this property has been used to recover gold from ores.
Elemental mercury can evaporate into toxic vapor. Methylmercury is a different chemical form, so mercury’s health effects depend in part on which form is involved.

overview.text: Python is a general-purpose programming language: people use it to give computers instructions, build programs, and automate tasks. Guido van Rossum began creating it in December 1989 as a language influenced by ABC; he chose “Python” as a working title while a fan of the comedy show Monty Python’s Flying Circus. A defining feature is that indentation—the spaces at the start of a line—groups related statements into code blocks. Van Rossum said this design helps make programs more readable. Python is interpreted and has an extensive standard library, along with third-party modules, giving programmers ready-made tools for many kinds of projects.

key_facts.text: Python’s creator, Guido van Rossum, started the project in December 1989 and named it after Monty Python’s Flying Circus, not the snake.
Python is a high-level, general-purpose programming language that supports several programming styles, including object-oriented, procedural, and functional programming.
Indentation determines how Python groups statements; inconsistent indentation can cause an error.
Python’s interpreter runs code, and the language’s extensive standard library supplies modules for common tasks; programmers can also use third-party modules.
Van Rossum said indentation reduces visual clutter and encourages a more uniform style, helping people read one another’s code.

overview.text: Stephen Hawking (1942–2018) was an English theoretical physicist and cosmologist whose research explored gravity, black holes, and the universe. Working with Roger Penrose, he used mathematics and Einstein’s theory of general relativity to study singularities—points where that theory breaks down—and the implications for the universe’s beginning. In 1974, Hawking proposed that black holes emit radiation, now called Hawking radiation; over time, this process can make them lose energy. His 1988 book A Brief History of Time introduced questions about the universe’s origin and fate to a broad readership. After an operation took away his natural speaking voice, a computer speech synthesizer became his distinctive means of communication.

key_facts.text: With Roger Penrose, Hawking developed mathematical work on singularities in general relativity; their results connected the theory to the universe’s beginning.
Hawking radiation is a theoretical prediction: black holes can emit radiation and gradually lose energy.
Hawking’s book A Brief History of Time, published in 1988, explained cosmology—the study of the universe—to general readers.
He was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the University of Cambridge from 1979 until 2009.
After a tracheotomy in 1985, Hawking lost his ability to speak; speech-synthesis software later enabled him to communicate with a computer-generated voice.

overview.text: Codebreaking, or cryptanalysis, analyzes codes and ciphers to defeat their protection and recover concealed information, sometimes without knowing the key. It is distinct from cryptography, which creates protective systems. Codebreakers may combine intercepted signals, clues about likely message wording, language skills, and tools for testing possible cipher settings. During World War II, teams at Britain’s Bletchley Park broke German, Italian, and Japanese ciphers, including German Enigma systems. The intelligence they produced contributed significantly to the Allied effort, showing how deciphering secret communications can affect military decisions.

key_facts.text: NIST describes cryptanalysis as attempting to defeat cryptographic protection without initially knowing the key.
Cryptography makes codes and ciphers; cryptanalysis attempts to break them.
Bletchley Park’s guide outlines steps including intercepting radio signals, working out how messages were encrypted, deciphering them, and using the results to build intelligence.
Bletchley Park codebreakers used clues about possible message wording to help machines check likely Enigma settings.
Bletchley Park’s wartime codebreaking grew into a large intelligence operation whose work provided vital intelligence and contributed significantly to Allied victory.

overview.text: Mass spectrometry (MS) is a family of analytical methods used to study what a sample contains. In a typical experiment, molecules are turned into gas-phase ions, separated according to their mass-to-charge ratios, and detected. The resulting mass spectrum displays signals from the detected ions; scientists use its peaks to investigate the masses and composition of substances. Different instruments and ionization methods suit different samples, so MS is not one single machine or procedure. It is significant in fields including chemistry and materials science, and can help identify components in complex mixtures. When paired with gas chromatography, it can analyze mixtures by separating their components before mass analysis.

key_facts.text: A mass spectrometer’s core tasks are creating ions, separating them by mass-to-charge ratio, and detecting them.
A basic mass spectrum plots detected-ion counts against mass-to-charge ratio.
Ionization methods include MALDI, which uses laser energy, and electrospray, which uses a strong electric field.
In gas chromatography–mass spectrometry, the mixture is separated into components before ions are analyzed; the resulting patterns can help identify its chemical makeup.
Early mass-spectrometry research provided the first evidence for stable, nonradioactive isotopes.

overview.text: The Higgs boson is an elementary particle associated with the Higgs field, a quantum field thought to fill space. It can be understood as a ripple, or excitation, of that field. Interactions with the field give mass to certain fundamental particles, including W and Z bosons, electrons, and quarks; the boson itself is not a particle that simply gives everything its mass. The field and the Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism help explain why the W and Z carriers of the weak force are massive. ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider announced the particle’s discovery in 2012. Its spin is zero, a distinctive property that helped establish its identity.

key_facts.text: The Higgs boson is a ripple, or wave, in the Higgs field; finding it provided evidence for the field.
The Brout–Englert–Higgs mechanism describes how interactions with the field give mass to certain fundamental particles, including W and Z bosons.
The photon does not interact with the Higgs field and has no mass.
ATLAS and CMS announced the discovery in 2012; further measurements helped confirm the particle’s spin-zero nature in 2013.
The Higgs mechanism was proposed in 1964 by Peter Higgs, François Englert, and other theorists.

overview.text: Turbulence is an irregular way that a fluid—a liquid or a gas—moves, unlike the smoother, layered motion of laminar flow. In turbulent flow, swirling structures called eddies appear at many sizes, and local velocities fluctuate around an average. These motions carry fluid across the main direction of flow, mixing and spreading dye, heat, or other materials more effectively than laminar motion. Turbulence matters in rivers, pipes, and air moving near objects because it changes momentum transfer and forces on surfaces. The Reynolds number compares inertia with viscosity; larger values favor turbulence, but there is no universal cutoff: boundaries and flow conditions can shift when turbulent motion begins.

key_facts.text: The Reynolds number compares a flow’s inertia with its viscosity. A higher value favors turbulent motion, but the transition depends on conditions such as boundary roughness and how the flow enters.
Turbulent flow combines a mean flow with fluctuating motion; eddies of different sizes can carry fluid across the main flow’s streamlines.
Eddies can spread dye and transport heat, momentum, and other material through a fluid, making turbulence important to mixing and flow behavior.
In an energy cascade, energy passes mostly from larger eddies to smaller ones; viscosity dampens velocity fluctuations at the smallest scales.
Near an object, its boundary layer can be laminar or turbulent; turbulent boundary layers contain unsteady swirling motion and affect aerodynamic forces such as drag and lift.

overview.text: An airplane is an engine-driven, heavier-than-air aircraft supported by air acting on fixed wings, distinguishing it from rotorcraft such as helicopters. As the airplane moves relative to the air, its wings redirect airflow to generate lift; an engine-powered propeller or jet provides thrust to counter drag. Movable controls let a pilot change the aircraft’s climb, descent, and turn. The Wright brothers’ Flyer was a milestone in aviation: after years of glider experiments, Wilbur and Orville Wright made successful powered, controlled flights at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903. Orville piloted the first; Wilbur’s final flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet.

key_facts.text: The FAA defines an airplane as engine-driven, heavier than air, and supported in flight by air acting on fixed wings.
Lift is produced as a wing moves relative to air and turns the airflow; both upper and lower wing surfaces contribute.
Lift opposes weight, while thrust moves an airplane forward against drag. Small airplanes may use propellers, while larger ones may use jet engines.
The Wright Flyer used a gasoline engine to drive two pusher propellers; its pilot used controls to manage climb, descent, and turns.
On December 17, 1903, Orville Wright piloted the Flyer’s first successful flight at Kitty Hawk; Wilbur’s final flight that day lasted 59 seconds and covered 852 feet.

overview.text: Blood type (blood group) is an inherited classification based on antigens—markers—on red blood cells, and it matters because a recipient’s immune system can react to incompatible donor cells. The best-known system, ABO, sorts blood into A, B, AB, or O according to whether red cells carry A antigens, B antigens, both, or neither. A second major system is RhD: the D antigen’s presence is called positive and its absence negative, creating familiar labels such as A+ and O−. Together ABO and RhD make eight common combinations. Many other red-cell antigens also exist, so “universal donor” is shorthand for O-negative red cells, not a substitute for medical testing and matching.

key_facts.text: Blood groups are inherited from parents.
In the ABO system, A and B describe which of those antigens are present on red cells: A has A, B has B, AB has both, and O has neither.
RhD-positive red cells have the D antigen; RhD-negative red cells lack it.
Combining ABO and RhD gives eight common labels, such as A+, O−, and AB+.
O-negative is called the universal red-cell donor type, but other blood-group antigens mean transfusions still require medical testing and matching.

overview.text: Teeth are hard structures anchored in the jaws that help animals grasp, cut, tear, crush, or grind food. Their shapes often reflect their jobs: in mammals, incisors cut, pointed canines can seize or tear, and broader premolars and molars crush and grind. A human tooth has a crown above the gum and a root set in the jaw; enamel covers the crown, dentin forms the hard layer beneath it, and a pulp chamber contains nerves and blood vessels. Teeth matter not only for feeding: because mammals have different tooth shapes, scientists can use teeth in skulls as clues to diet and way of life.

key_facts.text: A human tooth has a crown and a root; enamel covers the crown, while dentin surrounds the pulp, which contains nerves and blood vessels.
Human incisors are shaped for cutting, canines for tearing, and premolars and molars for crushing and grinding food.
Among mammals, tooth shapes vary with diet: for example, many plant-eaters have broad, flat molars for grinding vegetation, while carnivores often have sharp canines for catching and tearing prey.
Scientists can study a mammal’s teeth and skull to infer aspects of how it lived, including whether it ate meat, plants, or both.
The tissues that support teeth include the gums, periodontal ligament, and jawbone; the tooth root is covered by cementum.

overview.text: For a pure substance, the triple point is the particular temperature and pressure at which its solid, liquid, and gas phases coexist in thermodynamic equilibrium. On a pressure–temperature phase diagram, it is where the three phase-boundary curves meet; along each boundary, two phases coexist. The coordinates depend on the substance: water’s triple point is about 0.01 °C and 611 Pa, far below ordinary atmospheric pressure. This reproducible condition makes water’s triple point useful for calibrating thermometers. It also has a history in measurement science: until 2019, the water triple point defined the kelvin, which is now defined using the Boltzmann constant.

key_facts.text: At a triple point, all three phases coexist in equilibrium; it is distinct from a point on a phase boundary, where two phases coexist.
A pressure–temperature phase diagram shows phase regions and their boundaries; the three boundaries meet at the triple point.
Water’s triple point is about 0.01 °C and 611 Pa (about 4.6 torr), not its familiar freezing point at ordinary pressure.
Until 2019, the triple point of water defined the kelvin; the SI kelvin is now defined using the Boltzmann constant.
A water triple-point cell remains a practical, reproducible reference for calibrating thermometers.

overview.text: Natural selection is an evolutionary process in which inherited differences among individuals affect how many descendants they leave. When a trait gives an advantage in a particular environment, individuals carrying it tend, on average, to survive and reproduce more, so the trait may become more common over generations; selection acts on individuals, while populations change. It requires heritable variation and does not mean organisms change because they need to, or that the “fittest” are necessarily strongest. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace independently developed the idea and presented it jointly in 1858; Darwin expanded it in On the Origin of Species (1859). Finches studied over generations show selection as environmental conditions shift.

key_facts.text: Natural selection needs heritable variation in a population; differences caused only by non-genetic factors will not be passed on as an evolutionary change.
An advantage depends on the environment, and evolutionary fitness is about contributing offspring to later generations—not simply being strong or surviving.
Individuals are affected by selection; over generations, the frequencies of inherited traits change in populations.
Darwin and Wallace independently developed the idea and presented their work on natural selection together in 1858.
Studies of Galápagos finches documented shifts in average beak size associated with changing food availability, illustrating selection across generations.

overview.text: The Haber–Bosch process is the industrial method for making ammonia (NH₃) by reacting nitrogen gas with hydrogen: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃. A finely divided iron catalyst speeds the reaction, which is run at high pressure and high temperature; together, these conditions make ammonia production practical at factory scale. Fritz Haber demonstrated the laboratory chemistry, while Carl Bosch and BASF colleagues engineered it for industrial production; the first plant began operating at Oppau in 1913. Ammonia supplies nitrogen for fertilizers that help crops grow, but it has also been used to make nitrates for explosives. The process is both a landmark in industrial chemistry and a technology with agricultural and military uses.

key_facts.text: The balanced reaction is N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃; the gases pass over finely divided iron at high pressure and high temperature.
Haber developed the laboratory-scale synthesis; Bosch led the engineering work to make it industrially practical.
The first ammonia synthesis plant began operating at Oppau on September 9, 1913.
Ammonia is chiefly used as a starting material for nitrogen fertilizers, supporting crop growth.
Ammonia can also be converted into nitrates used in explosives, linking the process to wartime supply as well as agriculture.

overview.text: The eye is the roughly circular central region of a strong tropical cyclone. It has the storm’s lowest surface pressure, but its winds are generally light rather than guaranteed to be calm; stronger winds can extend into it. Air sinks in the eye, warming and drying as it descends, which often suppresses clouds and rain. The eye is ringed by the eyewall, a band of deep thunderstorms where the storm’s strongest surface winds and heaviest rain occur. The calmer conditions can be deceptive: once the eye passes, dangerous eyewall winds may return from the other side. Sinking air and eyewall thunderstorms are involved in eye formation, but the exact mechanisms are not fully understood.

key_facts.text: The eye is at the center of a strong tropical cyclone and contains its lowest surface pressure.
Sinking air in the eye helps suppress cloud formation, so skies there are often clearer and winds lighter than around it.
The surrounding eyewall is a ring of thunderstorms with the cyclone’s strongest surface winds and intense rainfall.
A lull as the eye passes does not mean the storm is over; dangerous winds can return as the opposite side of the eyewall arrives.
Not every tropical cyclone develops a visible eye; a defined eye and eyewall can be clues to a storm’s structure and intensity.

overview.text: Memory in psychology is the set of processes that lets people take in information, retain it, and bring it back to awareness. Psychologists commonly describe three linked functions: encoding (forming a representation), storage (retaining it), and retrieval (accessing it later). Memory is not one simple store: brief sensory traces, short-term or working-memory processes, and longer-lasting knowledge and experiences can be distinguished, although models of how these systems relate differ. Working memory helps people hold and work with information; short-term memory often refers to keeping information available briefly. Long-term memory includes conscious facts and personal events as well as learned skills, making memory important for learning, reasoning, and everyday activities.

key_facts.text: Encoding brings information into the memory system; storage retains it; retrieval brings it back into awareness.
Working memory is used to work with information, whereas short-term memory usually means briefly retaining it; psychologists do not always treat the terms as identical.
Long-term memory includes semantic memories of facts, episodic memories of personal events, and procedural memories for skills.
Retrieval includes recall (accessing information without cues), recognition (identifying previously learned information), and relearning.
Working memory supports tasks such as reasoning and comprehension, and is linked to learning across school years.

overview.text: Ethics, also called moral philosophy, is the branch of philosophy that examines moral principles and evaluates actions and values: what is right or wrong, and why. It includes normative ethics, which develops principles for how people ought to act; metaethics, which asks what moral judgments mean and whether morality exists; and applied ethics, which considers specific practices and dilemmas. Ethical theories offer different ways to reason: consequentialism emphasizes overall outcomes, deontology duties or rights, and virtue ethics character and the kind of life a person should cultivate. Ethics matters because it helps people reflect systematically on choices affecting themselves and others; Aristotle’s influential treatises linked ethical inquiry to living well and flourishing.

key_facts.text: A common way to organize ethics is into three branches: metaethics examines morality and moral judgments; normative ethics develops moral principles; applied ethics considers the permissibility of particular actions and practices.
Consequentialist theories assess actions by their outcomes, while deontological theories give a central role to duties or rights.
Virtue ethics makes moral character central and asks what kind of person one should be, rather than treating rules or outcomes as the basic focus.
Applied ethics addresses concrete issues in areas such as business and bioethics, often drawing on principles and questions from normative ethics and metaethics.
Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics explores virtue and human flourishing; the Stanford Encyclopedia notes that the title was added later and may refer to editing by his son, Nicomachus.

overview.text: Stanford University, legally Leland Stanford Junior University, is a private research university in California. Leland and Jane Stanford founded it in 1885 in memory of their son, and it opened in Palo Alto on October 1, 1891. Its founders envisioned a coeducational, nonsectarian school combining liberal arts with science and engineering—an approach that helped make Stanford part of the early movement toward the modern research university. Stanford’s research has since spanned fields including engineering, molecular biology, medicine, and economics. The university is also associated with controversial behavioral research: Philip Zimbardo’s 1971 prison simulation took place on campus and was stopped early after concerns arose about participants’ behavior.

key_facts.text: The university commemorates Leland Stanford Jr., who died of typhoid fever at age 15 in 1884; his parents founded the university the following year.
Its formal name is Leland Stanford Junior University. It opened on October 1, 1891, on the Stanford family’s Palo Alto property.
The founding vision included coeducation, a nonsectarian institution, and a combination of liberal arts with science and engineering.
Stanford’s characteristic early campus design features sandstone buildings, red-tiled roofs, arches, and quadrangles.
In 1971, 24 students selected from more than 70 volunteers took part in Zimbardo’s prison simulation; planned for up to two weeks, it ended after six days amid concerns about participants’ behavior.

overview.text: Classical conditioning, also called Pavlovian conditioning, is associative learning in which an organism learns that one stimulus predicts another, often producing an automatic response to a cue. In Ivan Pavlov’s well-known dog experiments, food naturally prompted salivation; after a tone was repeatedly paired with food, the tone alone could prompt salivation. The food is the unconditioned stimulus, the learned cue is the conditioned stimulus, and the learned reaction is the conditioned response. Pavlov’s research grew out of his work on digestion. Unlike operant conditioning, which concerns how consequences shape actions, classical conditioning focuses on associations between stimuli and responses.

key_facts.text: Classical conditioning is also known as Pavlovian conditioning.
In Pavlov’s example, food naturally elicits salivation; food is the unconditioned stimulus and salivation is the unconditioned response.
A previously neutral cue, such as a tone, can become a conditioned stimulus after being paired with food, and then elicit a conditioned response such as salivation.
Classical conditioning involves learning associations between stimuli; operant conditioning instead concerns associations between actions and their consequences.
Pavlov was a physiologist who studied digestion; observations of dogs’ learned responses to cues led to his experiments on conditioning.

overview.text: The ontological argument is a family of philosophical arguments that tries to establish God’s existence through reasoning about the concept or nature of God, rather than by observing the world. In Anselm of Canterbury’s influential eleventh-century version, God is understood as a being than which nothing greater can be conceived: Anselm argues that such a being could not exist only as an idea, since existing in reality would be greater. René Descartes later offered a related argument, claiming necessary existence belongs to the idea of a supremely perfect being. The reasoning has drawn criticism, including challenges to moving from an idea to real existence and to treating existence as a perfection.

key_facts.text: Anselm’s best-known version appears in his eleventh-century work Proslogion.
Anselm reasons that a greatest conceivable being cannot exist only in the mind, because existing in reality would make it greater.
Descartes’s related argument, discussed in his Fifth Meditation, claims necessary existence is included in the idea of a supremely perfect being.
Anselm’s contemporary Gaunilo challenged the reasoning with a parody involving a supposedly greatest conceivable island.
Kant’s famous criticism is that existence is not a real predicate or perfection that can simply be included in a concept.

overview.text: Voting is the formal expression of a choice—usually on a ballot, though sometimes by voice or show of hands—used to select public officials or express a preference on a political question. In representative government, voters choose officials to make decisions on their behalf; voting can also register choices among courses of action. Its distinguishing feature is that individual choices are counted under an electoral system, whose rules determine how votes translate into winners or legislative seats. Some ballots ask for a single choice, while preferential systems let voters rank candidates. In the United States, ballots may be cast in person, early, or by mail, depending on state rules; procedures are designed to keep choices private.

key_facts.text: A vote formally indicates a choice between candidates or courses of action; it may be expressed on a ballot, by hand, or by voice.
In representative government, elections let people convey authority to officials who make decisions on their behalf.
Electoral systems differ in what voters mark—such as a candidate, a party, or ranked preferences—and in how votes are translated into winners or seats.
In an alternative-vote system, voters rank candidates; if no one wins a majority of first preferences, lower-ranked candidates are eliminated and votes are reassigned according to later preferences.
In the United States, in-person Election Day, early in-person, and mail voting are options, but procedures vary by state; election officials keep voters’ choices private.

overview.text: Margaret Mead’s Coming of Age in Samoa is a 1928 anthropological study based on her 1925–26 fieldwork on Taʻū, in American Samoa. Mead focused chiefly on adolescent girls in three villages, while describing childhood, family life, community expectations, education, and relationships to explain their social setting. Her central argument challenged the idea that adolescent turmoil is universal: she reported that Samoan girls experienced less conflict and attributed the difference to culture. The book became influential in discussions of how society shapes development and brought the nature-versus-nurture debate to a broad audience. Its methods and portrayal of Samoan sexuality were later criticized, and scholars disputed those criticisms too; its conclusions are Mead’s interpretation, not a timeless description of Samoa.

key_facts.text: William Morrow published the book in New York in 1928; Franz Boas wrote its foreword.
Mead’s fieldwork in Samoa took place in 1925–26; the book’s case histories focus on girls in three Taʻū villages.
The book ranges beyond adolescence to discuss childhood, households, community life, education, and sexual relationships.
Mead argued that adolescence need not be universally turbulent and attributed the difference she reported in Samoa to cultural patterns.
The book became popular and a lasting case in the nature-versus-nurture debate; its methods and conclusions have been challenged, and the scholarly debate continued.

overview.text: Affirmative action is a broad label for proactive efforts to reduce barriers and widen opportunity for groups historically excluded from education or work; it names a family of policies rather than one fixed method. In the United States, its modern federal history includes President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 order, which used the term, and a 1965 order directing federal contractors to pursue equal employment opportunity. Approaches and legal rules have varied across settings. In 2023, the Supreme Court held the race-conscious admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina unlawful under the Equal Protection Clause. That decision reshaped college admissions, but addressed those programs, not every effort called affirmative action.

key_facts.text: President John F. Kennedy’s 1961 Executive Order 10925 used “affirmative action” in connection with measures to achieve nondiscrimination.
A 1965 executive order directed federal contractors to take affirmative action to ensure equal employment opportunity.
The 1969 Philadelphia Plan used employment goals and timetables; officials distinguished those tools from quotas.
In 2023, the Supreme Court ruled that the admissions programs at Harvard and the University of North Carolina in the cases before it could not be reconciled with the Equal Protection Clause.
The Court said universities may consider an applicant’s account of how race affected their life, while requiring evaluation of the individual’s experiences rather than race itself.

overview.text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Genevan Enlightenment philosopher, writer, and composer whose work influenced later political philosophy and Romantic thought. In his *Discourse on the Origin and Foundations of Inequality Among Men* (1755), he used a conjectural account of human development to examine how society and institutions produce inequality; this was philosophical speculation, not a verified history. In *The Social Contract* (1762), he asked how political authority could protect freedom and equality, arguing that legitimate laws should express the people’s “general will.” His *Émile* (1762) explored education through a child-centered approach. Together, these works made him a distinctive critic of modern society and a major thinker about civic life, human character, and education.

key_facts.text: Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712 and died in 1778; he also worked as a composer and music theorist.
His 1755 *Discourse on Inequality* explores how social development relates to inequality. Its account of humanity’s state of nature is conjectural, and scholars debate how literally to read it.
In *The Social Contract*, Rousseau argued that the people as a whole are sovereign and that laws should express the general will.
In *Émile*, Rousseau promoted an education that follows a child’s development and encourages learning through discovery.
Rousseau’s ideas influenced later political philosophers, including Immanuel Kant, and contributed to the Romantic movement.

overview.text: The Flynn effect is the observed rise in average scores on intelligence tests across generations, especially documented through successive editions or norming samples of IQ tests. Psychologist James R. Flynn’s 1984 analysis of U.S. Stanford–Binet and Wechsler test data estimated a 13.8-point increase from 1932 to 1978. Later researchers confirmed a broad trend while finding that its estimated size depends on which tests and comparisons are included. The effect matters because test norms can become outdated, making scores from tests standardized in different periods less directly comparable. It describes changing test performance; by itself, it does not settle why scores rose or prove that every aspect of intelligence changed.

key_facts.text: Flynn’s 1984 study estimated that U.S. IQ scores rose by 13.8 points between 1932 and 1978.
A meta-analysis of 285 studies estimated an average increase of 2.31 standard-score points per decade across its comparisons.
For a subset of modern Stanford–Binet and Wechsler tests, the meta-analysis estimated about 2.93 IQ points per decade.
The estimated size varies with the tests and comparisons used, so one rate should not be treated as universal.
Flynn discussed possible contributors such as education and test familiarity, but his analysis did not establish a single cause.

overview.text: Gertrude Elizabeth Margaret (G.E.M.) Anscombe (1919–2001), often called Elizabeth Anscombe, was a British philosopher whose work shaped debates about intentional action and how people should reason about right and wrong. Her book Intention (1957) examined how actions can be understood through an agent’s reasons and purposes. In “Modern Moral Philosophy” (1958), she criticized influential approaches to ethics; the essay helped renew attention to virtue ethics. A close student and friend of Ludwig Wittgenstein, Anscombe became his principal English translator, including of Philosophical Investigations. Her combination of action theory, moral philosophy, and Wittgenstein scholarship distinguishes her as a major twentieth-century philosopher.

key_facts.text: Anscombe was born in 1919 in Limerick, Ireland, and died in Cambridge, England, in 2001.
Her 1957 book Intention became an important work in the philosophy of action, exploring what it means to act intentionally.
Her 1958 essay “Modern Moral Philosophy” criticized prominent approaches to ethics and helped spur renewed interest in virtue ethics.
Anscombe was one of Wittgenstein’s literary executors and his main English translator; her translation of Philosophical Investigations appeared in 1953.
Her work ranged beyond ethics and action theory, including topics in mind, language, metaphysics, and logic.

overview.text: Section 230 is part of the Communications Act of 1934, added in 1996 as Section 509 of the Communications Decency Act, itself part of the Telecommunications Act. It is best known for two related protections: services generally cannot be treated as the publisher of content supplied by someone else, and they may have legal protection when they restrict material they consider objectionable in good faith. These rules matter because they address both hosting people’s online posts and moderating them. Section 230 is not blanket immunity: it does not generally protect a service from liability for content it develops itself, and the law includes exceptions.

key_facts.text: Section 230 was added to federal law by Section 509 of Public Law 104–104, enacted February 8, 1996.
The law generally bars treating a provider or user of an interactive computer service as the publisher or speaker of information supplied by another content provider.
A separate provision protects certain good-faith actions to restrict access to material considered objectionable.
The statute defines “interactive computer service” broadly; the Congressional Research Service notes that covered entities can include online services, internet access providers, and libraries.
The protections have express exceptions, and Section 230 does not generally shield providers or users from claims based on content they themselves develop.

overview.text: Swahili, also called Kiswahili, is a Bantu language rooted in East African coastal communities. It grew into a regional lingua franca: many people in Tanzania, Kenya, and neighboring countries use it to communicate across different first languages, and many speakers learn it as an additional language. Indian Ocean trade helped the language spread, while contact with other communities added loanwords, notably from Arabic; its linguistic identity remains Bantu. One distinguishing feature is its noun-class system, in which prefixes group nouns and influence related words. Today Kiswahili links regional communication and cultural history, and UNESCO observes World Kiswahili Language Day on July 7.

key_facts.text: Kiswahili is the name speakers use for the language; it belongs to the Bantu language family.
It serves as a lingua franca in East Africa, where many people speak it in addition to their first language.
The language’s coastal roots and growth as a trading language connect its history to Indian Ocean commerce.
Swahili has loanwords from Arabic and other languages, alongside Bantu-based grammar that includes noun classes.
Older Swahili texts used Arabic script; a Roman-script standard orthography was established by the 1930s.
UNESCO proclaimed July 7 World Kiswahili Language Day in 2021.

overview.text: Avram Noam Chomsky is an American theoretical linguist and influential public intellectual whose generative grammar helped redirect linguistics toward explaining the rules that produce sentences and contributed to the growth of cognitive science. His Universal Grammar proposal treats some foundations of language as innate; his “poverty of the stimulus” argument says children appear to know grammatical patterns not fully explained by the language they hear. This is an influential but contested account, not a settled fact. Beyond academia, Chomsky became known for political criticism: in Manufacturing Consent, co-written with Edward S. Herman, he and Herman presented a “propaganda model” to examine how institutional pressures can influence news coverage, including reporting on U.S. foreign policy.

key_facts.text: Chomsky’s generative grammar uses rules to explain how sentences can be generated, rather than merely cataloging sentence forms.
His work in generative grammar helped shape cognitive science, linking the study of language with questions about the human mind.
The poverty-of-the-stimulus argument holds that children’s linguistic knowledge includes patterns not fully explained by the evidence available to them as learners.
Universal Grammar is associated with the idea of innate contributions to language learning, but scholars also debate empiricist alternatives.
In Manufacturing Consent, Chomsky and Edward S. Herman proposed a propaganda model to analyze structural influences on U.S. news coverage and reporting on foreign policy.

overview.text: Human population size is the number of people counted in a defined geographic area—such as a city, country, or region—at a particular time and under a stated counting rule. It differs from population density, which describes how many people live per unit of land. Demography, the statistical study of human populations, examines their size, composition, and change. For a country or community, the count changes through births, deaths, and migration; births minus deaths form natural increase or decrease, while net migration adds the balance of movement in and out. These measures help governments and researchers understand changing needs and plan services, while population estimates help track people between censuses.

key_facts.text: The UN glossary defines total population as the de facto population of a country, area, or region on July 1 of the stated year; figures are presented in thousands.
Population density is not the same as population size: density measures the number of people living in a given area, usually per square kilometer.
Demography is the statistical study of human populations; it examines processes including birth, death, and movement, as well as population composition.
A basic accounting rule for population change is: new population = starting population + births − deaths + net migration (people moving in minus people moving out).
Census Bureau estimates track population change between decennial censuses; population information helps decision-makers understand where people live and plan for their needs.

overview.text: Utilitarianism is an ethical theory that judges choices—such as actions, laws, or policies—by their consequences, asking which option produces the greatest overall good or well-being. It is a form of consequentialism: unlike views that treat duties or intentions as decisive, it makes outcomes central. Utilitarians generally count each affected person’s good impartially, rather than giving one person’s happiness extra weight simply because it is their own. Classical utilitarianism took shape in nineteenth-century Britain, especially through Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill, and offered a way to assess laws and social practices by whether they improve lives. Versions differ over what counts as good and whether to judge individual acts or general rules.

key_facts.text: Jeremy Bentham developed the first systematic account of utilitarianism; Bentham and John Stuart Mill became its major classical thinkers.
Classical utilitarians used the theory to assess laws and social practices, with the aim of improving people’s lives.
In Mill’s formulation, actions are right insofar as they promote happiness, which he describes as pleasure and the absence of pain.
Mill argued that pleasures can differ in quality, so judging them need not depend only on how much pleasure they provide.
Act utilitarianism assesses individual actions by their results; rule utilitarianism assesses rules by the results of adopting them, then judges actions by those rules.

overview.text: The trolley problem is a family of hypothetical moral cases about what to do when every available choice risks someone’s death. In the familiar switch version, a runaway trolley is heading toward five people, and a bystander can divert it onto another track, where it will kill one. Philosopher Philippa Foot introduced trolley cases; Judith Jarvis Thomson later developed the familiar bystander-and-switch version and contrasted it with a case involving pushing someone from a footbridge. The puzzle is significant because it tests whether redirecting a threat to save more lives is morally different from using someone as a means. Variations help philosophers explore why seemingly small changes can alter moral judgments.

key_facts.text: In the standard switch case, diverting the trolley saves five people but places one person on the alternate track in danger.
Foot introduced trolley cases, and Thomson later developed the familiar bystander-and-switch setup.
Thomson contrasted switching the trolley with pushing a person from a footbridge to stop it, asking why the two cases may prompt different judgments.
One ethical question is whether redirecting an existing danger differs from making a person the means of saving others.
The cases are deliberately simplified, allowing discussion of moral choices with assumed outcomes.

overview.text: Unemployment describes a situation in which people in the labor force do not have jobs. In U.S. official statistics, a person generally counts as unemployed if they are not working, are available for work, and actively searched during the previous four weeks; an exception applies to people temporarily laid off and expecting recall. The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people divided by the labor force, not the whole population. Economists distinguish frictional unemployment, as people take time to move between jobs; structural unemployment, when workers’ skills or locations do not match available jobs; and cyclical unemployment, which rises when a recession reduces hiring. Frictional and structural unemployment can persist even in a healthy economy, so unemployment is not automatically zero.

key_facts.text: The labor force consists of employed and unemployed people; the official unemployment rate divides the unemployed by the labor force.

Under the U.S. Current Population Survey definition, unemployed people are generally jobless, available for work, and actively searching; people on temporary layoff who expect recall are an exception.
People who have stopped actively searching—including discouraged workers—are not counted as unemployed in the official U.S. measure.
Frictional unemployment occurs while people enter the job market or transition between jobs.
Structural unemployment results from a mismatch between workers’ skills or location and the jobs available.
Cyclical unemployment is linked to the business cycle: it tends to rise in recessions and fall during expansions.

overview.text: Capital in economics is productive wealth: resources or assets put to work to help make goods and services or generate further value. In the standard factors-of-production model, it most often means produced physical assets—tools, machines, equipment, and buildings—used with labor and natural resources. These assets differ from raw materials and from money: money can purchase capital goods, but does not itself perform productive work. Capital matters because equipment can help workers produce more. In Marx’s analysis, the term also describes value advanced through buying and production to return in expanded form; capitalism, by contrast, names an economic system based on competition and private ownership.

key_facts.text: Capital is one of the factors of production, alongside land, labor, and entrepreneurship.
Physical capital includes produced tools, machinery, equipment, and buildings used to make or deliver goods and services.
In the standard production-factor model, money can buy capital goods, but is not itself a productive resource.
Capital goods usually help workers produce more; for example, the Federal Reserve’s lesson describes tools raising bookmark-making productivity.
In Marx’s analysis, capital is value advanced through a cycle of buying and selling with the aim of returning as expanded value; capitalism is an economic system, not a synonym for capital.

overview.text: Bushidō (often translated “Way of the Warrior”) is an ethical ideal associated with Japan’s samurai, but it was not one timeless, universally enforced rulebook. Japanese warrior houses produced varied martial codes and advice texts over centuries; the familiar, organized doctrine took shape mainly during Japan’s modernization in the late 1800s. It drew on older Confucian, Buddhist, and Shintō ideas, while also reflecting newer European ideals of chivalry and national identity. In the early 20th century, educators and state thinkers promoted it as a national morality emphasizing martial virtue and loyalty to the emperor, giving Bushidō influence far beyond the samurai class.

key_facts.text: The phrase “Way of the Warrior” is a common translation of Bushidō.
Older samurai communities had martial codes and advice books, but not a single universally binding code.
Modern Bushidō combined Confucian, Buddhist, and Shintō influences with ideas that included European chivalry.
In the early 20th century, Bushidō was promoted in civilian and military education as national morality.
Modern Bushidō gave loyalty to the emperor a prominent role, unlike the broader Confucian virtue of loyalty from which it drew.

overview.text: Stoicism is an ancient Greek philosophical school founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE; its name comes from the Stoa Poikile, or “Painted Porch,” where early Stoics gathered. It became influential in the Roman world, where thinkers including Seneca, Epictetus, and Emperor Marcus Aurelius were associated with it. Stoics understood philosophy as an interconnected system of ethics, logic, and physics, not merely advice for staying calm. In ethics, they argued that virtue is the only true good, and that flourishing comes from living in agreement with nature by using reason well. Since humans are social as well as rational, virtuous living also entails responsibility toward others. Stoicism did not mean feeling nothing: it emphasized examining judgments that contribute to troubling passions.

key_facts.text: Zeno of Citium began the school in Athens around 300 BCE. Its name refers to the Stoa Poikile, the “Painted Porch” where early Stoics met.
Stoic philosophy included three connected areas: ethics, logic, and physics.
Stoics held that virtue is the only true good; health and wealth could be preferred, but were not themselves moral goods.
Living according to nature meant using human reason and recognizing people’s social responsibilities—not simply withdrawing from society.
Stoic “passions” were not simply automatic feelings; the school connected them to judgments. Its ideal was not emotional numbness.
Stoicism remained influential in the Roman period; notable Roman-era Stoics included Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius.

overview.text: Jean Piaget was a Swiss psychologist whose work helped establish the study of how children’s thinking develops. He proposed four broad stages—sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational, and formal operational—whose age ranges are approximate. In the first, usually placed in the first two years, infants learn about the world through their senses and actions. A key milestone in Piaget’s account is object permanence: understanding that something continues to exist when it is out of sight. His theory shaped later explanations of cognitive development, though newer research suggests infants show some understanding of objects earlier than Piaget’s original methods indicated; the stages are a theory, not an exact timetable.

key_facts.text: Piaget’s theory describes four stages in a consistent order, with each stage representing a change in how children think; the age ranges are approximate.
The sensorimotor stage is the first stage; infants learn through sensory experience and motor actions, and it covers roughly the first two years.
Object permanence means understanding that objects continue to exist when they cannot be seen; Piaget treated it as a major achievement of early cognitive development.
Piaget’s account of object permanence has been revised: later research using different methods found evidence of some object understanding at younger ages than his original tasks suggested.
Piaget held academic and research roles in Geneva and helped build international work on education and the study of knowledge.

overview.text: In economics, a monopoly is a market structure in which one seller is the sole supplier of a product with no close substitutes, giving it meaningful influence over price rather than forcing it to accept a market price. Its power often persists because barriers—such as legal protections, control of a key resource, or high fixed costs—make entry difficult. Unlike a firm in perfect competition, a monopolist chooses output with the market demand curve in view; standard models predict it may restrict output and charge more than a competitive market, creating inefficiency. In antitrust law, “monopoly” can refer more broadly to durable market power, and dominance alone is not automatically illegal.

key_facts.text: A monopoly differs from an oligopoly: the monopoly model has one supplier, while an oligopoly has a few competing firms.
Barriers to entry can include legal restrictions, control of a scarce resource, and cost advantages from economies of scale.
A natural monopoly may arise when one provider can serve a market at lower average cost than multiple providers duplicating costly infrastructure, such as water pipes.
In the standard economic model, a monopolist faces the market demand curve; unlike a competitive firm, it does not simply take the market price as given.
U.S. antitrust analysis distinguishes having a leading position from illegally maintaining monopoly power: courts examine market conditions and whether conduct improperly excludes competitors.

overview.text: Socialism is a broad political and economic tradition that challenges capitalism, especially private control of factories, land, tools, and other resources used to produce goods and services. Its central idea is that these productive resources should be owned or effectively controlled socially, rather than mainly by private owners; social control can take public, cooperative, or other forms. Many socialist arguments connect this change with greater democracy, equality, or solidarity, but socialists disagree about how to organize the economy and how much planning or market exchange to use. So socialism is not one fixed blueprint, and government ownership alone does not always mean that people collectively control economic decisions.

key_facts.text: “Means of production” refers to resources used to make goods and services, such as land, factories, tools, and raw materials.
The central ownership debate is about productive property—not ordinary personal belongings such as clothes or everyday items.
Socialists disagree about whether a socialist economy can use markets and profit-seeking firms, or should rely more on planning and production for use.
Equality, democracy, freedom, and solidarity are important ideals in many socialist arguments, though socialists differ on their meaning and application.
Some accounts distinguish social ownership from state ownership: state control without democratic public control may not count as social control.

overview.text: Niccolò Machiavelli’s The Prince (Il Principe) is a political treatise offering advice about gaining and keeping a principality. Written in 1513, after Machiavelli lost his Florentine government post, it was published after his death in 1532. Rather than describing an ideal ruler, it examines how political power works amid conflict and changing circumstances. Its distinctive idea of virtù means a ruler’s practical ability to adapt—not simply moral goodness—and Machiavelli weighs that skill against unpredictable fortune. The book’s discussion of whether it is safer to be feared or loved helped make it controversial. Its influence is lasting, but scholars disagree about its ethics and how it fits with Machiavelli’s republican writings.

key_facts.text: Machiavelli composed the work in 1513, after the Medici returned to power in Florence and he was dismissed from office; it appeared posthumously in 1532.
The treatise addresses different kinds of principalities, how rulers acquire them, military forces, and ways to avoid hatred and contempt.
Machiavelli’s virtù refers to practical political skill and adaptability, not simply conventional moral virtue; fortune represents forces that can disrupt political plans.
Chapter 17 asks whether a prince should be loved or feared; Machiavelli argues fear is safer when a ruler cannot secure both, while warning against being hated.
The book was dedicated to Lorenzo de’ Medici, and Machiavelli hoped the dedication might help him return to political service; scholars caution that the work’s political outlook remains debated.

overview.text: Okun’s law is an observed economic pattern, named for economist Arthur Okun, linking unemployment with production: when unemployment rises above its estimated natural rate, real output often falls below estimated potential output. Economists use it in two main ways: to relate changes in output growth to changes in unemployment, or to compare the output gap with the unemployment gap. The pattern is useful for understanding economic slowdowns and estimating unused productive capacity. But it is not a guaranteed formula: estimates vary across methods and time periods, and the relationship is statistical rather than proof that one change directly causes the other. Potential output and the natural rate of unemployment must also be estimated.

key_facts.text: Arthur Okun’s 1962 work connected unemployment with the gap between actual and potential output.
The “output gap” is the difference between actual output and estimated potential output; the “unemployment gap” compares actual unemployment with an estimated natural rate.
Okun’s original growth-rate estimate suggested that each percentage-point increase in real GNP growth went with an average 0.3-percentage-point decrease in unemployment.
The relationship is an empirical guide, not proof that output changes directly cause unemployment changes.
Productivity shifts and other structural changes can make the relationship less reliable, while estimates of potential output and the natural unemployment rate are uncertain.

overview.text: Money is something people generally accept as final payment for goods and services. It has three main functions: serving as a medium of exchange, a unit of account for comparing prices, and a store of value that can be saved for later. These functions make trading easier than relying on barter, where each person must find someone willing to trade for exactly what they want. Money is not limited to coins and banknotes: examples across history include shells and stone wheels, while modern systems also use electronic bank deposits. Commodity money gets value from its material; fiat money is not redeemable for a commodity and relies on public acceptance. Inflation can reduce money’s purchasing power over time.

key_facts.text: As a medium of exchange, money is widely accepted as a way to pay; this helps people trade without arranging a direct barter of goods or services.
As a unit of account, money gives buyers and sellers a shared way to state and compare prices.
Money can store value for future spending, but it is not a perfect store: inflation can erode its purchasing power.
Commodity money has value from the material it is made of, such as gold; fiat money is not convertible into gold or another asset and depends on public trust and acceptance.
Money can be physical or digital: examples include coins and banknotes, commercial-bank deposits, and digital balances held at nonbank providers.

overview.text: Cartesian dualism is René Descartes’s view that mind and body are fundamentally distinct kinds of substance. He treated the mind as a thinking, nonphysical thing and the body as extended in space and nonthinking. In his argument in the Sixth Meditation, Descartes maintained that each could exist without the other; this claim of possible separation does not mean he showed they actually exist separately. The view became a lasting framework for debates about consciousness and the mind–body problem. It also raises a central challenge: how could an immaterial mind influence a physical body, or bodily events produce conscious experiences?

key_facts.text: Descartes characterized mind by thought and body by extension—occupying space; he treated them as distinct substances.
In the Sixth Meditation, he argues from his distinct ideas of mind and body to the possibility that either could exist without the other.
Possible separate existence is not proof that minds actually exist apart from bodies, nor that the mind is immortal.
A key difficulty is explaining how a nonphysical mind and a physical body could affect one another, as when a decision moves an arm.
Descartes’s account helped shape later debates about the mind–body problem and became a standard starting point in philosophy of mind.

overview.text: English is a West Germanic language whose early form, Old English (also called Anglo-Saxon), developed in England after Germanic-speaking groups settled there from around the fifth century. It has changed substantially: Old English relied on many word endings to show grammatical roles, while modern English depends more on word order. Contact with French after the Norman Conquest of 1066 also added many words. English later developed regional and national varieties around the world. Its role as a global lingua franca lets people with different first languages communicate, but global use does not make English one uniform standard; speakers adapt it in diverse communities.

key_facts.text: English belongs to the West Germanic branch; Old English is also known as Anglo-Saxon.
University of Potsdam outlines several historical periods, from Old English (about 500–1150) to present-day English (about 1950 onward); period boundaries are approximate.
After the Norman Conquest of 1066, English adopted numerous words from French and later from Latin.
Old English used richer inflectional endings; modern English relies more on constrained word order, commonly Subject-Verb-Object.
English has developed many regional and national varieties, and is used as a lingua franca among people with different first languages.

overview.text: Universal Grammar (UG) is a hypothesis, associated especially with Noam Chomsky’s generative linguistics, that humans begin language learning with an inborn mental endowment constraining the grammatical patterns they can acquire. In one influential version, this initial state supplies general principles and adjustable choices; exposure to a community’s language helps children arrive at a particular grammar. UG is not simply a claim that all languages use identical words or surface rules: it concerns proposed structures of the human language-learning system. The idea is significant because it offers an explanation for how children build extensive grammatical knowledge from limited experience. Its exact content and whether innate grammatical constraints are needed remain debated.

key_facts.text: In Chomsky’s principles-and-parameters account, UG describes the language faculty’s initial state; children use linguistic input to arrive at a particular language’s grammar.
UG proposes unlearned, tacitly known constraints that assist language acquisition; it does not mean children consciously know a list of grammar rules.
A cognitive theory about an innate language faculty is different from simply observing that languages share a feature; shared features can have other explanations.
The proposal addresses how children can generalize beyond the language examples they have encountered, a problem Chomsky describes as central to explaining language learning.

Research on language learning also considers children’s sensitivity to their linguistic environment and statistical patterns in the input; how these processes relate to innate representations is debated.

overview.text: Linguistics, also called language science, is the systematic scientific study of human language—not simply learning to speak many languages. Linguists collect and analyze language data to understand what people know about language, how languages are structured, and how language shapes social interaction. Core areas include phonetics (speech sounds), phonology (sound patterns), morphology (word structure), syntax (sentence structure), and semantics (meaning). Related fields investigate how people acquire language, how languages vary and change over time, and topics such as sign languages and bilingualism. Linguistics matters because its research helps explain language’s many forms and uses, and can support the study and documentation of understudied or endangered languages.

key_facts.text: Linguistics studies language scientifically; speaking several languages is not a requirement for studying the field.
Phonetics examines the physical properties of speech sounds, while phonology studies sound patterns.
Morphology concerns word structure; syntax studies how phrases and sentences are organized; semantics studies meaning.
Other areas include language acquisition, bilingualism, historical linguistics, sign language, and sociolinguistics—the study of language in social contexts.
Linguists also document understudied and endangered languages and investigate language variation, contact, and change.

overview.text: David Hume (1711–1776) was a Scottish Enlightenment philosopher, essayist, and historian whose work examined how people form beliefs, understand causes, and make moral judgments. He treated experience as central to knowledge and argued that repeated pairings of events teach us to expect one after another, though we do not directly observe a necessary link between them. His challenge about induction asks whether past patterns can prove that unobserved cases—including the future—will match them; he argued that reason cannot establish this assumption, while habit helps explain why we still make such predictions. Hume also wrote the influential six-volume History of England, so he was known in his own time for history as well as philosophy.

key_facts.text: Hume was born in Edinburgh in 1711 and died in 1776.
His A Treatise of Human Nature appeared in 1739–1740; he later presented related ideas in the more accessible Enquiry concerning Human Understanding (1748).
Induction means reasoning from observed examples to unobserved cases or general rules. Hume questioned whether reason can justify expecting the future to resemble the past.
Hume argued that repeated experience and custom or habit explain why we expect familiar patterns to continue, even if reason cannot establish that they must.
Hume’s six-volume History of England was published from 1754 to 1762 and helped make him well known as a historian in his lifetime.

overview.text: Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche (1844–1900) was a German philosopher and cultural critic who began his career in classical philology and became a professor at the University of Basel at age 24. His forceful, often aphoristic books—including The Gay Science, Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Beyond Good and Evil, and On the Genealogy of Morality—questioned inherited European morality and religion and explored how people form values and identities. “God is dead” names not simply a proof against God but a cultural crisis: Christian belief had lost authority as a shared foundation for morality. His debated ideas of will to power and the Übermensch concern power, self-overcoming, and possible responses to that crisis; scholars disagree about their precise meaning.

key_facts.text: Born in Röcken in 1844, Nietzsche was appointed professor of classical philology at Basel in 1869, at age 24.
His first book, The Birth of Tragedy, explored Greek tragedy through the contrasting artistic forces associated with Apollo and Dionysus.
Nietzsche’s “death of God” describes a cultural loss of Christianity’s authority as a foundation for shared moral values, not merely the claim that God does not exist.
“Will to power” is a prominent but disputed idea: scholars interpret it in different ways, including as a drive to overcome resistance or to gain greater control.
The Übermensch, also translated as “Overman” or “Overhuman,” appears mainly in Thus Spoke Zarathustra; its meaning and significance remain debated.

overview.text: Carl Gustav Jung (1875–1961) was a Swiss psychiatrist whose work founded analytical psychology, an approach to studying personality and the conscious and unconscious mind. After working with Sigmund Freud, Jung and Freud parted ways in 1913, and Jung developed his own psychological ideas. He proposed that the unconscious includes a personal layer and a collective layer shared across humanity; he called recurring images and patterns that appear in myths, dreams, and symbols archetypes. He also described individuation as a process of movement toward psychological wholeness, and synchronicity as meaningful coincidence without a causal link. Jung’s theories influenced psychotherapy and discussions in the arts, humanities, and religion.

key_facts.text: Jung began his psychiatric career at Zurich’s Burghölzli hospital, where his word-association research contributed to his thinking about emotional complexes.
Jung met Freud in 1907; after their views diverged, they parted ways in 1913.
Jung’s proposed collective unconscious was a shared layer of the psyche; he associated archetypes with recurring images and patterns in dreams, myths, and symbols.
His 1921 book Psychological Types discussed personality differences, including introversion and extraversion.
Jung used “synchronicity” for coincidences he considered meaningful despite lacking a causal connection.
