overview.text: The unemployment rate, also called the jobless rate, measures unemployed people as a percentage of the labor force—not the entire population. In the U.S. official measure, the labor force consists of employed people plus those counted as unemployed. A jobless person generally must be available for work and have actively searched in the previous four weeks; people on temporary layoff awaiting recall are an exception. The rate is calculated as unemployed ÷ labor force × 100. Economists and policymakers watch it as an indicator of labor-market conditions, but it is not a complete picture: people who want work but recently stopped searching, and people working part time who want full-time work, are not fully captured by the headline rate.

key_facts.text: The labor force is the sum of employed and unemployed people; it is the denominator in the rate.

In the U.S. Current Population Survey, unemployed people generally had no job, were available for work, and actively searched during the prior four weeks. People awaiting recall from temporary layoff need not have searched.
The BLS calls its official unemployment measure U-3.
People who want and are available for work but have not actively searched in the last four weeks—including discouraged workers—are not counted as unemployed in the official measure.
The broader U-6 measure also includes marginally attached people and people working part time for economic reasons.

overview.text: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) is a membership-based international organization that works to support monetary cooperation and financial stability around the world. Delegates from 44 countries agreed to establish it at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference as part of a postwar effort to strengthen international economic cooperation; it formally came into existence in December 1945. Today, the IMF monitors economies and advises governments, lends to member countries facing financial difficulty, and provides technical assistance and training. Its member countries govern the organization, and their quota subscriptions are a main source of its resources. The IMF’s focus on monetary and financial stability distinguishes it from the World Bank, which was established to support reconstruction and economic development.

key_facts.text: The IMF was agreed to at the Bretton Woods conference in New Hampshire in July 1944, attended by delegates from 44 countries.
The IMF formally came into existence in December 1945, when its first 29 member countries signed its Articles of Agreement.
Its three core activities are economic monitoring and policy advice, financial assistance, and technical assistance and training.
Member countries’ quota subscriptions are the IMF’s main source of resources; quotas also help determine members’ voting power.
Each member country has a governor and an alternate on the Board of Governors; the Executive Board oversees the IMF’s day-to-day work.

references.title: Creation of the Bretton Woods System

overview.text: Friedrich Engels (1820–1895) was a German socialist thinker, political writer, and revolutionary whose work helped shape Marxism. Born in Barmen, he trained for business and worked at a family-connected cotton firm in Manchester, where he studied industrial workers’ conditions. His observations informed *The Condition of the Working Class in England*, published in 1845, a critique of workers’ living and working conditions. From 1844, Engels collaborated closely with Karl Marx and supported him financially; together they developed and published *The Communist Manifesto* in 1848. Engels was an independent writer as well as a collaborator, and after Marx’s death he edited and prepared some of Marx’s unfinished works for publication.

key_facts.text: Engels was born in Barmen, now part of Wuppertal, Germany, in 1820.
While working in Manchester from 1842 to 1844, he gathered material on workers’ lives and conditions.
His *The Condition of the Working Class in England*, published in 1845, criticized workers’ poor living and working conditions.
Engels and Marx collaborated from 1844; their jointly published *Communist Manifesto* appeared in 1848.
Engels helped support Marx financially and worked on Marx’s writings after Marx died in 1883.

overview.text: Filial piety, called xiao (孝) in Chinese, is a Confucian ethical ideal centered on how children treat parents and older family members. In the Analects, it means more than providing food: respect and a caring attitude matter, as do proper service while parents live and appropriate mourning and rites after their deaths. The tradition also connects family conduct with wider moral life: a passage spoken by the disciple You Ruo describes filial and sibling respect as a root of humaneness. Historically, the idea’s scope developed from ancestral sacrifice toward conduct toward living parents; it should not be reduced to unquestioning obedience.

key_facts.text: Xiao (孝) is the Chinese term commonly translated as “filial piety” or “filiality.”
In an Analects passage, Confucius says that providing for parents is not enough: filial conduct also requires reverence.
The Analects describes duties toward parents during life and after death, including proper service, burial, and ritual observance.
A saying by You Ruo in the Analects connects filial conduct and respect for siblings with the development of humaneness.
The concept’s meaning broadened over time: it was associated with ancestral sacrifice and also came to describe appropriate conduct toward living parents.

overview.text: Confucianism is a Chinese ethical and philosophical tradition shaped by teachings associated with Confucius (c. 551–479 BCE) and generations of later thinkers. Its texts do not present one unchanging doctrine: the Analects preserves selected sayings and episodes, while later writers developed and reinterpreted Confucian ideas. Central themes include learning and moral self-cultivation, humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), and responsibilities within relationships. Filial piety—care and respect toward parents and ancestors—serves as a starting point for wider ethical conduct. Confucian ideals influenced education, government, and social life in China and spread into broader East Asian intellectual traditions.

key_facts.text: Confucius is conventionally dated to c. 551–479 BCE; the tradition associated with him developed through later followers and interpreters.
The Analects collects sayings and accounts of Confucius’s actions; it is not a single, unified treatise presenting fixed doctrines.
Humaneness (ren), ritual propriety (li), learning, and moral self-cultivation are important themes in Confucian thought.
Filial piety connects conduct toward parents and ancestors with broader responsibilities; Confucian texts also relate family duties to public roles.
Confucian teachings became influential in Chinese education and government, including the training of officials, and later interpretations spread across East Asia.

overview.text: Plato’s *Apology* is a prose work presenting Socrates’ defense at his Athenian trial in 399 BCE; its title comes from Greek *apologia*, meaning “defense,” not an expression of regret. Socrates answers accusations of impiety and corrupting the young, while explaining why he questions citizens and values the examined life. Unlike most Platonic works, it is not a back-and-forth dialogue, though Socrates questions his accuser Meletus within it. The work is a literary account, not a guaranteed word-for-word court transcript: Plato was Socrates’ student, but scholars do not treat him as a mere recorder. Its lasting significance lies in its exploration of philosophy’s relationship to civic authority, education, and ethical living.

key_facts.text: The dialogue presents Socrates’ trial in Athens in 399 BCE, where he faced charges of impiety and corrupting the youth.
“Apology” translates the Greek *apologia*, a defense or speech in one’s own defense—not an admission of regret.
Although the work is mostly a defense speech rather than a typical Platonic dialogue, Socrates questions his accuser Meletus in it.
Socrates presents the examined life and the effort to clarify one’s thinking as central to living well.
The Apology has been influential as a work about the tensions between philosophical inquiry, education, and political life.

overview.text: Critical Race Theory (CRT) is a scholarly movement and analytical framework that took shape in U.S. law schools in the late 1970s and 1980s. It examines how race, racism, power, and legal institutions interact, asking not only whether a rule openly discriminates but also how laws and institutional practices may preserve or reduce racial inequality. CRT scholars have questioned whether colorblindness, formal equality, or gradual reform alone can address entrenched hierarchies, and some use narrative and lived experience to bring overlooked perspectives into legal analysis. The approach is not a single fixed doctrine: its central focus is critically studying law and society through race, and its influence has extended beyond legal scholarship into other fields.

key_facts.text: Duke describes CRT as beginning in the late 1970s in law schools; Columbia describes its emergence in the 1980s. Derrick Bell is often credited with its origination, but it had no single creator.
The framework examines how law can both worsen and help address racial and other inequalities.
CRT scholars question whether concepts such as colorblindness, formal equality, and merit are enough to eliminate racial hierarchies.
Some CRT scholars use narrative and storytelling to make marginalized people’s experiences more visible in legal analysis.
Although it began in legal scholarship, CRT has influenced fields beyond law.

overview.text: William James (1842–1910) was an American psychologist and philosopher whose work helped shape both fields. At Harvard, he taught early psychology courses and established an experimental psychology laboratory; his Principles of Psychology (1890) combined scientific and philosophical approaches to the mind. James also helped develop and popularize pragmatism, a U.S.-born philosophical tradition that examines ideas through their implications for experience and action. He presented pragmatism as a way to address philosophical disputes by asking whether choosing one answer over another would make a practical difference. His books The Will to Believe (1897) and The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) explore questions of belief and religious life.

key_facts.text: James was born in New York City in 1842 and died in 1910.
In 1875, he taught an early Harvard psychology course and established an experimental psychology laboratory.
His influential Principles of Psychology appeared in 1890 and helped introduce ideas such as the “stream of thought.”
Charles Sanders Peirce first defined and defended pragmatism; James later developed and popularized the tradition.
The Varieties of Religious Experience grew out of lectures James delivered in Edinburgh in 1901–1902 and was published in 1902.

overview.text: Persian, also called Farsi, is a New Iranian language in the Indo-Iranian branch of the Indo-European family. Its modern form developed gradually from earlier Persian, with historians describing continuity from Middle Persian rather than a sudden break. Today, closely related Persian varieties are associated with Iran, Afghanistan—where the variety is commonly called Dari—and Tajikistan, where it is called Tajik or Tajiki. Tajik’s Cyrillic writing system is one visible regional distinction. Persian’s importance extends beyond daily communication: it became a major language of poetry, scholarship, administration, and literary culture across a wide area of Asia. Its long literary tradition and regional varieties reflect the language’s historical reach and development.

key_facts.text: Persian belongs to the Indo-Iranian branch of the Indo-European language family.
New Persian developed gradually from earlier Persian; its emergence in written records is associated with the 9th–10th centuries.
The names Farsi, Dari, and Tajik/Tajiki are associated respectively with Persian in Iran, Afghanistan, and Tajikistan.
The Samanid rulers’ patronage helped Persian flourish as a literary language, including for poetry and epic traditions.
Tajik is written in a Cyrillic-based orthography, distinguishing its standard written form from Persian traditions using Perso-Arabic script.

overview.text: Capitalism is an economic system in which productive assets—such as businesses, tools, and factories—are chiefly privately owned and used to make goods or services for sale and profit. Owners invest capital, hire workers for wages, and seek returns; markets and competition help shape prices, production, and investment. This makes capitalism significant because it organizes who controls productive resources and how many decisions about making and selling goods are coordinated, while encouraging investment in new business ideas. It is not one identical blueprint: scholars note variations, and capitalist economies can include government ownership, laws, regulation, and public services. Thus, capitalism is not simply an economy without government.

key_facts.text: Capital is money or property invested in a business; after costs, investors may receive a share of profits and reinvest it.
Supply, demand, and competition help shape prices; competition among businesses can encourage lower prices or better quality.
Private ownership and profit-seeking are central features, but government can set rules, regulate businesses, and provide public goods.
Capitalist economies vary; they can combine mostly private businesses with government ownership or regulation in some areas.
Private investment can support new business ideas and innovation, one reason capitalism is associated with economic dynamism.

overview.text: Existentialism is a diverse philosophical movement that asks what it means to live as a human being, beginning with people’s concrete experiences rather than treating them as abstract examples. Its roots reach back to nineteenth-century thinkers Søren Kierkegaard and Friedrich Nietzsche, while it became especially visible in mid-twentieth-century France through Jean-Paul Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir. A key idea, often summarized as “existence precedes essence,” is that people are not simply born with a complete, fixed identity: they shape themselves through choices, commitments, and actions. Existentialist thinkers explore freedom and responsibility alongside anxiety, death, alienation, and the search for meaning. They disagree deeply, including about religion and how much freedom people have within real-life constraints.

key_facts.text: Existentialism is a loose movement, not one unified doctrine; many thinkers later grouped under the label did not call themselves existentialists.
“Existence precedes essence” means people are not fully defined by a fixed nature in advance; they shape themselves through choices made within their circumstances.
Existentialist thought includes both religious and secular approaches, so the movement as a whole is not simply atheistic.
Albert Camus is often discussed alongside existentialists, but he rejected that label and developed a distinct philosophy of the absurd.
Existentialist ideas have reached beyond academic philosophy into literature, visual art, film, and approaches to psychotherapy.

overview.text: Dreams are conscious experiences during sleep: a person may later recall images, speech, thoughts, or settings, though some dream reports contain an experience without remembered details. They are often linked with REM sleep, when brain activity resembles waking activity, but research also finds dreams during non-REM sleep, so dreaming is not confined to one sleep stage. Dreams matter both as a subject of sleep science and as material people interpret. In The Interpretation of Dreams (1900), Sigmund Freud argued that dreams could reveal unconscious mental processes and described them as disguised wish fulfillment; this was his psychoanalytic theory, not a settled explanation that every dream has a hidden message.

key_facts.text: Dreams can occur during REM and non-REM sleep; research summarized by NIH reports them less often in non-REM sleep.
During REM sleep, brain activity resembles waking activity, and muscles normally become limp, helping prevent people from acting out dreams.
In a study summarized by NIH, researchers distinguished reports with recalled dream content, reports of dreaming without recalled content, and reports of no experience.
Freud’s The Interpretation of Dreams was first published in 1900 and set out his theory of the unconscious.
Freud proposed that dreams fulfilled wishes in disguised form; this describes his psychoanalytic interpretation, not a proven rule for every dream.

overview.text: Feminism is both a body of ideas and a social movement seeking justice for women and an end to sexism. It challenges not only unequal laws or formal rights, but also social arrangements, cultural assumptions, and institutions that can restrict people’s opportunities. Feminist inquiry examines political, economic, social, and personal life, including work and family. Feminism is not one doctrine or a single agreed plan: activists and thinkers differ about what equality requires and how injustice works. Many also emphasize that gender-based injustice can overlap with racism, class inequality, and other forms of discrimination, so women’s experiences and priorities are not identical.

key_facts.text: Feminism is both a political movement and an intellectual commitment; its shared concern is justice for women and opposition to sexism, though its approaches and proposed remedies differ.
Feminist analysis can examine institutions and experiences often treated as private or ordinary, such as family life, care, work, sexuality, and the body.
The 1848 Seneca Falls women’s rights convention is commonly linked to the beginning of the organized U.S. movement; it called for rights including education, property, and political participation.
The history of women’s activism is broader than a simple sequence of “waves”; the wave metaphor can help describe eras, but their boundaries are not precise.
Intersectional approaches draw attention to how gender discrimination can combine with discrimination related to race, class, ethnicity, religion, or sexual orientation.

overview.text: Scrabble is a crossword-style word board game designed by American architect Alfred Mosher Butts. Its roots lie in Butts’s earlier games Lexiko and Criss Cross Words; in 1948, James Brunot refined the rules and renamed it Scrabble. Players draw letter tiles and place them in connected lines to make words across and down on a 15-by-15 grid. Each letter has a point value, while special squares multiply letter or word scores, so success combines vocabulary with choices about where to play. The Strong National Museum of Play inducted Scrabble into its National Toy Hall of Fame in 2004, recognizing its lasting place among popular games.

key_facts.text: Butts first called his early word game Lexiko, then developed a board version called Criss-Cross Words.
James Brunot took over production, adjusted the rules, and gave the game the name Scrabble.
In the standard game, players draw seven tiles and make connected words; new words must connect to tiles already on the board.
Letters have different point values, and colored premium squares can multiply a letter’s or a word’s score.
The Strong National Museum of Play records Scrabble’s induction into the National Toy Hall of Fame in 2004.

overview.text: A crossword puzzle is a word game in which numbered clues lead to words or phrases written across and down in a grid; intersecting answers share letters, helping solvers check or discover words. The American journalist Arthur Wynne is generally credited with creating an early modern crossword, published in the New York World in 1913, although word-form puzzles existed earlier. His puzzle was called “Word-Cross”; the familiar name reportedly followed an illustrator’s accidental reversal of the words. Crosswords became a popular newspaper pastime, and their clues and grids can vary: many standard U.S. puzzles use definition-style clues, while cryptic crosswords add wordplay involving the answer’s letters.

key_facts.text: Clues are usually numbered and grouped as “Across” and “Down,” depending on the direction each answer runs in the grid.
Arthur Wynne’s “Word-Cross” appeared in the New York World’s puzzle supplement in 1913; earlier word-form puzzles may have influenced it.
The name “Cross-Word” reportedly began when an illustrator accidentally reversed the words in “Word-Cross.”
Crossword collections helped fuel the puzzle’s popularity in the 1920s; the New York Times published its first crossword in 1942.
In cryptic crosswords, clues combine a definition with wordplay involving the answer’s letters; many U.S. crosswords more often use definition-style clues.

overview.text: Skiing is travel and sport on snow using skis, long pieces of equipment attached to the feet. Archaeological finds and rock art show that skis were used in northern Europe thousands of years ago, especially as practical tools for getting around; the evidence does not establish one simple birthplace. Over time, different ski designs and styles developed for varied terrain and activities. Modern skiing includes several distinct competitive branches, such as alpine skiing, cross-country, ski jumping, Nordic combined and freestyle—not only downhill skiing at resorts. The International Ski and Snowboard Federation, founded in 1924, governs major international disciplines and sets competition rules. Skiing’s significance reflects its transformation from winter transport into recreation and organized sport.

key_facts.text: Ski use in northern Europe dates back thousands of years: rock art and preserved skis provide evidence, though they do not prove where skiing first began.
Skis were practical equipment for winter travel, hunting and communication before skiing became a widespread sport and recreation.
Ski designs differ by activity; alpine and cross-country skis, for example, are among several specialized types.
FIS recognizes branches including alpine skiing, cross-country, ski jumping, Nordic combined and freestyle skiing, and sets international competition rules.
The Ski Museum at Holmenkollen, established in 1923, describes its collection as presenting 5,000 years of skiing history.

overview.text: Archery is the practice of using a bow to shoot arrows. Once used for hunting and warfare, it is now also a recreational activity and an organized sport built on precision, focus and control. Across cultures, people developed different bows and techniques using local materials; bows and arrows have also served as ceremonial objects and expressions of cultural identity. In Olympic target archery, competitors use recurve bows to shoot at circular targets 70 metres away, scoring by how close their arrows land to the centre. Individual and team match play make accuracy and consistency essential. Archery appeared in the modern Olympics in 1900, returned permanently in 1972, and remains a link between ancient technology and contemporary sport.

key_facts.text: Archery uses a bow to propel arrows; today, it is practiced both recreationally and competitively.
Historically, archery served hunting and warfare. Bows and techniques varied around the world, shaped by local materials and ways of life.

Evidence dates the practice to prehistory, but exact dating depends on the evidence described: World Archery cites flint arrowheads around 20,000 BCE and separately gives European signs around 10,000 BCE.
At the Olympics, archers use recurve bows and shoot at circular targets from 70 metres; the rings score from one point at the outer edge to ten at the centre.
Archery featured at the modern Olympics in 1900, 1904, 1908 and 1920; it returned in 1972 and has remained on the programme since.

overview.text: The National Football League (NFL) is a professional American-football league whose member clubs compete in an organized season. Formed in Canton, Ohio, in 1920 as the American Professional Football Association (APFA), it was intended to bring greater order to a sport then centered largely in Midwestern towns, where teams competed for players and schedules varied. The association adopted the National Football League name in 1922. Today its 32 teams are divided between two conferences—the AFC and NFC—with four four-team divisions in each. Each club plays 17 regular-season games over an 18-week schedule; a rotating formula helps determine opponents and ensures recurring matchups across the league.

key_facts.text: The league was organized in Canton, Ohio, in 1920, first under the name American Professional Football Association.
Jim Thorpe, a famous athlete of his era, was elected the association’s first president.
The association changed its name to the National Football League in 1922.
The NFL’s 32 teams are arranged into the AFC and NFC; each conference has four divisions of four teams.
Each team plays 17 regular-season games over 18 weeks, with one bye week.

overview.text: Ferrari is an Italian sports-car maker and racing organization closely associated with Maranello. Its founder, Enzo Ferrari, created Scuderia Ferrari in Modena in 1929; after starting a separate car-making venture, he moved his factory to Maranello during World War II, and the first Ferrari race car appeared in 1947. The company’s identity combines road-car production with top-level competition: Scuderia Ferrari has entered every Formula One World Championship season since the series began in 1950. Its prancing-horse badge is a defining symbol, and Ferrari remains the championship’s longest-running team, with 16 constructors’ titles.

key_facts.text: Enzo Ferrari founded Scuderia Ferrari in Modena in 1929; it initially worked with Alfa Romeo and managed the company’s sporting activity.
The first Ferrari race car appeared in 1947, after the factory moved to Maranello during World War II.
Maranello remains closely tied to Ferrari: the town’s history page identifies the Ferrari factory there and describes the long connection between the company and the town.
Scuderia Ferrari has competed in every Formula One World Championship season since the championship began in 1950.
The prancing horse is Ferrari’s distinctive emblem; Formula One’s 2026 team guide lists 16 constructors’ titles for Ferrari.

overview.text: The Denver Broncos are a professional American football team based in Denver, Colorado. Awarded a charter place in the American Football League (AFL) in 1959, they began playing in 1960. The team’s first major breakthrough came in 1977, when it reached the playoffs for the first time and won its first AFC championship; its defense became known as the “Orange Crush.” The Broncos have won three Super Bowls: XXXII, XXXIII, and 50. Their home is Empower Field at Mile High. The name “Broncos” was chosen through a statewide contest before the team’s inaugural season, giving the franchise a lasting Western-themed identity.

key_facts.text: The franchise was awarded in 1959 as a charter AFL member, and its first season was 1960.
Denver’s first playoff appearance and first AFC championship came in 1977; the team’s defense that year was nicknamed the “Orange Crush.”
The Broncos’ three Super Bowl titles are XXXII, XXXIII, and 50.
A statewide contest selected the name “Broncos” before the team began play; Ward M. Vining was named the contest winner.
The team’s home venue is Empower Field at Mile High in Denver.

overview.text: The Indianapolis 500, often called the Indy 500, is an annual automobile race held at Indianapolis Motor Speedway in Speedway, Indiana, as part of the NTT INDYCAR SERIES. The race covers 500 miles—200 laps of the Speedway’s 2.5-mile circuit. First run on May 30, 1911, it was planned as one major annual contest to attract attention to cars and their makers. Ray Harroun won the inaugural race in the Marmon Wasp. A distinctive tradition is the pace-car start: since the first running, a pace car has led the field before the race begins. The 1911 event is believed to have been the first major event to use a pace vehicle for its start.

key_facts.text: The inaugural race took place on May 30, 1911; Ray Harroun won in the Marmon Wasp.
The race distance is 500 miles, or 200 laps of the 2.5-mile Indianapolis Motor Speedway circuit.
The race was conceived as a single long annual contest intended to attract publicity and showcase automobiles and their makers.
A pace car has led the field at every Indianapolis 500 since 1911. The Speedway says the first race is believed to have been the first major event to use a pace vehicle for its start.
HISTORY describes the Indianapolis 500 as one of the world’s most famous motor-racing competitions.

overview.text: Diego Armando Maradona was an Argentine footballer celebrated for his close control, dribbling, vision and passing. His defining achievement came at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, where he led Argentina to the title and became the tournament’s standout player. In a quarter-final against England, he scored twice in a 2–1 win: first a controversial handball goal later nicknamed the “Hand of God,” then a celebrated solo run past several opponents and goalkeeper Peter Shilton. The contrast between those goals—one contentious, the other admired for its skill—helped make Maradona one of football’s most recognizable figures. ([bbc.co.uk](https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/44627510))

key_facts.text: Maradona scored twice in Argentina’s 2–1 quarter-final victory over England on June 22, 1986.
The first goal followed a handball; the referee allowed it to stand, and Maradona later described it as scored partly with his hand.
Four minutes later, Maradona ran from his own half, dribbled past English players and goalkeeper Peter Shilton, and scored what became known as the “Goal of the Century.”
At the 1986 World Cup, Maradona scored five goals and provided five assists; he also set up Jorge Burruchaga’s winning goal in the final.
His ball control, agility, vision, dribbling and passing were among the qualities that made him stand out as a player.

overview.text: The Big Ten Conference is an association of U.S. universities that organizes intercollegiate athletic competition. It took shape in 1896, when faculty representatives from seven universities established rules for college athletics, including student eligibility standards. Its name reflects its history: the media first called it the “Big Ten” in 1917, when it had nine members, and the conference formally adopted the name in 1987. In 2024, Oregon, UCLA, USC and Washington joined, bringing membership to 18 universities. The conference sponsors 28 sports and is distinctive for connecting athletic competition with an emphasis on academics.

key_facts.text: Seven universities established the conference’s foundations in 1896; the original goal included setting rules for intercollegiate athletics and student eligibility.
The conference’s name did not match its membership count for much of its history: media used “Big Ten” in 1917, and the conference formally adopted the name in 1987.
The University of Chicago, an early member, left the conference in 1946.
Oregon, UCLA, USC and Washington officially joined on August 2, 2024, bringing the conference to 18 member universities.
The conference sponsors 28 official sports: 14 for men and 14 for women.

overview.text: The University of Southern California (USC) is a private research university in Los Angeles, California. It opened in 1880, when Los Angeles was still a small frontier town, and grew from its first 53 students into a major institution with broad academic and research programs. Its sports teams are the Trojans, and USC’s athletic identity is especially visible through Traveler, a white horse ridden by a Trojan warrior at home football games; the tradition began in 1961. USC also has a notable athletic record, including a 26-year run of national team titles and a long Olympic history. USC officially joined the Big Ten Conference on August 2, 2024, alongside UCLA, Oregon and Washington.

key_facts.text: USC opened in 1880 with 53 students and 10 teachers.
USC describes itself as a private research university and links its work to Los Angeles and Southern California.
Traveler, the white horse ridden by a Trojan warrior, first appeared at USC football games in 1961.
USC’s Trojan teams won at least one national team title in 26 consecutive years, from 1959–60 through 1984–85.
USC became a Big Ten member on August 2, 2024, together with UCLA, Oregon and Washington.

overview.text: A baseball home run (HR, or “homer”) is a fair-ball play on which the batter scores without being put out or benefiting from an error. Most often, the ball flies over the outfield fence in fair territory: the batter is credited with all four bases, and any runners already on base score as well. A ball that hits a foul pole counts. The ball need not leave the field, however: when it stays in play and the batter safely touches all four bases, it is an inside-the-park home run. Because one swing can score several runs, homers can sharply affect a game; they are also used to gauge hitting power, although park dimensions and conditions influence totals.

key_facts.text: A home run hit over the fence in fair territory gives the batter all four bases and scores any runners already on base.
A ball that hits a foul pole is a home run; foul poles mark the boundary between fair and foul territory.
An inside-the-park home run happens when a batter keeps the ball in play but safely reaches all four bases without being put out.
Home runs are used to evaluate hitters’ power, but ballpark size, wall height, and wind can affect whether a hit clears the fence.
Home-run records have been celebrated milestones: the Baseball Hall of Fame describes Babe Ruth’s 60 home runs in 1927 as a major benchmark, while noting that later players surpassed it.

overview.text: Baseball is a bat-and-ball team sport played on a field. In Major League Baseball’s rules, two teams of nine players take turns on offense and defense: the batter tries to become a runner, while fielders try to stop runners advancing. A runner scores by legally touching first, second, third, and home; the team with more runs wins. A regulation MLB game is nine innings, though ties can extend play and games may be shortened in specified situations. Baseball’s rules took shape gradually: New York clubs used differing rules in the 1850s, and a 1857 convention produced a shared rulebook. The game’s history and cultural influence are closely connected with American life, but the story that Abner Doubleday invented baseball in Cooperstown in 1839 is a legend, not an established account.

key_facts.text: In MLB rules, a runner scores by touching first, second, third, and home in order.
MLB’s rulebook specifies nine players per team and nine innings for a regulation game, with exceptions.
New York clubs had differing rules in the 1850s; a convention in 1857 adopted a shared rulebook.
The Cooperstown story crediting Abner Doubleday with baseball’s invention in 1839 is described as legendary, not established history.
The Baseball Hall of Fame describes baseball as reflecting and influencing aspects of American life and culture.

overview.text: En passant (“in passing”) is a special capture made by a pawn. It is possible when an opposing pawn moves two squares from its starting square and ends beside your pawn. On your very next turn, your pawn may capture it as though it had moved only one square: your pawn moves diagonally to the square the enemy pawn crossed, and the enemy pawn is removed. The capture is optional, but the chance disappears after that turn. This rule accompanies the pawn’s first-move two-square advance and, in effect, stops that move from passing an adjacent pawn without a possible capture. Its unusual feature is that the capturing pawn lands on a different square from the captured pawn.

key_facts.text: Only a pawn can make an en passant capture, and only an opposing pawn can be captured this way.
The opposing pawn must have just advanced two squares from its original square and finished next to the capturing pawn.
The capturing pawn moves diagonally to the square the opposing pawn crossed; the captured pawn is removed from its destination square.
The capture is optional, but it is legal only on the move immediately after the two-square advance.
“En passant” is French for “in passing.”

overview.text: The Houston Astros are Houston, Texas’s Major League Baseball club, which began play in 1962 as the expansion Houston Colt .45s, a National League team. They beat the Chicago Cubs 11–2 in their first game at temporary Colt Stadium. Before the 1965 season, the franchise adopted “Astros,” a name linked in team history to Houston’s NASA-associated space program, and moved into the Astrodome. The domed venue made the team especially identifiable with Houston’s space-age image and was an engineering landmark; its field later became the first in baseball to use artificial turf, called AstroTurf. The franchise won its first World Series title in 2017 and a second in 2022.

key_facts.text: Houston’s first major-league team, the Colt .45s, debuted in 1962 and beat the Chicago Cubs in its first game.
The team name changed to the Astros before the 1965 season, reflecting Houston’s connection to the space program.
The Astros moved into the Astrodome in 1965; artificial turf was installed there in 1966 and became known as AstroTurf.
The franchise played in the National League through 2012 and moved to the American League in 2013.
Houston won its first World Series championship in 2017 and its second in 2022.

overview.text: Castling is a special chess move that shifts a king and one of its own rooks together as a single move: the king moves two squares toward that rook, and the rook moves to the square the king crossed. Players may castle kingside (0-0) or queenside (0-0-0). It stands out because it is the only move that moves two pieces at once, and the king’s only move of more than one square. In standard chess, castling is legal only if neither the king nor chosen rook has moved, the intervening squares are clear, and the king is not in check, crossing an attacked square, or landing on one. It can protect the king and help bring a rook toward the center; an attacked rook alone does not forbid castling.

key_facts.text: Castling is made with the king and a rook of the same color, as one move.
The king and the particular rook used must not have moved earlier in the game; moving one rook does not by itself remove the right to castle with the other.
The squares between the king and rook must be empty. The king cannot castle out of check, through an attacked square, or onto an attacked square.
Castling toward the kingside is written 0-0; castling toward the queenside is written 0-0-0.
Castling can improve the king’s safety and bring a rook into play; the rook being attacked does not, by itself, prevent castling.

overview.text: Bullfighting, or tauromachy, is a public spectacle best known as a Spanish tradition, with a related history in parts of Latin America. In the Spanish-style corrida de toros, a matador and assistants face a bull in a ring through a set sequence of events. First, the bull is drawn with a cape and confronted by mounted picadors; next, banderilleros place decorated barbed sticks; finally, the matador uses a smaller cloth called a muleta and usually kills the bull with a sword. The formal stages, specialized roles, costumes and audience rituals distinguish a corrida from an ordinary contest. Bullfighting has also influenced Spanish art and literature, though its meaning and acceptance vary among people.

key_facts.text: A corrida begins with a parade called the paseíllo; its three main phases are the tercio de varas, tercio de banderillas and tercio de muerte.
The matador leads the performance, assisted by picadors on horseback and banderilleros on foot.
In the final phase, the matador performs a sequence of passes with the muleta and typically uses a sword to kill the bull.
Bullfighting is strongly associated with Spain, and the tradition also has a long history in parts of Latin America.
Madrid’s tourism guide connects bullfighting with works by artists and writers including Goya, Picasso and Lorca.

overview.text: American football, also called gridiron football, is a team sport that developed in the United States from rugby and soccer. Rutgers and Princeton played a game commonly identified as the first college football game in 1869; in the 1880s, Yale player Walter Camp helped shape the rules of the developing American game. Teams take turns trying to advance an oval ball by running or passing it forward, while the opposing defense tries to stop them or gain possession. Under NFL rules, an offense has up to four downs to advance 10 yards for a new set of downs. Carrying or catching the ball in the opponent’s end zone scores a six-point touchdown; a kick through the goalposts scores a field goal. Rules can vary by level of play.

key_facts.text: Walter Camp helped codify the game in the 1880s; the Library of Congress credits him with innovations including the 11-player team and quarterback position.
Under NFL rules, an offense earns a new first down by advancing 10 yards within a series of up to four downs.
In the NFL, a touchdown is worth six points and a field goal is worth three; after a touchdown, a team can attempt to score extra points.
Professional football took shape in the 1890s, and team representatives formed a professional league in 1920 that later became the NFL.
The Pro Football Hall of Fame traces the game’s roots to both soccer and rugby, and describes Walter Camp’s rule changes as helping transform rugby into American football.

overview.text: Stephen Curry, born Wardell Stephen Curry II, is an American professional basketball guard for the Golden State Warriors. After starring at Davidson College, where he led the Wildcats to the 2008 NCAA tournament Elite Eight, he was selected seventh overall by Golden State in 2009. Curry is especially known for his three-point shooting: in 2015–16, he made an NBA-record 402 three-pointers and became the league’s first unanimous Most Valuable Player. His long-range accuracy and willingness to shoot from far beyond the basket helped change how the game is played, making him one of modern basketball’s defining players.

key_facts.text: His full name is Wardell Stephen Curry II; he was born in Akron, Ohio, on March 14, 1988.
At Davidson, he led the Wildcats to the 2008 NCAA tournament Elite Eight and was named the Midwest Regional’s Most Outstanding Player.
The Golden State Warriors selected Curry seventh overall in the 2009 NBA Draft.
In 2015–16, Curry made 402 three-pointers, then an NBA single-season record, and became the NBA’s first unanimous MVP.
On December 14, 2021, he broke the NBA record for career three-pointers made.

overview.text: Lionel Andrés Messi, widely known as Leo Messi, is an Argentine football forward born in Rosario on June 24, 1987. He became a defining player for FC Barcelona, where he spent 17 first-team seasons, scored 672 goals, and won 35 trophies; his eight Ballon d’Or awards are another landmark of his career. With Argentina, he helped end a 28-year wait for a Copa América title in 2021, earning the tournament’s best-player award. In 2022, he helped Argentina win the FIFA World Cup, scoring twice in the final and converting a penalty in the shootout. His exceptional club record and major international achievements distinguish his career.

key_facts.text: Messi was born in Rosario, Argentina, on June 24, 1987.
He spent 17 first-team seasons at FC Barcelona, scored 672 goals, and won 35 trophies with the club.
He won the Ballon d’Or eight times, with his eighth award coming in 2023.
Argentina won the 2021 Copa América; Messi was named the tournament’s best player and finished among its leading scorers with four goals.

overview.text: John Fetterman is a Pennsylvania Democrat and U.S. senator whose political career moved from local to state to federal office. Raised in York, he attended Albright College and, while teaching GED classes, was encouraged by students to run for mayor of Braddock; he served there for 13 years. In 2018, he became Pennsylvania’s 34th lieutenant governor. He won election to the U.S. Senate in 2022 and took office on January 3, 2023. In that election, he defeated Republican Mehmet Oz, receiving 2,751,012 votes to Oz’s 2,487,260, according to the Federal Election Commission’s results compilation. His path from a small-town mayoralty to statewide and national office distinguishes his political career.

He served as mayor of Braddock for 13 years after students encouraged him to run while he was teaching GED classes.
He was Pennsylvania’s 34th lieutenant governor, inaugurated in January 2019.

overview.text: Kansas is a Great Plains state whose history became nationally significant through antebellum conflict over slavery and later Black migration west. The 1854 Kansas–Nebraska Act let settlers decide whether slavery would be permitted in the territory; rival factions, contested elections, and violence came to be known as “Bleeding Kansas.” Kansas entered the Union as a free state on January 29, 1861, although slavery remained legal in the territory until statehood. In 1877, formerly enslaved African Americans founded Nicodemus in northwest Kansas, building a community that offered new opportunities after the Civil War. The sunflower, adopted as the state flower in 1903, gave rise to Kansas’s familiar nickname, the “Sunflower State.”

key_facts.text: The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854 established Kansas Territory and used popular sovereignty to let settlers decide the slavery question.
“Bleeding Kansas” refers to the sometimes-deadly conflict among pro-slavery supporters, Free-Staters, and abolitionists before statehood.
Kansas became the 34th state on January 29, 1861, under a free-state constitution.
Founded in 1877, Nicodemus was established by formerly enslaved African Americans, many of whom came from the Lexington, Kentucky area.
Kansas adopted the wild native sunflower as its state flower in 1903; “Sunflower State” became a common nickname.

overview.text: Al Capone (Alphonse Gabriel Capone, 1899–1947) was a Chicago organized-crime leader whose rise was tied to Prohibition, when federal law barred the manufacture, sale, and transportation of alcohol. After moving to Chicago around 1920, he advanced in Johnny Torrio’s criminal organization and became its boss in 1925. His operation profited from illegal liquor and other rackets amid violent gang rivalries. Capone’s mob was widely blamed for the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre, but investigators never proved his involvement; Capone was in Florida that day. Convicted of federal tax evasion in 1931, he served time in Atlanta and Alcatraz. His story illustrates how illegal alcohol trading helped organized crime grow in Chicago.

key_facts.text: Capone was born in Brooklyn, New York, in January 1899, and moved to Chicago around 1920.
He became the boss of Johnny Torrio’s Chicago organization in 1925.
Chicago became a major center for bootlegging during Prohibition; Al Capone was among the prominent gang leaders there.
Seven members or associates of the Bugs Moran mob were killed in the 1929 St. Valentine’s Day Massacre. Capone’s mob was generally blamed, but his involvement was not proven; he was in Florida.
After his 1931 federal conviction for tax evasion, Capone received an 11-year sentence and served time in Atlanta and Alcatraz.

overview.text: George Corley Wallace Jr. (1919–1998) was an Alabama politician whose career became closely associated with resistance to efforts to end racial segregation. Elected governor four times, he gained national notoriety in 1963 for defending segregation in his inaugural address and for standing in the doorway of the University of Alabama as two Black students sought to enroll. He eventually stepped aside after federal intervention. In 1968, Wallace ran for president as the American Independent Party’s candidate. He finished third, receiving 46 electoral votes; his campaign brought his segregationist politics and opposition to federal power to a national audience.

key_facts.text: Wallace was elected Alabama governor four times: in 1962, 1970, 1974, and 1982.
His 1963 inaugural address publicly defended segregation; later that year, he tried to block two Black students from enrolling at the University of Alabama.
Wallace stepped aside at the university after President Kennedy federalized the Alabama National Guard.
In 1968, he was the American Independent Party’s presidential candidate and received 46 electoral votes.
An assassination attempt at a 1972 campaign rally left Wallace paralyzed below the waist.

overview.text: The Federalist Papers, also called The Federalist, are 85 essays written by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay and published anonymously under the shared name Publius. Printed in New York newspapers in 1787–1788, they urged New Yorkers to ratify the proposed Constitution and answered objections raised during the debate. The essays explained how parts of the new government were intended to work, including how a large republic might manage competing interests and how separated branches could check one another. Their significance extends beyond the ratification campaign: historians and readers use them as an important source for understanding arguments about the Constitution, though they are essays advocating a position, not a neutral record of everyone’s views.

key_facts.text: The essays appeared in New York newspapers and were later collected in a two-volume edition.
Publius was a shared pen name for Hamilton, Madison, and Jay; the essays were published anonymously.
The essays promoted ratification amid opposition that included concerns about central power and the absence of a bill of rights.
Federalist No. 10 discusses factions and the possibility of governing a large republic.
The Library of Congress describes the essays as an important source for interpreting the Constitution’s intentions.

overview.text: John Adams (1735–1826) was a Massachusetts lawyer, Founding-era independence advocate, diplomat, and Federalist who became the United States’ first vice president and second president. As a delegate to the Continental Congress, he supported independence and served on the committee that prepared the Declaration of Independence. His diplomatic work in Europe included helping secure Dutch support and a loan for the Revolution; later he represented the new nation in the Netherlands and Great Britain. As president (1797–1801), he avoided war with France, though his administration’s Alien and Sedition Acts remain a major controversy. His defeat by Thomas Jefferson in 1800 produced the nation’s first transfer of power between political parties. He was married to Abigail Adams, with whom he shared a long partnership and correspondence.

key_facts.text: Born in Braintree, Massachusetts, Adams studied at Harvard and trained as a lawyer.
He defended British soldiers charged after the Boston Massacre, an episode that brought him public attention.
He married Abigail Smith in 1764; they shared a long life of public service and correspondence.
As a diplomat, Adams served in the Netherlands and Great Britain; in the Netherlands, he helped secure a loan for the American war effort.
His presidency avoided war with France, but also saw passage of the controversial Alien and Sedition Acts.
His 1800 defeat by Thomas Jefferson led to the first transfer of power between political parties in U.S. history.

overview.text: John Hancock (1737–1793) was a Boston merchant and Patriot politician whose wealth and public standing helped make him an influential revolutionary leader. Elected president of the Second Continental Congress in May 1775, he led it through the Declaration of Independence debate and was the first to sign the document in 1776. His bold, flamboyant signature became closely associated with the Declaration, though it was only one part of a long political career. After the Revolution, Hancock became the first governor under Massachusetts’s 1780 constitution and served again from 1787 until his death.

key_facts.text: Hancock inherited and took over his uncle’s Boston merchant business in 1764.
He was unanimously elected president of the Continental Congress in May 1775 and served until October 1777.
As Congress’s president, he presided over the Declaration of Independence debate and was its first signer in 1776.
Hancock’s flamboyant signature made him especially famous, although he also had a substantial business and political career.
He was Massachusetts’s first governor under its 1780 constitution and later returned to the governorship, serving until 1793.

overview.text: Passed by Congress on March 3, 1873, the Comstock Act was a federal law restricting mail circulation of certain materials. Named for Anthony Comstock, an anti-vice campaigner who lobbied for the measure and later served as a postal special agent, it targeted obscene publications as well as contraceptive devices and information. The law’s reach extended beyond sexual publications: National Archives examples include anatomy books and photographs of boxing matches. Because the statute did not define obscenity, its enforcement could extend to a broad range of material. The law drew organized opposition, including a petition seeking repeal or modification, and became a focus of birth-control activism and legal challenges.

key_facts.text: Congress passed the law on March 3, 1873; it became known by the name of anti-vice campaigner Anthony Comstock.
It restricted mailing obscene publications and contraceptive devices or information.
The National Archives notes that the law did not define obscenity and describes Comstock as a postal special agent who policed the mails.

In 1879, the National Defense Association submitted a petition with more than 70,000 signatures asking Congress to repeal or modify the law; it later supplied affidavits defending the signatures’ legitimacy.
A 1936 federal appeals court decision allowed doctors to distribute contraceptives across state lines, a change PBS describes as an important step in the law’s history.

overview.text: Connecticut Colony was an English colony in New England, in the region that is now Connecticut. It formed in 1636, when Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield joined as a political community. Its development drew together several settlements: Saybrook joined Connecticut in 1644, while New Haven remained separate until a 1662 royal charter began uniting it with Connecticut; the merger was completed in 1665. These English settlements arose on lands long inhabited by Indigenous peoples, including Pequots, Mohegans, Paugussets, and Schaghticokes. The colony’s distinctive early achievement was the Fundamental Orders, adopted in 1639 as a written framework for government by Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield. Often described as an early written constitution, the Orders helped give Connecticut its later “Constitution State” identity.

key_facts.text: Indigenous peoples, including Pequots, Mohegans, Paugussets, and Schaghticokes, lived in the region long before English colonial settlement.
The Connecticut Colony formed from Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield in 1636; the separate Saybrook Colony joined in 1644.
The Fundamental Orders were adopted on January 14, 1639; the date appears as 1638 in the document because of the calendar then in use.
The Orders set out a written government framework for Hartford, Windsor, and Wethersfield and operated from 1639 until the 1662 royal charter.
New Haven and Connecticut were separate colonies until the 1662 charter; their unification was completed in 1665.

overview.text: The Sons of Liberty were colonial resistance groups that first formed in Boston in 1765, amid opposition to the Stamp Act. Artisans, shopkeepers, and small merchants took part, using public protest and sometimes force to challenge British policies they considered violations of their rights. The movement spread to other colonies, where local groups organized protests and boycotts. In Boston, members helped organize resistance to the Tea Act; on December 16, 1773, some joined the destruction of East India Company tea in Boston Harbor, an act remembered as the Boston Tea Party. The name also belonged to groups outside Boston, including Rhode Island resisters involved in the 1772 burning of the customs schooner HMS Gaspee.

key_facts.text: The Boston group formed in summer 1765 as opposition to the Stamp Act grew.
Participants included artisans, shopkeepers, and small-time merchants; protests included effigies and attacks on officials’ property.
Sons of Liberty groups spread beyond Boston, while women’s boycotts and other actions also helped broaden resistance.
In Boston, members helped organize opposition to the Tea Act and, after efforts to return the tea failed, some joined the December 16, 1773 destruction of tea from three ships.
Rhode Island Sons of Liberty burned the customs schooner HMS Gaspee in 1772, before the Boston Tea Party.

overview.text: The California Gold Rush was the surge of migration and gold seeking that followed James Marshall’s discovery of gold flakes at a sawmill in Coloma on January 24, 1848. News spread, and by 1849 people were arriving by land and sea to seek gold, using methods such as panning and sluicing to separate it from river sediment. The rush accelerated California’s growth and helped it enter the United States as a state in 1850. It also brought severe harm to Native Californians: newcomers took land and resources, while laws and violence enabled forced labor and attacks. Marshall’s find sparked the famous rush, though it was not the first gold discovery in California.

key_facts.text: Marshall found gold flakes in the sawmill’s tailrace at Coloma on January 24, 1848; gold had been discovered in California before.
News spread quickly, but President James Polk confirmed the discovery to Congress in December 1848; a major influx of migrants followed in 1849.
Placer miners separated gold from river sediment with tools including pans, rockers, and sluices.
The population surge helped California enter the Union as a state in 1850 without first becoming a U.S. territory.
Native Californians faced dispossession, loss of resources, forced labor, and violence during the period; state and federal governments sometimes supported attackers.

overview.text: At the Ohio Women’s Rights Convention in Akron in May 1851, abolitionist and women’s-rights advocate Sojourner Truth spoke extemporaneously about women’s equality. Born enslaved as Isabella Baumfree, she challenged claims that women were too weak or intellectually unsuited for equal rights, linking arguments about women’s status with slavery and racial injustice. The speech is now widely called “Ain’t I a Woman?”—a title associated with the version published by Frances Gage in 1863. A report by Marius Robinson, published soon after the convention, differs and does not include that phrase. Because Truth spoke without a written text, the surviving versions are other people’s records, not a verbatim transcript.

key_facts.text: Truth was born Isabella Baumfree, was enslaved in New York, and spoke Dutch as her first language.
She spoke at the Ohio Women’s Rights Convention in Akron in May 1851; she delivered the speech extemporaneously.

The version reported by Marius Robinson appeared in the Anti-Slavery Bugle on June 21, 1851. It discusses women’s rights, labor, intellect, and biblical arguments, but does not use the familiar title phrase.

Frances Gage published a different account in 1863, twelve years after the speech. It popularized the phrase “Ain’t I a Woman?” and rendered Truth’s words in a Southern dialect despite her New York upbringing and Dutch first language.
The speech is significant for joining women’s-rights advocacy with abolition and for challenging claims that Black people and women were inferior.

overview.text: Warren G. Harding was an Ohio newspaper publisher and Republican politician who became the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923. Before reaching the White House, he served in Ohio politics and represented Ohio in the U.S. Senate. Elected in 1920 after promising a “return to normalcy,” Harding appealed to voters weary of wartime upheaval and reform-era politics. His short presidency is especially associated with Teapot Dome: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly leased a Wyoming naval oil reserve to a private company without competitive bidding. A Senate investigation uncovered Fall’s corruption, leaving the scandal a lasting stain on Harding’s administration.

key_facts.text: Harding built his early career as a newspaper publisher in Marion, Ohio, before entering state and national politics.
He served as president from 1921 to 1923 and died in office in August 1923.
“A Return to Normalcy” was the campaign slogan associated with his 1920 victory over Democrat James M. Cox.
Teapot Dome concerned Secretary of the Interior Albert Fall’s secret, no-bid lease of a Wyoming naval oil reserve to a private company.
The Senate inquiry into the lease led to Fall becoming the first former cabinet officer to go to prison.

overview.text: The U.S. Department of the Interior (DOI) is a Cabinet-level executive department created by Congress on March 3, 1849, to bring together federal offices handling the nation’s internal affairs. Today, it protects and manages natural resources and cultural heritage, provides scientific information, and honors federal trust commitments to Indigenous peoples and communities. Its distinguishing feature is its wide reach: specialized bureaus work on public lands, national parks, wildlife, geology, water, and Indian affairs, so DOI is not simply a parks agency. Its history also reflects changing federal policy: Indian Affairs moved into Interior in 1849, while the department now describes its work with tribes in terms that include self-determination and self-governance.

key_facts.text: Congress created the department on March 3, 1849, consolidating several offices, including the General Land Office, Indian Affairs Office, and patent and pension offices.
DOI’s stated mission includes managing natural resources and cultural heritage, providing scientific information, and honoring trust responsibilities or special commitments to Indigenous communities.

Its bureaus have distinct roles: for example, the National Park Service manages park sites, the Bureau of Land Management manages public lands, and the U.S. Geological Survey provides science about natural resources and hazards.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs was established within the War Department in 1824 and transferred to Interior in 1849; the name “Bureau of Indian Affairs” was formally adopted in 1947.
The Bureau of Indian Affairs fulfills trust responsibilities and promotes self-determination and self-governance for federally recognized tribes and Alaska Natives.

overview.text: The Wounded Knee Massacre took place on December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee Creek in southwestern South Dakota, when U.S. Seventh Cavalry troops opened fire on a Miniconjou Lakota camp while trying to disarm its people. The camp included women and children; the Lakota dead numbered more than 250, with some estimates reaching about 300. This violence followed rising official alarm over the Ghost Dance, a Native religious movement that many Lakota found hopeful, but the event should not be reduced to a simple armed uprising: the band was largely unarmed and was not engaged in combat when the shooting began. Remembered as a massacre and a symbol of coercive U.S. policy toward Native peoples, Wounded Knee became a lasting place of remembrance.

key_facts.text: The massacre occurred on December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee Creek in southwestern South Dakota.
Most victims belonged to the Miniconjou Lakota; the camp included women and children.
The shooting began during the Army’s attempt to disarm the Lakota camp; soldiers also fired Hotchkiss guns.
Casualty estimates differ: the University of Nebraska–Lincoln account reports more than 250 Lakota dead and notes estimates as high as 300.
The Ghost Dance was a Native religious movement; officials’ fears about it helped spur military intervention, while many Lakota adherents saw it as a source of hope.
Wounded Knee became a lasting symbol of the harm caused by U.S. policy toward Native peoples.

overview.text: The Battle of Shiloh, also called Pittsburg Landing, was fought in southwestern Tennessee on April 6–7, 1862, during the American Civil War. Confederate forces under Albert Sidney Johnston surprised Union troops commanded by Ulysses S. Grant near Pittsburg Landing, where Grant’s army was waiting for reinforcements before advancing toward Corinth, Mississippi—a key railroad junction. The first day brought fierce fighting and Union retreats, including at the Hornets’ Nest, a stretch of sunken road where Union defenders held off repeated attacks before Confederate forces surrounded them. After Johnston was killed and P. G. T. Beauregard took command, reinforcements arrived overnight; Grant’s Union forces counterattacked on April 7 and the Confederates withdrew. The battle’s heavy losses made clear how costly the war could become.

key_facts.text: The battle is also known as Pittsburg Landing, named for the landing where Grant’s army established its base.
Grant’s Union army was near Pittsburg Landing while awaiting Don Carlos Buell’s reinforcements and planning to advance toward Corinth.
The Hornets’ Nest was a stretch of Sunken Road where Union troops resisted repeated Confederate attacks before being surrounded and captured.
Confederate commander Albert Sidney Johnston died after being wounded on April 6; P. G. T. Beauregard then took command.
The Union victory helped open the way for Federal forces to advance toward Corinth, an important railroad center.

overview.text: The Spanish-American War was the 1898 conflict between the United States and Spain, fought amid Cuba’s long independence struggle and rising tensions after the USS Maine exploded in Havana Harbor; the explosion’s cause remained uncertain. Fighting spanned the Caribbean and Pacific: the first battle was a U.S. naval victory at Manila Bay, and U.S. forces also fought in Cuba. The Treaty of Paris, signed December 10, 1898, ended the war: Spain relinquished its claims to Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam, and the Philippines to the United States, selling the Philippines for $20 million. Cuba’s independence came later, while the new U.S. control of the Philippines brought resistance from Filipino nationalists.

key_facts.text: Congress voted for war on April 25, 1898, after tensions escalated over Cuba and the USS Maine’s destruction; the cause of the explosion was not established with certainty.
The first battle took place at Manila Bay on May 1, where Commodore George Dewey’s squadron defeated the Spanish naval force.
The Treaty of Paris ended the war; it guaranteed Cuba’s independence, transferred Puerto Rico and Guam to the United States, and provided for the United States to buy the Philippines from Spain.
The treaty was negotiated by Spanish and U.S. representatives without Cuban, Puerto Rican, or Filipino participation; Filipino nationalists opposed the transfer of their islands to U.S. rule.
Cuba became independent in 1902, after the war and treaty; the conflict helped establish the United States as a power with new overseas possessions.

overview.text: The 1992 Los Angeles riots—also called the uprising or civil unrest—began on April 29, after a jury acquitted four Los Angeles police officers charged over their videotaped beating of Black motorist Rodney King. Protests and unrest spread from South Los Angeles to other parts of the city and lasted six days. The upheaval included violence, looting, arson, and destruction of homes and businesses; Korean American merchants were among those whose livelihoods were devastated, while Black and Latino neighborhoods also suffered. Its meaning remains debated: the event became a defining national moment in discussions of police brutality, racial inequality, and urban poverty, while exposing divisions and prompting community dialogue efforts.

key_facts.text: The unrest began April 29, 1992, following the acquittal of four officers in the Rodney King beating case.
A bystander’s video of King’s 1991 beating was broadcast on local and national television.
The unrest lasted six days and was concentrated especially in South Los Angeles, though events occurred across the city.
Korean American store owners described businesses burned during the unrest and community efforts to aid affected families.
Federal mediators worked with Korean American, African American, and Latino community leaders, as well as law enforcement, to reduce tensions and restore peace.

overview.text: The Donner Party, also called the Donner-Reed Party, was a wagon-train group traveling from Illinois to California in 1846 under the leadership of George Donner and James Reed. Hoping to save time, the emigrants took Lansford Hastings’s cutoff across the Great Salt Lake region; delays instead depleted their supplies and left them reaching the Sierra Nevada late in the year. Heavy snow trapped members near Truckee Lake through the winter of 1846–47. As food ran out, some ate rawhide and the bodies of people who had died. The ordeal became a stark example of the dangers of overland migration, and the camp site is recognized as a National Historic Landmark for its connection to settlement of the West.

key_facts.text: George Donner and James Reed led the emigrant party, which left Illinois in April 1846.
The party took the Hastings Cutoff, promoted as a time-saving route, but delays along the route cost time and depleted supplies.
The emigrants reached Truckee Lake below the Sierra Nevada crest in October and were trapped by winter snow for about four months.
As food disappeared, party members ate rawhide; some also ate people who had died in order to survive.
The Donner Party camp site was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1961 for its significance in the settlement of the West.

overview.text: William Jennings Bryan (1860–1925) was a lawyer, Democratic congressman from Nebraska, and celebrated political orator. His 1896 “Cross of Gold” speech championed free silver, a monetary policy he argued would help ordinary workers, and helped win him the Democratic presidential nomination. He was the party’s nominee in 1896, 1900, and 1908, losing each time. President Woodrow Wilson appointed him secretary of state in 1913; Bryan resigned in 1915 over disagreement about Wilson’s response to German submarine warfare. In 1925, Bryan joined the prosecution of teacher John Scopes in Tennessee’s evolution trial, where defense lawyer Clarence Darrow questioned him about the Bible.

key_facts.text: Born in Salem, Illinois, Bryan moved to Nebraska, represented the state in Congress, and became known as “the Great Commoner.”
The 1896 “Cross of Gold” speech supported free silver and helped propel Bryan to the Democratic presidential nomination.
Bryan was the Democratic presidential nominee in 1896, 1900, and 1908, but lost all three elections.
He served as Woodrow Wilson’s secretary of state from 1913 until resigning in 1915 amid disagreement over the administration’s response to German submarine warfare.
During the 1925 Scopes trial, Bryan helped prosecute John Scopes for teaching evolution and was questioned by Clarence Darrow.

overview.text: Elizabeth Warren is a Democratic U.S. senator from Massachusetts, serving since 2013. Before entering elected office, she taught law and studied bankruptcy, commercial law, and the financial pressures on middle-class families; her research included analysis of bankruptcy court records. After the 2008 financial crisis, she chaired the Congressional Oversight Panel for the Troubled Asset Relief Program and served as a Treasury special adviser helping establish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). Congress created the CFPB through the Dodd-Frank Act to bring consumer financial protections together in one agency. Warren is particularly associated with the bureau’s creation and with advocacy for consumers facing financial products such as mortgages and credit cards.

key_facts.text: Warren has represented Massachusetts in the U.S. Senate since 2013; the Senate lists her as a Democrat.
Her academic specialties include bankruptcy and commercial law, and she researched the financial difficulties of middle-class households.
After the 2008 financial crisis, she chaired the Congressional Oversight Panel for the Troubled Asset Relief Program (TARP).
As a Treasury special adviser, Warren worked on establishing the CFPB; Congress created the bureau under the Dodd-Frank Act.
The CFPB was designed to consolidate federal consumer-finance protections and address unfair or deceptive practices involving financial products and services.

overview.text: The Hartford Convention was a secret meeting of New England Federalists held in Hartford, Connecticut, from December 15, 1814, to January 5, 1815, during the War of 1812. Angered by the war’s costs, threats to coastal trade, and federal policies, delegates sought greater regional control over defense and funds and recommended constitutional amendments. These included requiring a two-thirds congressional vote to declare war, limiting embargoes, and changing how representation and direct taxes were apportioned. Secession talk made the gathering politically explosive, but its documented recommendations focused on these demands and contemplated another convention if they failed. The Treaty of Ghent had been signed before the report appeared, making the recommendations seem out of step with a war that was ending.

key_facts.text: The convention met secretly at Hartford’s Old State House; delegates began meeting on December 15, 1814, and issued their final report on January 5, 1815.
Its delegates were New England Federalists opposed to the War of 1812; they objected to its effects on trade and to wartime federal policies.
Proposed amendments included a two-thirds vote in Congress to declare war, limits on embargoes, and a change to apportionment based on free persons rather than the Constitution’s existing count.

Secession rumors surrounded the meeting, though the Connecticut History account says most New England Federalists were moderate and feared that secession talk could lead to civil war; the National Park Service notes that some radicals considered it.
The Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814, while the convention was still meeting; news of the treaty reached the United States in January 1815.

overview.text: The Federalist Party was one of the United States’ first political parties, taking shape in the early 1790s as national leaders argued over the new Constitution and the power of the federal government. Led especially by Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton and associated with John Adams, Federalists favored a stronger national government than their Democratic-Republican rivals and drew support from commercial interests. They supported measures such as a national bank and a broad reading of federal powers. After Thomas Jefferson’s election in 1800, the Federalists lost national power. Their opposition to the War of 1812 became unpopular, and the party’s influence collapsed in the postwar political realignment.

key_facts.text: By the early 1790s, Federalists and Democratic-Republicans had emerged as recognizable political groups, though the Constitution did not provide for political parties.
Federalists were associated with Alexander Hamilton, John Adams, and John Jay; Federalists generally supported strengthening federal power.
Federalists drew support from commercial interests. A major dispute with Republicans concerned whether the Constitution’s implied powers allowed Congress to create a national bank.
The Federalists opposed the War of 1812 and voted against the war bill; their opposition became unpopular after the war.
Thomas Jefferson’s election in 1800–1801 swept the Federalists from national power, and the War of 1812 marked the party’s decline as political parties realigned afterward.

overview.text: The Battle, or Siege, of Yorktown was the decisive 1781 campaign in Virginia in which American and French forces under George Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau trapped British General Charles Cornwallis’s army. French Admiral de Grasse’s fleet kept control of Chesapeake Bay, blocking British naval support, while allied troops dug siege lines and bombarded Yorktown’s defenses. After the allies captured two key redoubts and a storm foiled a British escape attempt, Cornwallis sought terms. On October 19, his troops laid down their arms. Yorktown ended large-scale fighting in the Revolution and strengthened the push for peace, but the war formally ended with the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

key_facts.text: Allied siege operations began on September 28, 1781, after American and French troops marched from Williamsburg to Yorktown.
French control of Chesapeake Bay helped prevent British reinforcements from reaching Cornwallis and supported the allies’ blockade.
On October 14, French troops captured Redoubt 9 and American troops captured Redoubt 10, helping the allies complete their second siege line.
Cornwallis’s troops surrendered on October 19, 1781; the fighting at Yorktown was a turning point, not the formal end of the war, which came with the 1783 Treaty of Paris.

overview.text: Boston Massacre, also called the Bloody Massacre, was a deadly confrontation on King Street in Boston on March 5, 1770, amid growing tensions between colonists and British authorities and troops stationed in the city. British soldiers fired into a crowd, killing five people and wounding six. Among the dead was Crispus Attucks, a sailor of mixed African and Indigenous ancestry whose killing later made him a prominent symbol of Black participation in the struggle for liberty. In the aftermath, Bostonians disputed what had happened and what it meant; Patriot leaders used public funerals and images such as Paul Revere’s engraving to condemn British power. The episode helped turn local conflict into a widely remembered revolutionary symbol.

key_facts.text: The confrontation occurred outside Boston’s Custom House on King Street.
Five people died and six were wounded; Crispus Attucks was among those killed.
Attucks was a sailor of mixed African and Indigenous ancestry and was identified as the first victim.
The historical record does not establish when or how Attucks gained his freedom.
Boston’s public response included a large funeral procession, which helped shape how the event was remembered.
