overview.text: Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District is a 1969 U.S. Supreme Court case about whether public-school students could express political views at school. In December 1965, Iowa students Mary Beth and John Tinker and Christopher Eckhardt wore black armbands to oppose U.S. involvement in Vietnam and support a truce; school officials suspended them under a ban on armbands. On February 24, 1969, the Court ruled 7–2 for the students, finding their quiet, non-disruptive protest protected by the First Amendment, applied to state schools through the Fourteenth Amendment. The decision is significant for recognizing student expression rights while allowing schools to restrict speech that materially disrupts schoolwork or interferes with others’ rights.

key_facts.text: The Supreme Court decided the case on February 24, 1969, ruling 7–2 for the students.
The students planned to wear black armbands to oppose U.S. hostilities in Vietnam and show support for a truce.
School officials adopted a policy requiring students to remove armbands or face suspension; Mary Beth Tinker, Christopher Eckhardt, and John Tinker were suspended.
The Court found the students’ quiet, passive expression protected in the circumstances because it did not disrupt school or infringe others’ rights.
The Library of Congress describes the decision as a continuing reference point for assessing whether school discipline violates students’ First Amendment rights.

overview.text: Benedict Arnold (1741–1801) was a Connecticut-born merchant and officer whose Revolutionary War service first made him a prominent Patriot commander. In 1775, he helped capture Fort Ticonderoga alongside Ethan Allen, and later fought at Saratoga, where he was wounded in the leg. Disputes and disappointments within the Continental Army preceded his secret negotiations with Britain. While commanding West Point in 1780, Arnold shared military information with the British and plotted to hand over the strategic post on the Hudson River. The scheme was discovered before it succeeded; Arnold escaped and accepted a British military commission. His story is remembered for both his earlier service to the Patriot cause and his notorious betrayal.

key_facts.text: Arnold was born in Norwich, Connecticut, in 1741 and died in London in 1801.
In 1775, he and Ethan Allen shared command during the Patriot capture of Fort Ticonderoga.
At Saratoga in 1777, Arnold led an attack and was wounded in the same leg he had injured earlier in the war.
Arnold’s West Point plot was exposed after British contact John André was captured with documents that implicated him; André was later executed.
After escaping, Arnold served in the British Army, having been a general in both armies during the Revolutionary War.

overview.text: William Henry Seward (1801–1872) was a New York lawyer and politician who became a leading antislavery voice in the Whig and Republican parties. After losing the 1860 Republican presidential nomination to Abraham Lincoln, he served as secretary of state from 1861 to 1869, under both Lincoln and Andrew Johnson. During the Civil War, Seward worked to keep foreign governments from recognizing the Confederacy. In the Trent Affair, he helped defuse a crisis with Britain by agreeing to release Confederate envoys seized from a British ship. After the war, he negotiated the 1867 treaty purchasing Alaska from Russia, making him a prominent figure in U.S. diplomacy and territorial expansion.

key_facts.text: Seward was born in Florida, New York, in 1801 and graduated from Union College in 1820.
Before becoming secretary of state, he served as New York governor and U.S. senator, and became a leading antislavery politician.
In the 1861 Trent Affair, the U.S. Navy seized Confederate envoys from a British ship; Seward agreed to release them, helping ease the diplomatic crisis.
Seward negotiated the 1867 Alaska Purchase treaty with Russia; the U.S. Department of State’s National Museum of American Diplomacy reports the price as $7.2 million.
Seward survived an attempted assassination on the same night Lincoln was killed in 1865.

overview.text: The Alamo, in downtown San Antonio, began in 1718 as Mission San Antonio de Valero, one of several Spanish Franciscan missions along the San Antonio River. After moving to its present site in 1724, it grew into a community with a chapel, priests’ residence, homes, workshops, and irrigation ditches. Secularized in 1793, it later served as a military post. During the Texas Revolution, Mexican troops besieged the fortified compound for 13 days and captured it on March 6, 1836; the defenders’ deaths made the Alamo a powerful rallying symbol, but the battle did not end the war. The origin of its name is disputed: it may honor the soldiers’ former company or refer to nearby cottonwoods.

key_facts.text: The mission’s work involved Indigenous communities; Spanish authorities also used missions to advance territorial claims in Texas.
Two proposed explanations for “Alamo” are the name of the soldiers’ former company and the Spanish word for cottonwood; the name’s origin is uncertain.
The 1836 garrison included Tejanos as well as Americans, Anglo-Texians, and other European immigrants; families and enslaved people were also inside.
The chapel and Long Barrack are among the best-known surviving structures; much of the original mission compound is now beneath city streets and buildings.
The battle became a symbol of sacrifice and a rallying cry in the Texas Revolution; the war continued after the Alamo fell.

overview.text: On the evening of April 14, 1865, actor and Confederate sympathizer John Wilkes Booth shot President Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C., while Lincoln watched the comedy Our American Cousin. Lincoln was carried across the street to a boarding house and died at 7:22 a.m. the next morning. The attack came just five days after Confederate General Robert E. Lee surrendered at Appomattox, as Washington celebrated Union victory. Lincoln’s death abruptly turned that celebration into mourning. Booth’s attack was part of a wider plot that also targeted Secretary of State William Seward and Vice President Andrew Johnson, though Johnson was not attacked.

key_facts.text: Booth shot Lincoln during a performance of Our American Cousin at Ford’s Theatre on April 14, 1865.
Lincoln died in the Petersen Boarding House, across the street from the theatre, at 7:22 a.m. on April 15.
Booth had first plotted to kidnap Lincoln; as the Civil War neared its end, he shifted to a plan to murder him and target other leaders.
Lee’s surrender at Appomattox came five days before the assassination; Lincoln’s death halted Washington’s celebrations of Union victory.
Booth escaped after the shooting but was tracked down and killed in Virginia on April 26, 1865.

overview.text: The Battle of Gettysburg was a three-day Civil War clash fought near Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, July 1–3, 1863. Confederate General Robert E. Lee had moved north into Pennsylvania seeking supplies and a victory that might pressure the United States to make peace; Union forces under General George G. Meade met his army there. After fierce fighting around hills and ridges, the Union held its defensive line against the July 3 assault known as Pickett’s Charge. Lee withdrew toward Virginia beginning July 4, ending his invasion campaign in defeat but not the Civil War. On November 19, Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of a cemetery for Union dead.

key_facts.text: Lee’s move into Pennsylvania aimed partly to find supplies and win a victory that could increase pressure on the U.S. government to seek peace.
The battle began on July 1, when Confederate and Union forces met near Gettysburg; Union troops were pushed through town and regrouped on high ground south of it.
The Union defensive position across Cemetery Ridge, Cemetery Hill, Culp’s Hill, and Little Round Top formed a line often described as a fishhook.
On July 3, Pickett’s Charge attacked the Union center on Cemetery Ridge and failed; Lee began retreating to Virginia the next day.
Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of the Soldiers’ National Cemetery; the war continued after the battle.

overview.text: Jamestown is a historic settlement on Jamestown Island in Virginia, founded by the Virginia Company in 1607 as England’s first permanent settlement in North America. English colonists established it amid the homelands of Indigenous Powhatan peoples, whose interactions with the newcomers included trade, assistance, and conflict. Jamestown became Virginia’s colonial-government center; a representative assembly met there in 1619, and tobacco exports helped make the colony profitable. In 1676, Bacon’s Rebellion—a complex conflict involving political and economic grievances and escalating violence against Indigenous communities—culminated in rebels burning much of the town. In 1699, Virginia’s capital moved to Williamsburg, and Jamestown declined as an urban center.

key_facts.text: The Virginia Company’s colonists selected Jamestown on May 13, 1607; the settlement was named for King James I.
Powhatan people were important to the colony’s early survival, and relations between the communities included both cooperation and conflict.
John Rolfe introduced a tobacco strain in 1612; tobacco became an important source of profit for the Virginia Company.
Jamestown hosted Virginia’s first representative legislative assembly in 1619.
During Bacon’s Rebellion in 1676, rebels burned Jamestown; historians describe the uprising as a complex crisis, not simply a precursor to the American Revolution.
Virginia’s government moved its capital to Williamsburg in 1699.

overview.text: The World’s Columbian Exposition was Chicago’s 1893 world’s fair, organized to commemorate the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus’s arrival in the Americas. It opened on May 1 and ran through October on grounds that included Jackson Park and the Midway Plaisance. Art, architecture, technology, and cultural displays made it an ambitious showcase of the era. Its white buildings and nighttime electric lighting helped earn it the nickname “White City.” The fair’s most famous innovation was the world’s first Ferris wheel, designed as a spectacle to rival Paris’s Eiffel Tower. Yet its legacy was not simply celebratory: racist portrayals of non-Western peoples and the exclusion of Black Americans drew protest from Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass. Objects exhibited there also helped form the collections of Chicago’s Field Museum.

key_facts.text: The fair opened May 1, 1893, and commemorated 400 years since Columbus’s arrival in the Americas.
Landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted and architect Daniel Burnham collaborated on the fairgrounds’ waterways, natural areas, and grand architecture.
The first Ferris wheel was invented for the exposition as an attraction intended to rival the Eiffel Tower.
Electric lights illuminated the fair’s buildings at night; the exposition also helped renew interest in neoclassical architecture.
Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass protested Black Americans’ lack of representation; the fair also included racist depictions of non-Western people.
Exhibits and other objects from the fair became part of the collections of Chicago’s newly established Field Museum.

overview.text: César Chávez (1927–1993) was a Mexican American labor and civil-rights organizer who became a prominent leader of the farmworker movement. After growing up doing migrant farm labor, he left the Community Service Organization to focus on organizing agricultural workers. In 1962, he and Dolores Huerta, with other organizers, formed the National Farm Workers Association (NFWA). During the 1965 Delano Grape Strike, the NFWA joined Filipino farmworkers organized by Larry Itliong; the groups later united in the organization that became the United Farm Workers (UFW). Chávez helped lead strikes, marches, consumer boycotts, and fasts to press for better wages and working conditions, bringing farmworkers’ concerns to national attention. His work connected labor organizing with Latino civil-rights activism.

key_facts.text: Chávez was born near Yuma, Arizona, in 1927, and experienced migrant farm labor after leaving school following eighth grade.
In 1962, Chávez, Dolores Huerta, and other organizers formed the National Farm Workers Association, a predecessor to the UFW.
The 1965 Delano Grape Strike began with Filipino farmworkers organized by Larry Itliong; Chávez’s NFWA joined their strike.
The movement used nonviolent tactics including strikes, marches, consumer boycotts, and fasts to draw attention to farmworkers’ conditions.
Chávez died in Arizona in 1993; his organizing helped make farmworker rights a major public issue.

overview.text: The First Great Awakening was a broad Protestant revival movement in Britain’s American colonies. Local revivals grew in the 1730s, and the movement became part of a wider evangelical surge across the English-speaking world; its colonial reach continued into the 1770s. Its central message was that individuals needed personal conversion, often called the “new birth,” and revival preachers used forceful, emotionally charged sermons. Itinerant minister George Whitefield carried the message across colonial regions, while Jonathan Edwards helped interpret and publicize revival. The movement invigorated religious life but provoked disputes over emotional preaching, traveling ministers, and church authority, dividing some congregations into supporters called New Lights and opponents called Old Lights.

key_facts.text: The earliest colonial revivals emerged among Presbyterians in Pennsylvania and New Jersey, then spread to Congregationalists and Baptists in New England and later to the South.
Whitefield’s colonial preaching tour from 1739 to 1741 was a high point of the movement; he preached outdoors when churches would not admit him.
Edwards’s Northampton revival of 1734–1735 was an early sign of the larger movement. He described revival experiences and preached “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God.”
The “new birth” meant a personal conversion from sin through preaching. Revivalists emphasized heartfelt religious experience, while critics objected to emotionalism and itinerant ministers.
The revival’s disputes split some Congregationalist and Presbyterian communities: supporters were called New Lights (or New Side), and opponents Old Lights (or Old Side).

overview.text: The Mayflower Compact was an agreement made aboard the Mayflower in 1620, after the English settlers landed outside the area governed by Virginia’s authorities. It joined the passengers into a self-governing community and gave them a shared basis for making rules and maintaining order as they established Plymouth. The agreement was important as an early example of settlers organizing government by mutual promise, but it was not a declaration of independence or a complete constitution. The original document has not survived; its text was copied into the manuscript history of Plymouth written by governor William Bradford, now held by the State Library of Massachusetts.

key_facts.text: The agreement was signed aboard the Mayflower in 1620.
The settlers created it because Plymouth was outside the jurisdiction of Virginia’s government.
It served as a self-governing agreement for the Plymouth settlers.
The original agreement was not preserved; William Bradford recorded its text in his manuscript history.
Bradford’s manuscript, which documents Plymouth’s early history, is held by the State Library of Massachusetts.

overview.text: Founded on February 12, 1909, after years of racial violence and the 1908 Springfield race riot, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) brought together Black leaders and white reformers to oppose racial discrimination and secure constitutional rights. The organization pursued change through legal challenges, public advocacy, local branches, and journalism. In 1910, W.E.B. Du Bois became its director of publications and research and edited The Crisis, the NAACP’s magazine, which covered civil rights and Black life and culture. The NAACP’s sustained legal campaign against school segregation helped bring cases before the Supreme Court; in 1954, Brown v. Board of Education ruled public-school segregation unconstitutional.

key_facts.text: The NAACP was founded in 1909; its founding call followed the 1908 Springfield race riot and was signed by Black and white participants.
Early aims included opposing lynching and racial injustice and securing rights protected by the 13th, 14th, and 15th Amendments.
The NAACP launched The Crisis in 1910, with W.E.B. Du Bois as editor; the magazine reported on the organization and covered race, politics, and Black culture.
The NAACP’s legal campaign challenged school segregation over many years and contributed to the cases leading to Brown v. Board of Education.
On May 17, 1954, the Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation in public schools violated the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause.

overview.text: Helen Adams Keller (1880–1968) was born in Tuscumbia, Alabama, and became deafblind after an illness at 19 months; the illness remains unidentified. In 1887, teacher Anne Sullivan began teaching her by spelling words into her hand, opening a path to communication and formal education. Keller attended Radcliffe College and graduated in 1904, the first deafblind person to earn a college degree. She published The Story of My Life in 1903, wrote many other works, and became a prominent advocate for people with disabilities, women’s suffrage, and workers’ rights. Her significance lies in both her literary career and decades of public advocacy for greater opportunity and access.

key_facts.text: On April 5, 1887, Sullivan fingerspelled “W-A-T-E-R” into Keller’s hand as water flowed over it; Keller connected the word with what she felt.
Keller graduated cum laude from Radcliffe in 1904, becoming the first deafblind person to earn a college degree.
Her autobiography, The Story of My Life, was published in 1903, while she was a student at Radcliffe.
Keller was a committed socialist, supported women’s suffrage, and became an early member of the American Civil Liberties Union.
From 1924, she worked as a public spokesperson for the American Foundation for the Blind, advocating for people with vision loss.

overview.text: Colin Luther Powell (1937–2021) was a U.S. Army officer and diplomat who rose from ROTC at New York’s City College to become a senior national-security official. He served two tours in Vietnam, became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989, and oversaw U.S. military operations including the 1991 Gulf War. Appointed by President George W. Bush, Powell served as secretary of state from 2001 to 2005—the first African American to hold that office. His legacy also includes his February 2003 presentation to the UN Security Council arguing that Iraq possessed weapons of mass destruction; later reviews found some of the intelligence behind the presentation was erroneous.

key_facts.text: Powell was born in Harlem to Jamaican immigrant parents and grew up in the South Bronx.
After joining ROTC at City College of New York, he was commissioned as an Army second lieutenant in 1958 and served two tours in Vietnam.
He became chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff in 1989; during his tenure, he oversaw the 1991 Gulf War operation, Desert Storm.
Powell served as secretary of state from 2001 to 2005 and was the first African American to hold the position.

In his February 5, 2003, UN Security Council address, Powell presented U.S. intelligence supporting claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. Later official reviews found some of the intelligence was erroneous and that serious doubts about a key source had not reached Powell before the speech.

overview.text: Donald John Trump (born June 14, 1946, in Queens, New York) is an American businessman and politician. Before entering national politics, he led his family’s real-estate company, later known as the Trump Organization, and became widely recognized through property projects and the television program The Apprentice. He won the presidency in 2016 and served as the 45th president from January 2017 to January 2021; after winning again in 2024, he returned to office in January 2025 as the 47th president. His terms are nonconsecutive, a rare distinction in U.S. history: he is the second president to serve that way, after Grover Cleveland.

key_facts.text: His full name is Donald John Trump; he was born in Queens, New York, on June 14, 1946.
In 1971, he took over his father’s real-estate company and renamed it the Trump Organization.
He launched the reality television show The Apprentice in 2004.
His first presidential term ran from January 20, 2017, to January 20, 2021.
He returned to office on January 20, 2025, as the 47th president; the U.S. government lists him as the current president.
Trump is the second U.S. president to serve two nonconsecutive terms; Grover Cleveland was the first.

overview.text: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is a federal agency whose mission is to protect human health and the environment. President Richard Nixon proposed creating it in Reorganization Plan No. 3 in July 1970 to bring environmental responsibilities that had been spread across government into one agency. December 2, 1970—the day the Senate confirmed EPA’s first administrator, William Ruckelshaus—is traditionally treated as the agency’s birthday. EPA was designed to study pollution across air, water, and land, monitor environmental conditions, and work with states on standards and enforcement. It carries out laws passed by Congress by developing regulations, enforcing them, conducting research, providing grants, and cooperating with state, local, and Tribal governments.

key_facts.text: EPA’s traditional birthday is December 2, 1970, when the Senate confirmed its first administrator; Nixon had signed the reorganization plan calling for the agency in July.
Its mission is to protect human health and the environment, including by supporting clean air, land, and water.
When Congress passes an environmental law, EPA helps implement it by writing regulations; it also enforces regulations and may work with states and Tribes on national standards.
EPA’s creation consolidated environmental responsibilities that had been scattered among parts of the federal government, including responsibilities related to air pollution and water quality.
EPA also studies environmental problems in laboratories and provides grants for work such as scientific studies and community cleanups.

overview.text: John Wesley Powell (1834–1902) was an American geologist, explorer, and Union Army officer whose fieldwork advanced scientific study and mapping of the American West. Wounded at Shiloh in 1862, he lost his right arm but returned to service and rose to major. In 1869, he led an expedition down the Green and Colorado rivers, including through the Grand Canyon—a landmark journey, though not the first human exploration of these river canyons. His later surveys documented western landscapes, and he became the second director of the U.S. Geological Survey (1881–1894) and the first director of the Smithsonian’s Bureau of Ethnology.

key_facts.text: Powell lost his right arm at the Battle of Shiloh during the Civil War, returned to active duty, and was promoted to major.
His 1869 expedition traveled down the Green and Colorado rivers; the NPS notes that Indigenous people and others had explored the river canyons before Powell’s party.
The expedition’s later 1871–1872 journey produced photographs of landmarks and an accurate map of the area.
Powell served as the second director of the U.S. Geological Survey from 1881 to 1894.
Powell directed the Smithsonian’s Bureau of Ethnology from 1879 until his death in 1902.

overview.text: Plymouth Colony was an English settlement established at Plymouth, in present-day Massachusetts, in 1620 by the Pilgrims, religious separatists who crossed the Atlantic aboard the Mayflower. After reaching Cape Cod and signing an agreement for self-government, they explored before settling at Plymouth. The Mayflower Compact helped organize the settlers as a political community, but Plymouth remained distinct from the larger Massachusetts Bay Colony for most of the seventeenth century; the two were combined under a royal government in 1691. The settlement arose on Wampanoag homeland, and its history includes both an early alliance with Wampanoag leader Massasoit and later strained relations. Understanding the colony therefore requires attention to both Indigenous and English experiences.

key_facts.text: The Mayflower Compact was signed at Cape Cod on November 11, 1620, before the settlers chose Plymouth.
The Pilgrims were religious exiles who had separated from the Anglican Church; some had lived in Holland before sailing to America.
Much of the land that became Plymouth Colony was Wampanoag homeland. Massasoit sought an alliance with the English settlers.
Relations between Indigenous people and Pilgrims included both cooperation and conflict, making both perspectives important to the colony’s history.
Plymouth was a separate colony from Massachusetts Bay for much of the seventeenth century; the two were combined under royal government in 1691.

overview.text: The United States of America is a country whose national territory, for Census Bureau reporting, comprises 50 states and the District of Columbia. Its origins as an independent nation lie in the break between Britain and its thirteen North American colonies: the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776. The Declaration announced separation from British rule, while a later Constitution established the national government. Written in 1787 after debate over how power should be shared between the states and the central government, the Constitution created a federal framework that began operating in 1789. These founding documents and the continuing balance of national and state authority are key features of U.S. history and civic life.

key_facts.text: The Census Bureau defines the nation as 50 states and the District of Columbia.
The Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence on July 4, 1776; all thirteen colonies had signified approval by July 9.
The Declaration announced the colonies’ separation from British rule; the parchment copy was signed by delegates over time, with the signing recorded on August 2, 1776.
Delegates signed the Constitution on September 17, 1787, establishing the government of the United States.
The Constitution replaced the Articles of Confederation, and the First Federal Congress opened in March 1789.

overview.text: King Philip’s War, also called Metacom’s or Metacomet’s War, was a conflict in New England from 1675 to 1678 involving Wampanoag and other Native forces, English colonies, and Native allies of the English. Metacom, a Wampanoag sachem, was called King Philip by the English. The conflict grew amid disputes over English expansion onto Native lands and political authority; historians caution that it may have begun without Metacom’s approval. Fighting spread across the region, including the Great Swamp Fight against the Narragansett in December 1675. Major hostilities in southern and central New England subsided in 1676, though fighting continued in Maine until 1678. The war caused severe losses and transformed Native peoples’ position in the region.

key_facts.text: Metacom (also spelled Metacomet) was a Wampanoag sachem; “King Philip” was the English name associated with him.
The conflict involved multiple Native nations and English colonists, with Native people also allied with the English; it was not simply a war between two uniform sides.
In December 1675, colonial forces attacked the Narragansett winter settlement in the Great Swamp in present-day Rhode Island; the attack helped bring the Narragansett into the war.
The war’s chronology varies by region: hostilities in southern, central, and western New England subsided by August 1676, while fighting in Maine continued until 1678.
The war was a major turning point: historian James D. Drake describes it as reshaping New England society and leaving Native peoples politically marginalized.

overview.text: The Confederate States of America (CSA), also called the Confederacy, was a breakaway government formed by Southern states that claimed to leave the United States during the Civil War. Seven states organized it at Montgomery, Alabama, before Abraham Lincoln took office in March 1861; after fighting began at Fort Sumter, four more slave states seceded, bringing its membership to eleven. Jefferson Davis served as its president. The Confederacy’s constitution resembled the U.S. Constitution but stressed state sovereignty, set a six-year presidential term, and protected slavery. Secession grew from conflict over slavery and fear that it would be restricted. The Union rejected secession’s legality, defeated the Confederacy in 1865, and preserved the United States as one nation.

key_facts.text: The Confederacy included eleven states: Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana, Tennessee, Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia, Florida, South Carolina, North Carolina, and Virginia.

Delegates from the first seven seceding states formed the government at Montgomery, Alabama, and selected Jefferson Davis as president; four more slave states seceded after fighting began at Fort Sumter.
Its Constitution, adopted March 11, 1861, resembled the U.S. Constitution but emphasized state sovereignty, allowed slavery in its territories, and set a six-year presidential term.
Slavery was central to secession: leaders feared the federal government would eventually end the institution on which their region’s economy depended.
The Union won the Civil War in 1865; the U.S. government did not accept secession as legally valid.

overview.text: The Tuskegee syphilis study was a U.S. Public Health Service project conducted with Tuskegee Institute in Macon County, Alabama, from 1932 to 1972 to observe untreated syphilis. It involved 600 Black men: 399 who already had syphilis and 201 who did not; participants were not deliberately infected for the study. Researchers did not obtain informed consent or offer treatment, even after it became available. Community members thought the project was a special government health-care program. After news reports and an advisory review, the study ended in 1972. Its legacy includes federal human-subject research protections and the Belmont Report, which outlined principles including respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.

The study included 399 men who already had syphilis and 201 men who did not; participants were not deliberately infected.

Community members understood the study as a special government health-care program.
The 1974 National Research Act established a national commission on human-subject protections; the Belmont Report, published in 1979, outlined three guiding ethical principles.

overview.text: Annie Oakley (born Phoebe Ann Moses, 1860–1926) was an American sharpshooter and stage performer from rural Darke County, Ohio. As a child, she hunted and sold game to help support her family; marksmanship later became both her livelihood and her route to public fame. After performing with her husband, Frank Butler, she joined Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West in 1885, where she became a featured star known for trick shooting, including splitting cards and shooting corks from bottles. Her fame challenged assumptions about women in a male-dominated sport: she encouraged women to learn firearms for self-protection. During World War I she offered to raise a women’s sharpshooter regiment and train troops, but the offer was not accepted. Her career made her one of the era’s best-known female entertainers.

key_facts.text: Oakley was born Phoebe Ann Moses in Darke County, Ohio, in 1860.
As a child, she hunted and sold game to help support her family.
She joined Buffalo Bill Cody’s Wild West in 1885 and became the show’s star sharpshooter.
Her performances included splitting playing cards and shooting corks from bottles.
She encouraged women to learn firearm skills for self-protection and offered during World War I to raise a women’s sharpshooter regiment; the offer was declined.

overview.text: The President of the United States, often called the U.S. President or POTUS, leads the federal executive branch, serves as commander in chief of the armed forces, and is the nation’s head of state. Article II of the Constitution vests executive power in the office and sets a four-year term, selection through electors, and eligibility requirements: natural-born citizenship, at least 35 years of age, and 14 years’ U.S. residence. The president is responsible for carrying out federal laws and may veto legislation, while important powers such as making treaties and appointing officials involve the Senate’s advice and consent. Checks and balances among the executive, legislative, and judicial branches limit the concentration of government power.

key_facts.text: Article II establishes the presidency as the holder of federal executive power and provides for a four-year term.
Voters choose electors who cast votes for president; this process is known as the Electoral College.
The Constitution’s listed eligibility requirements are natural-born citizenship, age 35 or older, and at least 14 years’ residence in the United States.
The president is commander in chief and must take care that federal laws are faithfully executed.
Presidential powers are checked by other branches: for example, Congress can override a veto, and the Senate confirms many presidential nominees.

overview.text: Mehmet Oz, commonly known as Dr. Oz, is an American cardiothoracic surgeon and television personality whose public profile connects medicine, mass media, and politics. A Columbia University profile describes him as a cardiac surgeon and professor who brought health education to television: he appeared regularly on The Oprah Winfrey Show before hosting his own health-focused daytime program. In 2022, he ran as the Republican candidate for a Pennsylvania U.S. Senate seat; Federal Election Commission results show Democrat John Fetterman won the general election. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services now lists Oz as its administrator. His career is distinctive for carrying a physician’s celebrity platform into electoral politics and leadership of a major federal health agency.

key_facts.text: Oz earned an undergraduate degree at Harvard and a joint MD and MBA from the University of Pennsylvania and Wharton, according to his CMS biography.
A 2009 Columbia Magazine profile identifies Oz as a cardiac surgeon and professor at Columbia, as well as an attending surgeon at New York-Presbyterian at that time.
The Columbia profile says Oprah Winfrey began inviting Oz onto her show in 2004; he became a regular guest before hosting his own health-focused program.
In the 2022 Pennsylvania Senate general election, Republican Mehmet Oz received 46.27% of the vote, while Democrat John Fetterman received 51.17%.
As of September 24, 2026, the CMS website lists Oz as Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

overview.text: Abigail Adams (née Abigail Smith, 1744–1818) was a Massachusetts writer and public figure, wife of John Adams and mother of John Quincy Adams, who later became the sixth U.S. president. Her long correspondence with John—written while he was often away in public service—preserves her views on family life, the Revolution, and politics. In a March 1776 letter, she urged him to “remember the ladies” when shaping new laws, arguing that women should not be subject to laws without representation. She also argued that girls needed education, since educated women could help prepare future citizens. As the wife of the second president, she served as First Lady and advised him politically.

key_facts.text: Born Abigail Smith in Weymouth, Massachusetts, she educated herself by reading her father’s books because formal schooling was generally unavailable to girls.
In her March 1776 letter to John Adams, she called for women to be considered in new laws and objected to laws imposed without women’s representation.
In another 1776 letter, she argued that girls’ education mattered because educated women could help prepare future citizens.
When John Adams was away during the Revolutionary War, she managed family and farm responsibilities and described those challenges in her letters.
She was the wife of the second U.S. president and the mother of John Quincy Adams, the sixth president.

overview.text: The Harlem Renaissance was a major period of African American artistic and cultural activity that grew around Harlem after World War I and continued into the 1930s. Writers, musicians, performers, and visual artists created poetry, fiction, theater, jazz, blues, painting, sculpture, and photography. The Great Migration helped bring Black communities together in northern cities, including Harlem, while partnerships and debate supported artistic collaboration. The work asserted pride in Black life and identity, explored discrimination and modernity, and ranged from traditional poetic forms to experiments with blues-inspired rhythms and modern visual styles. The Renaissance expanded recognition of African American culture and influenced later artists and movements, including civil rights activism.

key_facts.text: The National Gallery of Art places the movement between the end of World War I and the 1930s, with the Great Depression weakening its artistic momentum.
The Great Migration helped shape the movement; African Americans settled in cultural centers including Harlem, Washington, D.C., and Chicago.
Its creative work crossed disciplines, including literature, theater, dance, jazz, blues, painting, sculpture, printmaking, and photography.
There was no single artistic style: some poets used established forms, while others drew rhythms from blues and folk culture.
Artists asserted pride in Black identity and addressed inequality; the movement later inspired artists and helped lay groundwork for civil rights and the Black Arts Movement.

overview.text: The Intolerable Acts were punitive laws passed by the British Parliament in 1774 after the Boston Tea Party. British officials called them the Coercive Acts; the name “Intolerable Acts” reflected colonial opposition. The four principal measures closed Boston Harbor until compensation was made for the destroyed tea, curtailed Massachusetts self-government, allowed certain trials to be moved outside the colony, and changed rules for quartering troops. The Quebec Act is sometimes grouped with them, though it was not passed as punishment for the Tea Party. Rather than isolating Massachusetts, the measures helped unite colonial resistance and prompted the First Continental Congress in 1774.

key_facts.text: The four principal Coercive Acts were the Boston Port Act, Massachusetts Government Act, Administration of Justice Act, and Quartering Act.
The Boston Port Act closed Boston Harbor to commercial traffic starting June 1, 1774, until conditions including restitution for the destroyed tea were met.
The Massachusetts Government Act replaced an elected council with a crown-appointed one and restricted town meetings, reducing local self-government.
The Administration of Justice Act allowed certain trials to be moved to another colony or Great Britain; colonists objected that this threatened trial by local peers.
The Quebec Act is sometimes counted among the Intolerable Acts, but it was not related to punishing Massachusetts for the Boston Tea Party.

The First Continental Congress met in Philadelphia in September 1774; its declaration named the Boston port, Massachusetts government, and justice laws among Parliament’s recent measures and set out colonial grievances.

overview.text: Powhatan, often identified by his personal name Wahunsenacawh (also spelled Wahunsunacock), was the mamanatowick, or paramount chief, of Tsenacomoco, the Powhatan chiefdom in Tidewater Virginia. By the English arrival at Jamestown in 1607, he had expanded an inherited core of six tribes through diplomacy and force; roughly 28–32 tribes or chiefdoms paid him tribute. His authority was powerful but not absolute, since local chiefs and councils retained roles. Werowocomoco served as his principal residence and political center. He managed relations with English colonists through negotiation and exchange as well as resistance to their growing presence. Pocahontas was his daughter. His leadership made him central to Virginia’s earliest English-colonial encounters; his death was reported in 1618.

key_facts.text: Mamanatowick was the title for Tsenacomoco’s paramount chief; Powhatan held that role when the English arrived in 1607.
Tsenacomoco covered much of Tidewater Virginia, from the James River north toward the Potomac, with boundaries that shifted with Powhatan’s influence.
Powhatan inherited a core of six tribes and extended his influence through diplomacy and force; local chiefs and councils also held political roles.
The famous account of Pocahontas saving John Smith comes from Smith’s account; scholars have debated how to interpret the event.
Powhatan’s death was reported in 1618; after his death, leadership passed first to his brother or kinsman Opitchapam.

overview.text: Kamala Devi Harris (born 1964 in Oakland, California) is an American lawyer and Democratic politician whose career moved from prosecution and California state government to national office. After serving as San Francisco district attorney and California attorney general, she represented California in the U.S. Senate from 2017 to 2021. She became the 49th vice president on January 20, 2021, serving until January 20, 2025, with President Joe Biden. Harris was the first woman, African American, and Asian American to serve as vice president, a milestone in U.S. political representation. Her path through elected prosecutorial offices, the Senate, and the vice presidency distinguishes her public career.

key_facts.text: Harris was born in Oakland, California, on October 20, 1964. She earned a bachelor’s degree from Howard University and a law degree from the University of California, Hastings College of Law.
Before entering the Senate, she worked as a deputy district attorney in Oakland, served as San Francisco district attorney, and was California’s attorney general from 2011 to 2017.
She became California’s first African American senator when her Senate service began on January 3, 2017.

Harris served as vice president and president of the U.S. Senate from January 20, 2021, to January 20, 2025; she was the first woman and the first African American and Asian American to hold the vice presidency.
Harris is the daughter of immigrants from Jamaica and India; she attended Howard University, a historically Black college and university (HBCU).

overview.text: The Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) is a U.S. civilian agency that gathers and analyzes intelligence about foreign countries and global issues for national-security decision-makers. Established by the National Security Act of 1947 and formally created on September 18, it was charged with coordinating national intelligence and sharing assessments affecting U.S. security. Its institutional roots include the World War II Office of Strategic Services (OSS) and the postwar Central Intelligence Group (CIG), but the CIA was a distinct successor organization. Today, it collects foreign intelligence, produces analysis, and may conduct covert action when directed by the president. It informs policymakers rather than making policy, and is not a law-enforcement agency—features that distinguish its mission from domestic policing.

key_facts.text: The National Security Act of 1947 established the CIA as an independent civilian agency in the executive branch; September 18, 1947, marks its formal establishment.
The CIA’s predecessors included the World War II Office of Strategic Services and the postwar Central Intelligence Group.
Its work includes collecting foreign intelligence, producing analysis, and conducting covert action when directed by the president.
The CIA provides intelligence to policymakers; it does not make policy or operate as a law-enforcement organization.
The CIA seal uses an eagle, shield, and compass rose to represent alertness, defense, and global intelligence collection.

overview.text: Stephen Arnold Douglas (1813–1861) was an Illinois Democrat and U.S. senator whose political career became closely tied to the conflict over slavery’s expansion. Known as the “Little Giant,” a nickname linked to his short stature and political influence, he championed popular sovereignty: letting settlers in U.S. territories decide whether to permit slavery. His Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 put that idea into law, overturned the Missouri Compromise’s restriction, and helped fuel violent conflict in Kansas. In 1858, Douglas debated Abraham Lincoln for an Illinois Senate seat; his response at Freeport to Lincoln’s question about slavery became known as the Freeport Doctrine. Douglas ran for president in 1860, lost to Lincoln, and later supported the Union.

key_facts.text: Douglas was born in Vermont on April 23, 1813, and died in Chicago on June 3, 1861.
The Kansas-Nebraska Act used popular sovereignty to let settlers decide whether slavery would be permitted in the territories.
At the 1858 Freeport debate, Douglas argued that local legislatures could make slavery difficult to sustain by withholding laws that protected it.
Douglas and Lincoln held seven debates while campaigning for an Illinois Senate seat; Douglas won reelection.
Douglas ran as the Northern Democratic candidate in the 1860 presidential election and lost to Lincoln.

overview.text: The Republic of Texas was an independent nation that declared independence from Mexico on March 2, 1836, during the Texas Revolution. Its leaders had to build a government amid continuing conflict with Mexico and serious financial difficulties. The United States recognized Texas in 1837, but annexation was delayed by concerns including possible war with Mexico and the dispute over admitting Texas as a slave state. Congress approved annexation in 1845, and Texas became the twenty-eighth U.S. state on December 29 that year. The formal transfer of sovereignty followed on February 19, 1846, marking the end of the republic’s diplomatic relations with the United States.

key_facts.text: A delegation adopted the Texas Declaration of Independence at Washington-on-the-Brazos on March 2, 1836.
The United States recognized Texan independence in 1837; this was distinct from annexation, which came later.
The United States’ annexation debate involved concerns about provoking Mexico and admitting another slave state.
Texas entered the Union as the twenty-eighth state on December 29, 1845; the formal sovereignty-transfer ceremony took place on February 19, 1846.
Mexico recognized Texas independence in 1845, but the republic’s leaders accepted annexation rather than continuing as an independent nation.

overview.text: The “Cross of Gold” speech was delivered by William Jennings Bryan, a former Nebraska congressman, at the 1896 Democratic National Convention in Chicago. Bryan urged “free silver”—allowing silver to be coined as money—and defended bimetallism, a monetary system using both gold and silver, against reliance on the gold standard alone. The debate unfolded amid economic hardship following the Panic of 1893. In the speech, Bryan cast the monetary question as a struggle affecting farmers and working people, and ended with a vivid warning against a “cross of gold.” His forceful address helped win him the Democratic presidential nomination; he later lost the election to Republican William McKinley. The speech became a memorable expression of the era’s monetary and political conflict.

key_facts.text: Bryan’s speech addressed a dispute over monetary policy, not a literal cross: he opposed the gold standard and advocated including silver in the nation’s money.

The Federal Reserve History account explains that under the gold standard, Treasury notes could be redeemed for a fixed amount of gold; falling gold reserves were one source of concern during the Panic of 1893.
Bryan presented his cause as defending farmers and working people, and contrasted their interests with those he associated with the gold standard.
The speech helped Bryan secure the Democratic nomination on the convention’s fifth ballot, according to Teaching American History’s introduction.
Bryan lost the 1896 presidential election to Republican William McKinley.

overview.text: The Scopes trial (State of Tennessee v. John Thomas Scopes) was a 1925 case in Dayton, Tennessee, in which high-school teacher John T. Scopes was prosecuted under the Butler Act for teaching evolution in a public school. The ACLU backed a test case against the law, while Dayton boosters also hoped to attract attention to their town. The courtroom confrontation featured defense lawyer Clarence Darrow and prosecutor William Jennings Bryan, making the case a national symbol of conflict over evolution, religious belief, and public-school curricula. A jury convicted Scopes and imposed a $100 fine, but Tennessee’s supreme court later reversed the conviction on a technicality; it did not strike down the law, which remained in force for decades.

key_facts.text: The Butler Act prohibited teaching theories that contradicted its account of divine creation and human origins as described in the Bible.
The ACLU offered to support a test case, and Dayton civic leaders pursued one partly to publicize their town.
The trial’s high-profile lawyers included Clarence Darrow for the defense and William Jennings Bryan as a special prosecutor.
The judge excluded expert testimony about evolution’s scientific status; Darrow’s questioning of Bryan about the Bible became a dramatic moment in the trial.
The Tennessee Supreme Court reversed Scopes’s conviction over the fine procedure, not by invalidating the Butler Act; the law was repealed in 1967.

overview.text: The Manhattan Project was a top-secret U.S. government program during World War II to develop the first atomic weapons, driven by fear that Nazi Germany might build them first. The Army Corps of Engineers organized it as the Manhattan Engineer District under General Leslie Groves, combining military, scientific, and industrial work across the country. Its three main centers had distinct roles: Oak Ridge enriched uranium, Hanford produced plutonium, and Los Alamos designed the bombs under physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer. On July 16, 1945, the plutonium “Gadget” succeeded in the Trinity test, the first human-caused nuclear explosion. The United States used atomic bombs against Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945; the project helped usher in the nuclear age and raised enduring ethical and environmental questions.

key_facts.text: The project pursued two bomb-making routes in parallel: uranium-235 and plutonium, each requiring different production methods.
The three main sites were not interchangeable: Oak Ridge enriched uranium, Hanford made plutonium, and Los Alamos developed bomb designs.
The federal government acquired the main sites using wartime eminent-domain powers, displacing Indigenous communities, farmers, and homesteaders.
Although the project employed a huge workforce, very few workers knew its true purpose.
After Trinity, the United States dropped the uranium-fueled Little Boy on Hiroshima on August 6, 1945, and the plutonium-fueled Fat Man on Nagasaki on August 9.

overview.text: Harry S. Truman was the 33rd president of the United States, serving from 1945 to 1953. He took office after Franklin D. Roosevelt died, just 82 days after Truman became vice president. A Missouri farmer and World War I artillery officer before entering politics, Truman gained national attention in the Senate for investigating waste in the wartime defense program. His presidency spanned the end of World War II and the early Cold War; his administration supported the Marshall Plan to help rebuild Western Europe. In 1948, despite expectations of defeat and a split in his party over civil rights, Truman won reelection after an energetic campaign.

key_facts.text: Truman was born in Lamar, Missouri, on May 8, 1884, and worked as a farmer before his political career.
As a U.S. senator, he chaired an investigation into waste and fraud in the wartime defense program, helping make him a national figure.
Truman became president on April 12, 1945, after Roosevelt’s death; he had become vice president only 82 days earlier.
The Marshall Plan, proposed by Secretary of State George C. Marshall in 1947, led to U.S. funding for Western Europe’s postwar rebuilding.
Truman issued executive orders to desegregate the armed forces and prohibit racial discrimination in federal employment.
He won the 1948 election despite predictions of defeat and a breakaway faction of Southern Democrats opposed to his civil-rights position.

overview.text: The New Deal was a broad, evolving package of federal policies advanced by President Franklin D. Roosevelt and enacted with Congress, beginning in 1933 as the United States faced the Great Depression; major laws continued through 1938. Its central aims were relief for people in need, economic recovery, and financial reform. Rather than a single program, it reached banking, farming, labor, public works, and later social security. Agencies such as the CCC and FDIC addressed distinct problems, while the WPA hired workers for construction and cultural projects. By creating lasting federal responsibilities and protections, the New Deal significantly expanded government’s role, though its programs eased suffering without ending the Depression.

key_facts.text: The New Deal’s commonly described goals were relief for people in need, economic recovery, and financial reform.
During Roosevelt’s first 100 days, Congress passed 15 major laws establishing New Deal agencies and programs, including the FDIC and CCC.
The Agricultural Adjustment Administration sought to aid farmers through production limits and federal subsidies.
The Second New Deal, beginning in 1935, included Social Security, which created unemployment insurance, old-age pensions, and public assistance programs.
The WPA combined employment and public works with cultural programs, including federal theater, arts, music, dance, and writers’ projects.

overview.text: Pennsylvania, officially the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, is a U.S. state whose capital is Harrisburg. William Penn received a royal charter for the colony in 1681, although Indigenous peoples—including the Susquehannock, Lenape, Shawnee, and Nanticoke—already lived in the region. Philadelphia gives the state a central place in U.S. founding history: the Declaration of Independence was adopted there in 1776, and delegates drafted the Constitution there in 1787. Pennsylvania ratified the Constitution on December 12, 1787, becoming the second of the original 13 states to join the Union. Its “Keystone State” nickname reflects its important place among the colonies and in the early Union.

key_facts.text: William Penn petitioned for land in America in 1680, and the king signed Pennsylvania’s charter in 1681.
The Commonwealth’s educational page identifies the Susquehannock, Lenape, Shawnee, and Nanticoke among the Indigenous peoples who lived in the region before European colonization.
Harrisburg is Pennsylvania’s capital.
Pennsylvania ratified the U.S. Constitution on December 12, 1787, becoming the second of the original 13 states to join the Union.
Philadelphia hosted the Constitutional Convention at the Pennsylvania State House, now called Independence Hall; the Declaration of Independence was adopted there 11 years earlier.
“Keystone State” refers to Pennsylvania’s central position among the 13 colonies and its role in holding together the newly formed union; the nickname caught on in the 1800s.

overview.text: John Marshall (1755–1835), a Virginia lawyer, Revolutionary War officer, and public official, became the fourth Chief Justice in 1801, serving until his death in 1835. Before joining the Court, he had been John Adams’s Secretary of State and was still acting in that role during the dispute that became Marbury v. Madison. In the 1803 case, Marshall wrote the Court’s opinion: it denied William Marbury’s request for a writ because the statute authorizing it conflicted with the Constitution. The decision helped establish judicial review—the courts’ power to test laws against the Constitution—and strengthened the Supreme Court’s role in federal government. His long leadership and opinions shaped the early judiciary.

key_facts.text: Marshall was the fourth Chief Justice and served from 1801 until 1835.
Before becoming Chief Justice, he served in the Revolutionary War, studied law, and held public office.
Marshall was Adams’s Secretary of State before and during the transition to his Chief Justiceship.
In Marbury v. Madison, Marshall wrote the opinion refusing Marbury’s requested writ because the authorizing law conflicted with the Constitution.
The decision helped establish judicial review and the Supreme Court’s role in the federal government.

overview.text: Frederick Douglass (1818–1895), born enslaved in Maryland, escaped in 1838 and became a leading African American abolitionist, orator, author, and journalist. His speaking career began after an 1841 address impressed members of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society. He published his first autobiography, Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, in 1845, and founded and edited the antislavery newspaper The North Star in 1847. His 1852 address “What to the Slave Is the Fourth of July?” challenged the celebration of liberty in a nation that still enslaved people. Douglass also advocated women’s rights and later held federal government posts.

key_facts.text: In 1838, Douglass escaped slavery by traveling to New York disguised as a sailor.
As a boy in Baltimore, he began learning to read and write with help from Sophia Auld, despite laws against educating enslaved people.
Douglass founded and edited The North Star, an antislavery newspaper, in 1847.
He delivered his famous Fourth of July address on July 5, 1852; the speech asks audiences to confront the gap between American ideals of liberty and slavery.
During the Civil War, Douglass helped recruit for the 54th and 55th Massachusetts regiments; his sons Lewis and Charles served in them.

overview.text: The Silent Sentinels were suffrage activists organized by Alice Paul’s National Woman’s Party (NWP), who began picketing the White House on January 10, 1917. Standing quietly at the gates, often six days a week, they held banners urging President Woodrow Wilson to support a federal constitutional amendment for women’s voting rights. Their tactic made them the first group to picket the White House and brought attention to the campaign. During World War I, wartime hostility met the protesters with arrests, jail sentences, and abuse. On November 14, 1917, imprisoned picketers were beaten at Occoquan in what became known as the “Night of Terror.” Reports of mistreatment strengthened public sympathy, though the eventual suffrage victory came through a much broader movement and political struggle.

key_facts.text: The first White House picket began on January 10, 1917; the first group included twelve women.
The protesters stood silently with banners, including questions asking Wilson when women would gain suffrage.
The NWP sought a federal constitutional amendment and pressured Wilson to support it, rather than relying only on state-by-state campaigns.
During World War I, picketers faced arrests and imprisonment; some went on hunger strikes and were force-fed.
The “Night of Terror” refers to the November 14, 1917, beating of suffragists at Occoquan Workhouse; accounts of their treatment helped build sympathy for suffrage.

overview.text: The Interstate Highway System is the federally supported network of major highways formally named the National System of Interstate and Defense Highways. Its origins predate the 1956 law: a 1944 act called for a national network connecting major cities and industrial centers while serving national defense, but construction lacked dedicated funding. On June 29, 1956, President Dwight D. Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, which expanded the planned system to 41,000 miles, established the Highway Trust Fund, and assigned the federal government 90 percent of project costs. Designed to uniform standards, Interstates feature controlled access—drivers enter and exit at designated points—and generally have at least two lanes in each direction. They serve military and civilian travel alike.

key_facts.text: The Interstate idea developed before Eisenhower’s presidency: the 1944 Federal-Aid Highway Act called for a national system of up to 40,000 miles.
Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act on June 29, 1956; it increased the proposed system to 41,000 miles.
The 1956 law created the Highway Trust Fund, using federal motor-vehicle taxes to support highway construction, and set the federal share of Interstate project costs at 90 percent.
The 1956 act called for uniform design standards, including full control of access and a minimum of two travel lanes in each direction.
Eisenhower’s experience in a 1919 U.S. Army transcontinental convoy and his observations of German autobahns helped shape his support for better highways.

overview.text: William Tecumseh Sherman (1820–1891) was a Union general and a leading commander in the Civil War’s Western Theater. After graduating from West Point in 1840, he served with Ulysses S. Grant in the campaign to capture Vicksburg. In November and December 1864, Sherman led about 60,000 troops from Atlanta across Georgia to Savannah in the March to the Sea. His army cut its communications with other Union forces and lived off the land, destroying food stores and other resources. The campaign brought severe hardship to civilians as Sherman sought to weaken the Confederacy’s economy and will to fight. After the war, he served as commanding general of the U.S. Army from 1869 to 1883.

key_facts.text: Sherman graduated from the U.S. Military Academy at West Point in 1840.
The March to the Sea began in Atlanta on November 15, 1864, and ended in Savannah on December 21.
Sherman’s force numbered about 60,000 troops and advanced in two main wings.
The army cut communications with other Union forces and relied on supplies gathered from the land, causing destruction and hardship for civilians.
Sherman served as commanding general of the U.S. Army from 1869 to 1883 and published his memoirs in 1875.

overview.text: Seminole refers to Indigenous people whose communities took shape in Florida from the 1700s onward—not simply a single Creek band. Lower Creek migrants joined other Native peoples, and people of African ancestry also lived among them. The name’s origin is uncertain; it may derive from the Spanish word cimarrón, rather than a proposed Creek expression. Seminole history is significant for sustained resistance to U.S. efforts to take Florida lands and force people west. The United States identifies three Seminole Wars, from 1817 to 1858. Many Seminoles were forced to Oklahoma, while others remained in Florida; Seminole communities are present in both states today.

key_facts.text: Seminole communities formed in Florida from a diverse mix that included Lower Creek migrants and other Native peoples.
The National Park Service says the name may come from Spanish cimarrón, but notes that its origin is uncertain.
Florida’s Department of State dates the three wars to 1817–1818, 1835–1842, and 1855–1858.

overview.text: Ethan Allen (1738–1789) was a military and political leader whose story is closely tied to Vermont’s early history and the American Revolution. Amid a dispute over land grants claimed by New York and New Hampshire, he helped organize and lead the Green Mountain Boys, a local militia that defended settlers’ claims. In May 1775, Allen, Benedict Arnold, and their forces captured the British-held Fort Ticonderoga. After a failed 1775 campaign in Canada, Allen was captured and held prisoner until 1778. Later, he advocated for Vermont’s recognition as a state. His bold reputation grew through his own accounts and later storytelling, so the celebrated folk-hero image should be distinguished from the documented events.

key_facts.text: Allen was born in Litchfield, Connecticut, in 1738, and died in 1789.
The Green Mountain Boys were a local militia formed amid disputes over land claims in the New Hampshire Grants; Allen became one of its leaders.
Allen and Benedict Arnold shared leadership in the capture of Fort Ticonderoga on May 10, 1775.
Allen was captured during a failed campaign against Montreal in 1775 and remained a British prisoner until 1778.
After his release, Allen lobbied for Vermont to be recognized as a state; he also wrote on Vermont politics and philosophy.

overview.text: Decided on June 24, 2022, Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization concerned a Mississippi law barring most abortions after 15 weeks of pregnancy. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, a clinic, and one of its doctors challenged the law. Six justices voted to uphold it, while five joined the broader ruling that overturned Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey, which had recognized a constitutional right to abortion. Writing for the majority, Justice Samuel Alito concluded that the Constitution does not confer that right and that abortion regulation was returned to elected representatives. The decision ended the federal constitutional protection for abortion recognized by Roe and Casey.

key_facts.text: The Supreme Court issued its decision on June 24, 2022; it had heard arguments on December 1, 2021.
The case arose from a challenge to Mississippi’s Gestational Age Act, which generally prohibited abortion after 15 weeks, with exceptions for a medical emergency or severe fetal abnormality.
The clinic Jackson Women’s Health Organization and one of its doctors brought the challenge, arguing that the law conflicted with earlier Supreme Court precedents.

The Court upheld Mississippi’s law 6–3; five justices joined the majority opinion overturning Roe v. Wade and Planned Parenthood v. Casey. Chief Justice John Roberts agreed with upholding the law but did not join that broader ruling.
The majority held that the Constitution does not confer a right to abortion and replaced the earlier cases’ viability and undue-burden standards with rational-basis review for abortion restrictions.

overview.text: Jefferson Davis (1808–1889) was a Mississippi politician and former U.S. Army officer who became the only president of the Confederate States of America during the Civil War. After graduating from West Point and serving in the Mexican War, he represented Mississippi in Congress and the Senate, then served as President Franklin Pierce’s secretary of war from 1853 to 1857. Davis defended slavery and supported Mississippi’s secession; he left the U.S. Senate in January 1861 and was chosen to lead the Confederacy the following month. His presidency placed him at the head of the secessionist government that fought the United States. Union troops captured him in 1865; he was imprisoned for two years, indicted for treason, but never tried.

key_facts.text: Davis was born in Kentucky on June 3, 1808, and died in New Orleans on December 6, 1889.
He served as U.S. secretary of war under Franklin Pierce from 1853 to 1857.
Davis resigned from the U.S. Senate on January 21, 1861, after Mississippi seceded from the Union.
He was inaugurated as Confederate president in Montgomery, Alabama, on February 18, 1861.
Davis defended slavery and supported Mississippi’s secession; the Senate history account connects secession to fears about slavery.
Captured in 1865, Davis was imprisoned for two years and charged with treason, but the case never went to trial.

overview.text: The Gettysburg Address was a short speech by President Abraham Lincoln, delivered at Gettysburg, Pennsylvania, on November 19, 1863, during the dedication ceremony for Soldiers’ National Cemetery, created to bury Union dead from the battle. The famous orator Edward Everett spoke for about two hours; Lincoln’s remarks lasted about two minutes. Rather than merely dedicate the ground, Lincoln honored the dead and urged the living to continue their “unfinished work.” By linking the Declaration of Independence’s equality principle to the war’s purpose, and calling for a “new birth of freedom” and government by the people, he gave the speech lasting meaning for American democracy.

key_facts.text: Lincoln spoke at the Soldiers’ National Cemetery dedication on November 19, 1863, several months after the Battle of Gettysburg.
Edward Everett delivered the principal oration; Lincoln had been asked to make only “a few appropriate remarks.”
In the address, Lincoln connected the nation’s founding commitment to equality with the question of whether a nation built on that principle could endure.
Lincoln described the living as responsible for continuing the “unfinished work” of those who died and resolving that their deaths would not be in vain.
The Library of Congress holds two of the five known handwritten manuscript copies of the address: the Nicolay and Hay copies.

overview.text: The Democratic Party is one of the United States’ two major political parties. It took shape around Andrew Jackson’s supporters in the 1820s; in the 1828 election, they called themselves Democrats, and their organized campaign helped make the party a durable force in national politics. Its nineteenth-century membership was not ideologically uniform: disputes over slavery split Democrats into northern and southern wings in 1860, with Stephen Douglas representing the Northern ticket. State affiliates gave the national party local roots. In Hawaiʻi, John A. Burns built a Democratic coalition with organized labor and Japanese American veterans; it won control of the territorial legislature in 1954. Today the state lists the Democratic Party of Hawaii as a qualified political party.

key_facts.text: Andrew Jackson’s supporters called themselves Democrats; their organized 1828 campaign helped establish the party as a national political force.
The party’s nineteenth-century membership included competing regional wings; Democrats split into Northern and Southern tickets in the 1860 presidential election.
Stephen Douglas, a Northern Democrat, promoted the Kansas-Nebraska Act, which allowed settlers to decide whether slavery would be permitted in those territories.
In Hawaiʻi, John A. Burns worked with organized labor and Japanese American veterans to build a Democratic coalition that took control of the territorial legislature in 1954.
Hawaiʻi’s Office of Elections lists the Democratic Party of Hawaii among the state’s qualified political parties.

overview.text: The 1930s (1930–1939) were a defining decade in U.S. history, shaped by the Great Depression and an expanded federal response. As unemployment, bank failures, foreclosures, and migration strained households and communities, President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal created programs for relief, jobs, farm support, and economic regulation. Its importance lies not only in emergency action: federal involvement in public welfare and economic life grew, and the 1935 Social Security Act established federal old-age benefits alongside unemployment insurance and assistance programs. New Deal laws reached banking, labor, agriculture, public works, and the arts, while political disputes over federal power continued. By the decade’s end, international tensions and debates over isolationism also shaped U.S. politics.

key_facts.text: In 1933, at the Depression’s height, 24.9% of the U.S. workforce was unemployed; many families also faced foreclosure or migrated in search of work.
Roosevelt launched the New Deal after taking office in 1933; its programs included work relief, farm support, and measures affecting industry and banking.
The Civilian Conservation Corps provided jobs for unemployed young people, while the Works Progress Administration funded jobs that included arts projects.
The 1935 Social Security Act established federal old-age benefits and included unemployment insurance and assistance for several groups, including dependent children and people who were blind.
The New Deal expanded federal involvement, but it did not bring complete economic recovery during the 1930s; its policies also faced political opposition.
Late in the decade, Congress debated U.S. involvement in growing international conflicts, with isolationists resisting deeper engagement.

overview.text: Amelia Earhart (1897–1937) was an American pilot whose record-setting flights made her a prominent aviation pioneer. On May 20–21, 1932, she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, a landmark that helped define her career. She also became the first person to fly solo from Hawaii to the U.S. mainland. In 1937, Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan set out to circle the globe; they disappeared over the Pacific while heading toward Howland Island. Radio records show communication difficulties before contact ended, but the sources do not establish their final fate.

key_facts.text: Earhart was born in Atchison, Kansas; the National Park Service identifies the Otis House there as her birthplace and childhood home.
On May 20–21, 1932, she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic; she received the Distinguished Flying Cross for the achievement.
She was the first person to fly solo from Honolulu, Hawaii, to Oakland, California.
Earhart and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared during their 1937 round-the-world attempt, over the Pacific as they traveled toward Howland Island.
The U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca’s radio log records communication problems and a final message from Earhart’s plane on July 2, 1937; the plane’s fate remains unestablished in these records.

overview.text: The Montgomery Bus Boycott was a mass protest against racial segregation on city buses in Montgomery, Alabama. After Rosa Parks was arrested on December 1, 1955, Black community organizers—including the Women’s Political Council and E. D. Nixon—helped launch a boycott that began December 5. The Montgomery Improvement Association coordinated the year-long campaign, with Martin Luther King Jr. as its president. Participants stayed off buses, walking or using carpools despite pressure and harassment. The boycott ended in December 1956 after the U.S. Supreme Court upheld a ruling against segregated bus seating in Browder v. Gayle. Its success demonstrated the power of organized mass protest and influenced later civil rights campaigns.

key_facts.text: The boycott began on December 5, 1955, four days after Parks’s arrest; earlier activists, including Claudette Colvin, had also challenged bus segregation.
The Women’s Political Council and Jo Ann Robinson helped organize the initial protest; E. D. Nixon also helped bring local leaders together.
The Montgomery Improvement Association (MIA) coordinated the continuing boycott, and its members elected Martin Luther King Jr. president.
Boycotters walked or relied on carpools and other rides rather than city buses, sustaining the campaign for more than a year.
The legal victory came through Browder v. Gayle, a case brought by four Black women; the Supreme Court affirmed the ruling against bus segregation in November 1956.
The campaign drew national and international attention and became an example for later nonviolent civil rights campaigns.

overview.text: The War of 1812 was fought between the United States and Great Britain from 1812 to 1815, after Congress declared war amid disputes over British interference with U.S. trade and the impressment of American sailors, as well as tensions over expansion and control of North American territory. Battles took place on the Atlantic, Great Lakes, and U.S.-Canada frontier. British forces burned Washington’s White House, Capitol, and other public buildings in 1814, while U.S. victories at Lake Erie and Baltimore bolstered American fortunes. At Fort McHenry, Francis Scott Key’s poem after a British bombardment became “The Star-Spangled Banner.” The Treaty of Ghent restored prewar boundaries and ended fighting upon ratification in February 1815, while Native nations faced further displacement.

key_facts.text: The causes included disputes over trade and impressment, but also U.S. expansion, relations with Indigenous nations, and territorial control.
On September 10, 1813, Oliver Hazard Perry’s fleet captured the British squadron on Lake Erie, securing American control of the lake.
After the British victory at Bladensburg, British forces burned the White House, Capitol, and other government buildings in Washington in August 1814.
Francis Scott Key wrote a poem after witnessing the bombardment of Fort McHenry; it became “The Star-Spangled Banner,” designated the U.S. national anthem in 1931.
The Treaty of Ghent was signed on December 24, 1814; after ratifications were exchanged on February 17, 1815, the war officially ended and prewar territory was restored.
Indigenous nations lost a crucial British ally after the war, and U.S. westward expansion brought further displacement and loss of Indigenous lands.

overview.text: The Great Chicago Fire was a devastating urban conflagration that swept Chicago from October 8 to October 10, 1871. Strong winds, unusually dry conditions, and a city filled with wooden buildings helped it race across the central business district and northern neighborhoods; the precise ignition point remains unknown, and the familiar story that Mrs. O’Leary’s cow started it is legend, not established fact. The blaze destroyed more than 17,000 structures, killed about 300 people, and left roughly one-third of Chicago’s residents homeless. Its aftermath exposed unequal burdens of recovery, while rebuilding helped spur the use of terra-cotta fireproofing, an innovation that supported taller buildings and became part of Chicago’s architectural identity.

key_facts.text: The fire began on October 8, 1871, and the last flames were extinguished on October 10.
Its exact origin is unknown; the story blaming Mrs. O’Leary’s cow is a legend, not a confirmed explanation.
Strong winds, dry conditions, and extensive wooden construction helped the blaze spread through Chicago.
The fire destroyed more than 17,000 structures, killed an estimated 300 people, and left about one-third of the city’s residents homeless.
In the rebuilding era, Chicago’s use of terra-cotta fireproofing helped make taller buildings possible and shaped the city’s architecture.

references.title: 150 Years Ago: The Great Chicago Fire
